title: Capture working hours and confirm the timezone before handing off to Google Calendar
design:
Capture the practice's general hours and confirm the timezone the FIRST TIME they open the calendar, before the Google setup.

THE TRIGGER IS THE CALENDAR FIRST-RUN STATE, not a step inside the Google OAuth flow and not another onboarding step. A therapist opens the calendar, has no availability rules, and that empty calendar is the moment to ask: it is the one screen where the absence is self-evident and the answer is obviously worth giving.

WHY HERE. Connecting a calendar before any availability rule exists produces a sync that cannot do anything useful: free/busy has no frame to sit in, and reminders, offers and self-booking all key off availability rules. A therapist who finishes Google setup with zero rules has a connected calendar and a product that still cannot offer a time.

WHAT EXISTS (verified on main 2026-09-10; re-locate before editing):
- frontend/app/(dashboard)/dashboard/calendar/page.tsx already gates a first-run wizard: showWizard = googleCalendarEnabled && preferences !== undefined && !preferences.calendar_setup_complete, rendering frontend/src/components/calendar/connect/CalendarSetupWizard.tsx (steps: Connect, Clients, Sessions, Review; the wizard's proposal/timezone at :384 is the Google import proposal, not availability). The page already reads useAvailabilityRules() and derives a working-hours window from it.
- frontend/src/components/onboarding/ScheduleStep.tsx (with app/onboarding/schedule/page.tsx) is a unit-tested weekday hours grid that creates one working_hours rule per checked weekday. Reuse it; do NOT write a second hours picker.
- backend/app/services/availability_parse_service.py is the natural-language rules parser; its result schema carries a confidence signal.
- user.timezone exists and is auto-detected from the browser on first save (backend/app/models/user.py:78-80).

WHAT TO BUILD: a new FIRST step in the calendar first-run state that captures weekday hours and confirms the timezone, shown when the practice has zero availability rules and skipped silently when rules already exist.

PRE-ANSWERED, the gate: the hours step is keyed on "zero availability rules", independent of whether Google Calendar is enabled for the deployment. When Google is enabled it is step one of CalendarSetupWizard, ahead of Connect; when Google is disabled it is the calendar's first-run state on its own. The existing Google steps keep their existing gate (calendar_setup_complete) untouched. Completing or skipping the hours step must not by itself set calendar_setup_complete.

THE STEP IS THE PARSER, NOT A FORM. Shape: a single natural-language box, above a row of CLICKABLE example chips that fill it ("I see clients Monday to Thursday, 9 to 5", "No appointments before 10am", "Two intakes a week, Tuesdays only", "Fridays are admin, no clients"). Clicking a chip is the same code path as typing it; the chips exist because a blank box is the classic failure of natural-language input, and they double as documentation of the vocabulary.

NON-NEGOTIABLE: ECHO BACK BEFORE SAVING. A form cannot silently misunderstand; a parser can. Every parse renders as an editable plain-language summary the practice confirms ("Got it: Monday to Thursday, 9:00 to 17:00, America/New_York") and nothing is written until they accept. Low confidence asks rather than guesses.

KEEP THE GRID AS THE FALLBACK. Offer ScheduleStep's grid behind a "pick from a grid instead" affordance, and fall back to it automatically when the parser is unavailable or repeatedly unsure, so a practice can never be blocked by a model being down. Render the grid through ONE shared control: if ScheduleStep's grid is not already a reusable component taking rules in and emitting rule changes out, extract it so the onboarding page and this step render the same control. Do not leave a second picker in the tree.

TIMEZONE: CONFIRM, DO NOT ASK COLD. Show the detected user.timezone pre-filled and let it be corrected in one click. A wrong silent value is the real risk (a practice that signed up while travelling), so it must be visible and correctable, not merely stored.

SKIPPABLE, but skipping states plainly what will not work until hours exist (offers, reminders, self-booking).

FILES: frontend/app/(dashboard)/dashboard/calendar/page.tsx, frontend/src/components/calendar/connect/CalendarSetupWizard.tsx (+ a new hours step component beside it), frontend/src/components/onboarding/ScheduleStep.tsx (extract the grid; keep its tests green), the availability parse client in frontend/src/lib/api/, and tests for the step, the gate and the fallback.

Commit and PR text: plain and human-toned; no tracker ids.
acceptance_criteria: 1. Opening the calendar with zero availability rules presents the hours + timezone capture as its first-run state; opening it with rules present never shows it. 2. Input is parser-first: a natural-language box with clickable example chips that fill it, chips and typing sharing one code path. 3. Nothing is written until the practice confirms an editable plain-language echo of what was understood; low confidence asks rather than guesses. 4. The existing grid remains reachable as an explicit alternative and is used automatically when the parser is unavailable or repeatedly unsure; the onboarding schedule page and this step render the same grid control and the existing ScheduleStep tests stay green. 5. The timezone is shown pre-filled from the detected user.timezone and is correctable. 6. Skipping is allowed and states plainly what will not work until hours exist. 7. Completing it creates the same working_hours rules the onboarding step would have. 8. The Google connect steps keep their existing gate; completing or skipping the hours step does not set calendar_setup_complete. 9. make check green.
notes:
Filed by the eng-head pass 2026-09-10 (evening, interactive, Kurt-directed) from the SaaS board's spec (Kurt's 2026-09-04 direction: parser-first, echo before save, grid as fallback), rehomed here because the calendar first-run wizard lives in this repo. Six gates walked on the SaaS twin; outside the never-dispatch set (calendar UI + existing parser, no PHI, no auth).

title: Ask the clinician instead of refusing when a hand-booked appointment hits an availability rule
design:
Manual booking asks instead of refusing. Sibling work already shipped the calendar grid shading (unavailable time rendered in the editorial day/week views); this is the other half: when a clinician books by hand into a window an availability rule covers, ask, do not refuse.

BACKEND

1. backend/app/models/scheduling.py: add to CreateAppointmentRequest (:60), CreateRecurringAppointmentRequest (:79) and UpdateAppointmentRequest (:109):
       rule_override: bool = False
   Document it as: the clinician has been shown the conflicting rules and confirmed. Default False, so every existing caller is unchanged.

2. backend/app/scheduling_engine/services/scheduling.py: thread it into _check_availability_rules (:83) as keyword-only rule_override: bool = False. When True, do NOT raise RuleViolationError; return the messages for EVERY conflict (hard and soft) so the caller records them as warnings. When False, behave exactly as today. Call sites: :203 (create), :302 (update), :531 (recurrence expansion).

3. backend/app/routes/scheduling.py: pass the flag through at create (:416), update (:~530) and the recurring path. When an override actually suppressed a hard conflict, record the overridden rule types on the audit trail alongside APPOINTMENT_CREATED (backend/app/services/audit_service.py). Rule types and enforcement levels only; no patient identifiers.

FRONTEND

4. frontend/src/types/availability.ts: add CheckConflictsResponse (conflicts[] of {rule_type, enforcement, message}, has_hard_conflicts, configured), mirroring backend/app/models/scheduling.py:284.
5. frontend/src/lib/api/availability.ts: add checkConflicts(body, token) posting to /api/availability/check.
6. frontend/src/hooks/useAvailability.ts: add a mutation-style useCheckConflicts(). POST on demand at save time; NOT a useQuery that fires as the therapist types.
7. frontend/src/lib/api/scheduling.ts and the appointment request types: carry rule_override.
8. NEW frontend/src/components/calendar/RuleOverrideDialog.tsx. Shape it on frontend/src/components/dashboard/CompanionGetDialog.tsx: <Dialog> + <Image> on an existing /pablo-*.webp from frontend/public. Pick one that reads as a gentle question, not an alarm. No red/destructive styling; the therapist is not doing anything wrong.
9. frontend/src/components/calendar/AppointmentModal.tsx: on save, call checkConflicts for the chosen window first. Empty conflicts -> save as today. Any conflict (hard OR soft) -> open the dialog. Confirm -> save with rule_override: true. Cancel -> save nothing, modal stays open with the form intact.

SUMMARISING MULTIPLE RULES (load-bearing). One window commonly trips SEVERAL rules at once: a blocked weekday plus a per-day cap plus a buffer. The dialog must read as a reason, not as an export of the settings page. Do NOT render a bulleted dump of per-rule strings. Write summarizeConflicts(conflicts): string in the dialog's own module: lead with the most specific/strongest conflict, hard before soft; join at most two or three into one natural sentence, then "and N more"; full per-rule detail goes in a collapsed details area; singular/plural must read correctly at 1, 2 and 5 conflicts. summarize(rule) already exists for a SINGLE rule (frontend/src/components/settings/AvailabilitySettings.tsx:208, exported) and is the vocabulary the settings page uses. Match its wording and tone. Do NOT move or edit that file; converging the two vocabularies is a filed follow-up.

THE DIALOG STATES THE REASON AND OVERRIDES ONE EVENT. Shape:
    This appointment is blocked because of "no meetings on Fridays".
    Do you want to override this event?
        [ Override this event ]        [ Cancel ]
The reason is stated in the therapist's own words and the question is about THIS event only.

DECIDED, NOT OPEN: the dialog NEVER modifies a rule. No "unblock Fridays", no delete, no disable, no edit-rule link that mutates anything. Do not call useDeleteAvailabilityRule or any rule mutation from this dialog or anywhere in the save path. The dialog does not care whether one rule or five produced the conflict; it names them and asks one question. Copy reflects enforcement: a soft rule is a preference ("You usually don't book Fridays"), a hard one is a boundary ("You've blocked Fridays"). Same buttons, same mechanics.

WHAT CANNOT BE KNOWN BEFORE SAVING. The save-time engine check is the ONLY authoritative answer. Any pre-check, including the grid shading, is an approximation. If the server still refuses a save the therapist confirmed, surface that refusal rather than swallowing it. Recurrence is all-or-nothing today: create_recurring expands every occurrence and one hard conflict aborts the whole series (scheduling.py:519-531). Keep that. With rule_override: true the series books in full. The dialog says the series conflicts with the therapist's rules; it does NOT report which occurrences or offer to skip them.

DECISIONS CLOSED: opt-in flag, default False; do not invert it, key it off a role, or add a server-side "is this a human" heuristic. Hard and soft raise the SAME dialog. One conflict check per save attempt, at save time. Reuse POST /api/availability/check; no new endpoint, no dry-run mode on create. Recurrence stays all-or-nothing.

DO NOT TOUCH: frontend/src/components/calendar/editorial/** (already shipped, owned elsewhere); frontend/src/components/settings/AvailabilitySettings.tsx (read its exported summarize; do not move or edit it).

TESTS. Backend: hard conflict with rule_override=False still 422s; same request with True creates and returns the messages as warnings; soft with False keeps today's create-with-warnings behaviour; a recurring series with one conflicting occurrence still aborts without the flag and books in full with it. Existing backend/tests scheduling + availability tests must pass UNEDITED. Frontend vitest: summarizeConflicts at 1, 2 and 5 conflicts; dialog renders the summary and fires override / cancel; AppointmentModal save path (no conflicts saves directly, conflicts open the dialog, override re-saves with the flag, cancel writes nothing); assert that NO rule mutation is reachable from the dialog.

Commit and PR text: plain and human-toned; no tracker ids.
acceptance_criteria: 1. With a hard rule blocking Fridays, booking a Friday appointment from the calendar opens a dialog carrying a Pablo image, stating the reason in the therapist's own words and asking whether to override this event. 2. Confirming writes the appointment; the therapist never has to delete the rule to book. 2a. The dialog offers NO way to change, delete or disable a rule, and no rule mutation is reachable from the save path. 2b. A window tripping several rules at once produces one readable summary, correct at 1, 2 and 5 conflicts. 3. Cancelling writes nothing and the form keeps its values. 4. A soft rule opens the same dialog rather than writing and warning after the fact. 5. POST /api/appointments WITHOUT rule_override behaves exactly as today: hard conflict 422s with violations, soft creates and returns warnings. 6. Every existing backend scheduling and availability test passes UNEDITED. 7. An overridden booking records the overridden rule types on the audit trail, with no patient identifiers. 8. Nothing under frontend/src/components/calendar/editorial/ is modified. 9. make check green.
notes:
Filed by the eng-head pass 2026-09-10 (evening, interactive, Kurt-directed) from the SaaS board's spec, rehomed here because the work lands in this repo. Six gates: spec unambiguous with verified pointers; done-signal = named tests + CI; blast radius bounded to the named files; self-contained; no collision with in-flight PRs; single target repo. Never-dispatch walk: no PHI handling change, no money/entitlement, no prod infra, no auth/RLS design, no vendor dashboard, no outbound send, not on a claim surface. Chain order for the booking set: link-to-type -> type-scoped rules -> exclusivity -> parser; the dependency edges enforce it.

title: Reconnecting a different Google account inherits the old account's calendar
description:
Three things in the Google Calendar connect path, found once the app-calendar
target could actually complete a connect for the first time.

**1. A reconnect to a different Google account reuses the old account's calendar.**

`_get_or_create_app_calendar_id` now reuses the `calendar_id` on the stored
token record rather than asking Google, because the app-calendar grant
(`calendar.app.created`) cannot call `calendarList.list`. That is right when the
row is absent or the account is unchanged — but `handle_callback` can run while
a row still exists (reconnecting without disconnecting first), and then a
*different* Google account inherits a calendar id living in the previous
account. Its credentials cannot write there, so every push afterwards fails.

`disconnect()` deletes the row outright, so the disconnect-then-reconnect path
is unaffected. It is only reconnect-in-place that breaks.

When the reuse was introduced there was no evidence about what
`calendar.app.created` permits beyond the refusal we had already seen, so an
existence check was deliberately left out: if `calendars().get` were refused too,
a failing check would create a duplicate calendar on every reconnect. A live
connect has since shown `calendars().insert()` succeeding under that scope, so
calendar-level operations are permitted and the check is now the right call.

**2. Settings shows the raw calendar id.**

`GoogleCalendarSettings.tsx:38` and `CalendarConnectStep.tsx:43` both render
`{status.calendar_id ?? "Connected"}` as the heading. For the primary target
that is the therapist's email and reads fine, which is why it went unnoticed —
the app-calendar target is the only one that yields an opaque
`...@group.calendar.google.com` hash, and it has never rendered before. The line
beneath already says "A calendar Pablo made for your sessions", so the heading
is both unreadable and redundant.

**3. The attestation audit record calls a calendar an account.**

`set_event_titling` stores `attested_account = calendar_id`, and the
`CALENDAR_NAME_DISCLOSURE_ATTESTED` row records it under `calendar_account`.
For an app-calendar connection that value is a calendar id, not an account.

The *enforcement* is fine and this is not a hole: `_effective_style` compares
`titling_attested_account` against `calendar_id`, both sides the same value, and
`handle_callback` rebuilds the token doc without carrying the attestation
forward — so it is wiped on every reconnect and cannot follow a therapist to
another account. This is an evidence-quality problem in a disclosure record, not
a live one.
design:
**1. Verify the stored calendar before reusing it.**

In `_get_or_create_app_calendar_id`, when the token record carries a
`calendar_id` for the app-calendar target, confirm it is reachable with the
credentials just granted — `service.calendars().get(calendarId=stored)` — and
reuse it only if that succeeds. On any `HttpError`, fall through and create a
fresh one: the calendar was deleted, or belongs to an account this grant no
longer speaks for.

The cost of a wrong guess is now bounded the right way. Previously a refused
check meant a duplicate calendar on every reconnect; with `insert` proven to
work under this scope, a refusal is unlikely, and the failure it prevents
(silently writing to a calendar in someone else's account) is worse than a
stray calendar.

**2. Give the status response a display name.**

Add `calendar_name: str | None` to `GoogleCalendarStatusResponse`, filled from
`get_sync_status`:
- app-calendar → `_APP_CALENDAR_SUMMARY` ("Pablo Sessions")
- primary → `None`

Both components become `{status.calendar_name ?? status.calendar_id ?? "Connected"}`,
so the primary path is untouched and the string stays in one place server-side
rather than being duplicated into the frontend.

**3. Make the audit row self-describing.**

Do not rename `calendar_account` — historical rows carry that key and queries
over them should keep working. Add `write_target` alongside it, so a reader can
tell whether the value is an account (primary) or a Pablo-made calendar. Fix the
comment that calls it "which account it covered", and the docstrings on
`titling_attested_account` and `_effective_style` that describe the comparison
as being about an account.
acceptance_criteria: Reconnecting in place with a different Google account creates a new Pablo-owned calendar rather than reusing an id from the previous account; reconnecting the same account still reuses its calendar and does not leave a second one behind. Settings and the connect wizard show a readable calendar name for the app-calendar target, and the therapist's email for the primary target as before. The attestation audit row records write_target so a reader can tell whether calendar_account names an account or a Pablo-made calendar. make check passes.
close_reason: Fixed in pablo#1077 (squash ebcf6236): calendars().get reachability check before reusing a remembered app-calendar id; calendar_name on the status response so settings shows a readable label; write_target recorded alongside calendar_account in the attestation audit row. Enforcement was never affected -- corrected in the PR body.

title: A webhook does not say which tenant it is for, so we ask all of them
description:
A clearinghouse webhook names a transaction and nothing else. It does not say
which practice the claim belongs to, so ingest_transaction_event finds out by
ASKING EVERY PRACTICE IN TURN:

    for practice in active_practices(max_tenants=_WEBHOOK_MAX_TENANTS):  # 50
        ...
        for user_id in practice.user_ids:
            with tenant_db_session(practice.schema, user_id):
                claims.get_by_control_number(...)

A linear scan over practices multiplied by clinicians, per delivery, inside
the vendor's delivery timeout. There is no platform-level index of control
numbers — checked 2026-09-10, platform_models.py has none.

It cannot currently be otherwise: one clearinghouse account serves every
tenant, so fetching the transaction proves nothing about who owns it. Row
visibility is the only discriminator available.

Three consequences, worst first.

1. _WEBHOOK_MAX_TENANTS = 50 IS A SILENT CLIFF. Practice 51 never matches.
   The delivery returns "unmatched", which is indistinguishable from "no claim
   of ours" and alerts nobody. That is exactly the failure shape PABLO-1qox
   was about, lying in wait at a specific customer count.

2. COST IS O(practices x clinicians) PER WEBHOOK, each iteration a schema
   switch and a query. Twenty practices with five clinicians is a hundred
   tenant sessions to route one document, against a timeout.

3. FIRST-MATCH-WINS IS ONLY CORRECT WHILE CONTROL NUMBERS ARE GLOBALLY
   UNIQUE — and the uniqueness constraint is PER-SCHEMA. Two tenants may
   legitimately hold the same control number, and then a payer's money posts
   to whichever practice the loop happened to visit first. This is the
   cross-tenant blast radius of PABLO-z7te, and it is considerably worse than
   that bead's own "a claim fails to file".
design:
Write a platform-level routing index when a claim is filed:

    control_number -> practice_id

Routing then becomes one lookup followed by one tenant session, instead of a
scan. It removes the scan, removes the 50-tenant cliff, and makes a
cross-tenant control-number collision impossible to MIS-ROUTE, because the
index's own uniqueness constraint refuses the second write instead of
silently accepting it.

DECISIONS TO CLOSE BEFORE BUILDING, not while building:
- The index is cross-tenant metadata outside the practice schemas, which cuts
  against the isolation model. The mitigating argument is that it holds a
  control number and a practice id and NOTHING else — no PHI, no clinical
  content, no patient identifier — and that platform.email_tenant_mappings is
  already exactly this class of object. Make that argument explicitly in the
  model's docstring or somebody will delete it on isolation grounds.
- Decide what happens when the index has no row: fall back to the scan, or
  refuse? A fallback keeps old claims working but keeps the cliff alive for
  them. Backfilling from every practice schema is the alternative.
- The scan should not simply be deleted while claims filed before the index
  exists are still open.

DO NOT fold this into PABLO-z7te. That bead is about how a control number is
generated; this one is about how a document is routed. They meet only at the
uniqueness question.
acceptance_criteria: 1. A clearinghouse webhook routes to the owning practice by lookup, not by scanning practices. 2. A deployment with more than _WEBHOOK_MAX_TENANTS practices routes correctly to a practice beyond the cap — a test proves it. 3. Two practices holding the same control number cannot mis-route: the second index write is refused. 4. Claims filed before the index existed still route. 5. make check passes.
notes: Confirmed live on dev 2026-09-10: six real 277CA deliveries between 22:52 and 23:39 all logged outcome=unmatched (clearinghouse_webhook_processed). Fix in pablo#1081 — routing index replaces the bounded scan.
close_reason: Fixed in pablo#1081 and verified on the dev deployment: four webhook deliveries routed (recorded / not_applicable) at 01:02 and 01:12 UTC, where every delivery before the deploy returned unmatched.

title: The app-calendar connect calls an API its own scope forbids
description:
Connecting a Google Calendar with the app-calendar write target fails at the
OAuth callback with:

```
googleapiclient.errors.HttpError: <HttpError 403 when requesting
https://www.googleapis.com/calendar/v3/users/me/calendarList?alt=json
returned "Request had insufficient authentication scopes.">
```

Observed on dev 2026-09-10T15:22:01Z, immediately after a successful token
exchange — so the grant itself worked and this is the first API call made with
it.

`_PUSH_TO_APP_CALENDAR` requests exactly one scope,
`https://www.googleapis.com/auth/calendar.app.created`. That scope is the whole
point of the app-calendar target: it reaches only calendars this app created and
cannot touch anything else on the account (`NarrowingEnforcement.PROVIDER_ENFORCED`).

But `_get_or_create_app_calendar_id` (google_calendar_service.py:1189) opens with
`service.calendarList().list()`, and Google refuses that under
`calendar.app.created`. So the connect path's first call is one its own scope
cannot authorize, and the app-calendar target can never complete a connect.

The docstring above the call states the assumption that fails: "Under the
app-calendar grant the calendar list only contains calendars this app created."
Whatever the list would contain, the caller is not allowed to ask.

This is the third distinct bug on this path today, which is why it surfaced only
now — an `InvalidGrantError` (02:30) and a missing `googleapiclient` dependency
(03:41, fixed in #1045) each had to be cleared before the request could get far
enough to be refused for scopes.
design:
Two ways out, and they pull in opposite directions.

Broadening the grant (adding `calendar.calendarlist.readonly`, or
`calendar.readonly`) would make the list call legal, but it gives up exactly the
property the app-calendar target exists to offer: a grant Google itself confines
to calendars Pablo created. The wizard copy promises that reach
(`reach="the calendar Pablo creates for your sessions"`,
`PROVIDER_ENFORCED`), so widening the scope would make the consent screen say
something the code no longer means.

So: drop the list call instead.

The identity of the app calendar is already ours to remember —
`GoogleCalendarTokenDoc` persists `calendar_id` alongside `write_target`. The
list call is re-deriving, through an API we are not entitled to use, a fact we
already store. Read it from the token record:

- If a stored record for this user has a `calendar_id` and its `write_target` is
  the app-calendar one, reuse that id. No API call at all.
- Otherwise create the calendar with `calendars().insert()`, which
  `calendar.app.created` does authorize, and let the existing save path persist
  the id.

That keeps "reconnecting finds the existing calendar rather than leaving a second
one behind" — the behaviour the docstring is protecting — while making zero calls
the grant cannot cover.

`_get_or_create_app_calendar_id` and `_resolve_calendar_id` both need `user_id`
threaded in; `handle_callback` already has it.

Deliberately not doing a `calendars().get()` existence check on the stored id:
if that call is also refused under this scope, every reconnect would silently
create a duplicate calendar — a worse failure than the one being fixed, and one
that only shows up in the user's account. A calendar the user deleted on
Google's side surfaces as a push error later; recovering from that is separate
work.
acceptance_criteria: Connecting a calendar with the app-calendar write target completes without a 403. The connect path makes no Google API call outside what calendar.app.created authorizes -- in particular it no longer calls calendarList.list. Reconnecting an account that already has a Pablo-created calendar reuses it rather than creating a second one. The requested scope set is unchanged (no broadening). make check passes.
close_reason: Fixed in pablo#1072 (squash 7c147bd1): app calendar id read from the stored token record instead of calendarList.list, which calendar.app.created does not authorize. Scopes unchanged. Needs a live connect against dev to confirm calendars().insert() is permitted under the same scope.

title: A blocking auth round trip in DatabaseSessionMiddleware freezes the whole worker
description:
`DatabaseSessionMiddleware.dispatch` is `async`, but the first thing it does is
call `_verify_and_stash_clinician_identity(request)` — a synchronous function
that performs a blocking HTTPS round trip to the identity provider
(`firebase_auth.verify_id_token(token, check_revoked=True)`; `check_revoked`
forces a remote user-record fetch on every authenticated request).

A blocking network call inside `async def dispatch` runs **on the event loop**,
so while it is in flight the entire worker makes no progress — every other
in-flight request, and every log write, is frozen.

Observed on dev 2026-09-10 15:05:02Z. The provider stalled for ~152s. Effects:

- 24 concurrent requests all froze at once and all failed at the same instant.
- 62 seconds with zero application log output — the loop was blocked, not busy.
- Requests that had already opened a transaction (middleware resolves the
  practice schema from the DB at `_resolve_schema_from_request`, before
  `call_next`) sat idle-in-transaction. Postgres reaped all ~20 pooled
  connections at the 30s `idle_in_transaction_session_timeout`.
- When the loop unblocked, every request touched a dead socket and returned
  500 with `OperationalError: SSL connection has been closed unexpectedly`.
- `statement_timeout` never fired, because no statement was ever running.

`pool_pre_ping`, `pool_recycle` and TCP keepalives are all already enabled and
are irrelevant here: the connections did not go stale in the pool, they were
killed while checked out.

The same shape applies to `_resolve_schema_from_request` and
`set_tenant_schema`, which also perform blocking DB I/O directly on the event
loop in `dispatch`. The auth round trip is the acute case because it depends on
an external provider with no timeout.
design:
Two changes, both in the request hot path.

1. Get the blocking work off the event loop.
   `DatabaseSessionMiddleware.dispatch` should run its synchronous prelude
   (token verification, schema resolution, `set_tenant_schema`) via
   `starlette.concurrency.run_in_threadpool` rather than calling it inline.
   This converts "one slow provider call freezes the worker" into "one slow
   request is slow", which is the whole of the blast radius.

   Ordering must be preserved exactly: verify-and-stash still happens before
   schema resolution, and both before `call_next`. `_request_session` is a
   ContextVar and the session is created on the loop, so the threadpool hop
   has to keep the ContextVar binding intact — set the ContextVar on the loop
   side, and pass the session explicitly into the offloaded callable.

2. Bound the provider call.
   The Firebase Admin SDK is initialized with a default transport that has no
   read timeout, so a provider stall blocks indefinitely. Configure an explicit
   connect/read timeout in `initialize_firebase_app()` so a stall surfaces in
   seconds. A timeout must NOT surface as 401 — that would sign users out
   during a provider blip. It should surface as 503.

Deliberately out of scope, filed as follow-ups:
- Caching the `check_revoked` result per subject with a short TTL. It would
  remove the remote call from steady state, but it trades away part of a
  revocation guarantee in an auth path; that deserves its own decision.
- Not holding a transaction open across `call_next`.
acceptance_criteria: A slow or hanging identity-provider call no longer blocks the event loop: concurrent requests that need no provider call continue to be served and logged while one is in flight. The provider call is bounded by an explicit timeout and surfaces as 503, not 401, when it expires. Middleware ordering is unchanged (verify-and-stash before schema resolution, both before call_next) and the request-scoped session ContextVar is still bound correctly inside route handlers. make check passes.
close_reason: Fixed in pablo#1070 (squash 6e7ef724): prelude moved to a worker thread, tenant-schema ContextVar re-applied on the loop, Admin SDK HTTP calls bounded at 10s, provider timeout answers 503 not 401.

title: Google API client is imported but never declared, so calendar connect dies after the token exchange
design:
Connecting a Google Calendar fails after a successful token exchange:

  File "app/services/google_calendar_service.py", line 262, in _build_calendar_service
    from googleapiclient.discovery import build
  ModuleNotFoundError: No module named 'googleapiclient'

google-api-python-client is not declared in pyproject.toml, so it is absent from the
deployed image and from a fresh poetry venv. _build_calendar_service imports it lazily, so
nothing fails at boot or at import time — the module is only reached once a real OAuth
exchange has succeeded and the service goes to resolve the calendar id.

Never worked, and never could have. Two things hid it:
  - the lazy import means no startup or CI import error;
  - every unit test patches _build_calendar_service, so no test ever imports the real one.

Third in a sequence of first-run failures on a path that had never run end to end
(PABLO-awt2 auth race, PABLO-y01q PKCE verifier, this). Each one was only reachable once
the previous was fixed.

Fix: declare google-api-python-client in pyproject.toml and lock it.

Worth considering alongside: a test that imports _build_calendar_service for real (without
patching) would have caught this, and would catch the next dependency that is only reached
behind a live credential. The tests cannot call Google, but they can prove the module
imports.

Acceptance criteria:
- google-api-python-client is in pyproject.toml and poetry.lock.
- A connect on dev gets past _resolve_calendar_id.
- Something in the suite fails if the dependency is removed again.
close_reason: Shipped in #1045 (merged 2026-09-10): the Google API client is declared.

title: The e2e fake clearinghouse no longer serves the path claims are submitted to
description: Claim submission moved to the vendor's native API in pablo#1032. The fake clearinghouse in the e2e stack still serves only the legacy compatibility path, so a claim filed from a browser against the harness now 404s. Nothing caught it because no e2e spec files a claim.
design:
PROVEN by curl against the running stack on 2026-09-09:

    POST /2024-04-01/change/medicalnetwork/professionalclaims/v3/submission -> 400 (route exists)
    POST /professional-claim-submissions                                    -> 404
    POST /2025-03-07/professional-claim-submissions                         -> 404

`backend/app/claims/stedi_sdk.py` sets the SDK's `endpoint_uri` from
`ClearinghouseCredentials.base_url`, and the e2e stack sets
`CLEARINGHOUSE_BASE_URL=http://fake-clearinghouse:8080`, so the SDK posts a
claim to the fake at the NATIVE path. `scripts/fake_clearinghouse.py` only
routes `@app.post(f"{HEALTHCARE}/change/medicalnetwork/professionalclaims/v3/submission")`.

This is a regression from pablo#1032 and the lesson is worth keeping: a
protocol change was shipped with a live vendor lane proving it against the
real API, and nothing proved the FAKE still matched. The live lane and the
fake test different things and both have to move together.

BUILD: teach the fake the native submission endpoint.
* `POST /professional-claim-submissions` accepting the native body shape
  (see `backend/app/claims/sdk_submission.py` for exactly what is sent:
  payer.id, submitter, insured, patient, authorization, encounter, billing,
  service_lines, idempotency_key).
* Answer with the native response: `{claimId, submissionId}` on acceptance
  and `{claimId, submissionId, errors:[{description}]}` for an edit
  rejection - NOT the legacy `{status, controlNumber, claimReference, ...}`
  envelope.
* `claimId` must be stable across resubmissions of the same patient control
  number, because that is the property the product now relies on.
* Keep the existing control-number rules (REJ-DX / REJ-PTR / REJ-SUB) working
  by mapping them onto the native `errors` array.
* Honour `idempotency_key` from the BODY (it is no longer a header): the same
  key with the same body replays the same claimId and starts no new timers;
  the same key with a different body is refused, as the vendor does.
* Keep serving the legacy path too until nothing calls it - eligibility,
  payer search, transactions and reports still go through httpx.

The 277CA and 835 timers key on the patient control number and can stay as
they are.

DO NOT widen this into the partial-payment work; that is PABLO-4emu.
acceptance_criteria:
1. A claim filed through the adapter against the fake is accepted and returns a native `claimId`.
2. Resubmitting the same patient control number returns the same `claimId`.
3. The same idempotency key with the same body replays; with a different body it is refused.
4. The REJ-DX / REJ-PTR / REJ-SUB control numbers still produce edit rejections, carried in the native `errors` array.
5. The legacy endpoints the httpx adapter still uses keep working.
6. A test proves the harness path end to end, so this cannot regress silently again.
notes:
worker exited with PR (open) — office poll tagged pr-open
PR closed unmerged — reconciled
close_reason:
Merged in pablo#1056 (4d1cd8bd). The fake clearinghouse serves POST /2025-03-07/professional-claim-submissions, the native endpoint claim submission moved to in pablo#1032, alongside the legacy compatibility path.

Came in whole from the fleet's branch (work/e2e-clearinghouse-claims-path, ac47461b) rather than being reimplemented — #1052 is closed pointing here.

And the reason this went unnoticed is now closed too: 'nothing caught it because no e2e spec files a claim' was the bead's own diagnosis, and frontend/e2e/specs/claims.spec.ts now files one through a browser and asserts the endpoint it lands on.

title: A second payer's remittance is dropped, and the client's balance is summed across payers
description: apply_posting writes a patient_resp ledger row for every remittance it posts. A claim with secondary coverage gets a remittance from each payer, so the client is billed once per payer for a single session.
design:
X12 RFI #2548 settles what each remittance means: "The secondary payer
should not re-report prior payer patient responsibility amounts. The secondary
payer should report PR adjustments that they have assigned per their
adjudication." So each remittance states what the client owes AFTER that
payer adjudicated - it is a restatement of the balance, not an addition to it.

`backend/app/claims/remittance.py` `apply_posting` writes
`charges.add_ledger_row(kind="patient_resp", amount_cents=posting.
patient_responsibility_cents, claim_id=...)` unconditionally when the amount
is positive. The receipt idempotency key is `f"{claim.id}:{posting.source_id}"`
where source_id is the vendor's payment-entry id, so a SECOND payer produces a
DIFFERENT entry id, passes the idempotency guard, and writes a SECOND row.

Worked example. $150 session, primary allows $150, pays $120, assigns $30
coinsurance. Secondary then pays that $30 and assigns nothing. Correct final
client balance: $0. What happens today: a $30 row from the primary, and the
secondary either writes nothing (leaving the client owing $30 they do not) or
writes its own assignment on top.

DECISIONS CLOSED - do not re-litigate:
1. Post the DELTA, not the amount. Sum the patient_resp rows already written
   against this claim, subtract from what this remittance says, write the
   difference. A negative delta is a credit row and is correct - that is a
   payer paying down a balance we already billed.
2. Write NOTHING when the delta is zero. Re-reading an unchanged remittance
   must stay a no-op even if it gets past the receipt guard.
3. Do NOT sum patient responsibility across remittances. That is the bug.
4. Keep it inside the same branch that records the receipt, so the receipt
   idempotency still covers the ordinary single-payer case.
5. Do NOT attempt to model COB ordering, OA-23, or which payer is primary.
   The delta reading is correct without knowing any of that, and RFI #2535
   says OA-23 is what the provider has already posted - not something to post
   again. Widening this into COB modelling is a separate bead.

The ledger rows carry `claim_id` and `kind` and `PatientPaymentRepository.
list_charges(patient_id)` returns them, so no new repository method is needed.

DIAGNOSIS CORRECTED once the code was actually run. The description above is
half right: the delta write is necessary but was never the whole bug, and
"bills the client twice" was not what today's code does.

There were THREE faults, all the same mistake in different places.

1. THE AGGREGATION (the real one). `ClaimTimeline.patient_responsibility_cents`
   SUMMED the patient responsibility of every money entry. A primary
   assigning $30 and a secondary assigning $10 reported $40 owed, when the
   client owes $10. That is over-billing inside a SINGLE posting, so it did
   not need a second posting to happen at all. Fixed: what the client owes is
   what the LATEST adjudication says, not a sum. Each payer reports only what
   it assigned itself (RFI #2548), so every entry is already a complete
   statement of the balance after that payer finished.

   Same change fixes a second thing: the old sum counted only entries where
   money moved, so a denial that leaves the client owing the whole charge -
   a non-covered service, which is ordinary in behavioural health - reported
   ZERO owed. Denials now count.

2. THE STATE MACHINE. `partial` and `paid` had no outgoing transitions at
   all, so a second payer's remittance was not double-posted - it was
   SILENTLY DROPPED by the `next_state(...) is None` guard in `apply_posting`,
   logged as `remittance_not_applicable`. The client kept owing the primary's
   coinsurance forever and the secondary's payment never reached
   `total_paid_cents`. Added `(partial, pay)`, `(partial, pay_partial)`,
   `(paid, pay)`, `(paid, pay_partial)`.

   `TERMINAL_STATES` keeps all four members: what callers actually ask it is
   "is this claim still waiting on somebody" - the watchdog does not time
   these out and an acknowledgement does not reject them - and a revised
   adjudication does not make a claim start waiting again. The invariant test
   now asserts the real rule (a settled claim never moves to a state that
   waits) instead of "takes no event", and `denied`/`rejected` still take
   nothing at all.

3. THE LEDGER WRITE. As described above: post the difference from what this
   claim has already billed, never the amount. Needed because a revised
   adjudication arrives as a separate posting.

Landed together; none of the three works without the others.
acceptance_criteria:
1. A primary remittance assigning the client $30 writes one $30 row, as today.
2. A secondary remittance on the same claim that assigns the client nothing brings the client to $0 - by writing a -$30 row, not by leaving $30 standing.
3. A secondary remittance assigning $10 leaves the client owing $10 in total, not $40.
4. A remittance that changes nothing writes no row at all.
5. The single-payer path is unchanged, and the existing patient-responsibility tests still pass untouched.
6. `make check` passes.
close_reason: Landed in pablo#1042: latest-adjudication balance, adjudicated states re-enterable, ledger writes the difference

title: PKCE verifier does not survive the calendar OAuth round trip, so every exchange is rejected
design:
Connecting a Google Calendar fails at the token exchange with:

  oauthlib.oauth2.rfc6749.errors.InvalidGrantError: (invalid_grant) Missing code verifier.

google-auth-oauthlib 1.4.1 generates a PKCE verifier inside flow.authorization_url() and
sends Google the derived challenge. The verifier lives on that Flow instance, in memory,
for the life of that request. _build_flow (google_calendar_service.py:236) is called
independently by each half of the round trip, so the callback builds a fresh Flow whose
code_verifier is None, fetch_token() sends no verifier, and Google rejects the exchange.

This has never worked. It was masked by PABLO-awt2 — until that landed, no authorization
code ever reached fetch_token, so the exchange was never actually attempted.

Fix: keep PKCE and persist the verifier across the round trip.

  - authorize: capture flow.code_verifier after authorization_url(), store it keyed by the
    nonce already inside the minted state, TTL matched to MAX_STATE_AGE_SECONDS (600s).
  - callback: after verify_state passes, look the verifier up, delete it, and set it on the
    Flow before fetch_token.

Store is Redis (backend/app/redis_client.py; USE_REDIS=true on both dev and prod, verified
2026-09-09).

Do NOT put the verifier in the OAuth state. State is HMAC-signed but not encrypted — the
payload is plain base64 JSON — and it travels in URLs, so it reaches access logs, browser
history and Referer headers. A verifier there would sit next to the code it protects and
nullify PKCE entirely.

Do NOT copy idle_session's "if redis is None: return" pattern. There a missing Redis
degrades an idle check; here it would silently drop PKCE from the flow, which is an
invisible security downgrade. Calendar connect is infrequent and retryable, so it should
fail loudly instead.

Deleting the verifier on use also makes the state single-use, which closes the replay
window verify_state cannot close on its own (it is stateless by design, so the nonce makes
values unguessable but does not stop re-presentation inside the 600s window).

Acceptance criteria:
- A full connect completes against Google with PKCE still on (challenge sent, verifier
  presented).
- A second exchange with the same state fails, because the verifier is gone.
- A verifier that has expired or is absent fails the connect with a clear error rather than
  retrying without PKCE.
- Unit coverage that the authorize half stores what the callback half reads, without a live
  Google or a live Redis.
close_reason: Shipped in #1040 (merged 2026-09-10): the PKCE verifier now survives the round trip.

title: Availability rule params are unvalidated JSONB — a typo'd key is silently a different rule
design:
SCOPE NOTE (2026-09-10): this change lands the Pydantic tagged union at the API boundary and deletes the mirrors. It does NOT add a database CHECK constraint, so acceptance item 6 (surveying existing rows on live databases) is not part of this change; that survey is a separate step that precedes any later DB constraint. Say so in the PR.

RAISED BY KURT 2026-09-09 while reviewing patient self-booking: "is there a
reason we don't want columns that are typed?"

There is a reason for the JSONB, and it is not being paid for.

availability_rules.params is JSONB carrying disjoint fields per rule_type:

  working_hours          day_of_week (0=Mon), start, end   ("HH:MM")
  block_day_of_week      day_of_week
  block_time_range       day_of_week, start, end
  block_date_range       start_date, end_date              ("YYYY-MM-DD")
  block_specific_dates   dates (list)
  max_per_day            max
  buffer_before          minutes
  buffer_after           minutes
  session_defaults       duration default

Plus `enforcement`: hard (refuses) or soft (permitted, flagged — TimeSlot.over_cap).

WHY JSONB IS DEFENSIBLE. Nine types with almost no shared fields. Typed columns
mean either one wide sparse table where every row is mostly NULL, or nine tables
with nine repositories. Adding a rule type stays a code change rather than a
migration.

WHY IT IS A LIABILITY AS IT STANDS. Nothing validates the shape at any layer:

  * API boundary: `params: dict[str, Any]` (app/models/scheduling.py:192, 200,
    210, 237).
  * Repository: `params=row.params` straight through
    (repositories/postgres/availability_rule.py:72, 83).
  * Database: no CHECK constraint on the table.

And the engine reads with bare subscripts — rule.params["day_of_week"],
["start"], ["end"], ["max"], ["minutes"], ["start_date"], ["dates"]
(scheduling_engine/services/availability.py:250-427). So:

  * a missing key is a KeyError at request time, on the availability path, as a
    500 — not a validation error at save time;
  * day_of_week: 9, start: "25:00", minutes: "thirty" all store happily;
  * WORST: a typo'd key does not error, it silently becomes a DIFFERENT RULE. A
    buffer_after row carrying `minute` instead of `minutes` is a gap rule that
    enforces nothing, and looks correct in the UI.

That last one is the same failure class as two things fixed today: booking_policy
and scheduling_policy diverging invisibly because their defaults were identical,
and the log-incident parser that agreed with the belief that wrote it
(THERAPY-br0ws). A writer and a reader agreeing only by convention drift — and
drift HERE means a therapist's blocked time quietly stops blocking, or a booking
lands in a gap they thought they had.

SUGGESTED SHAPE, not a migration to typed columns: a tagged union of per-
rule-type Pydantic models discriminated on rule_type, applied where rules are
created and updated. Turns a 500-at-booking-time into a 422-at-save-time, costs
one module, needs no schema change, and leaves the open-ended shape available for
rule types that do not exist yet. A per-type DB CHECK is the belt-and-braces
version if the guarantee should survive something writing outside the app.

Deliberately NOT folded into the patient self-booking PR, which is already a
feature plus a new auth gate.
acceptance_criteria:
1. ONE authority for rule params: a Pydantic tagged union discriminated on
   rule_type. The create/update API validates through it, so a malformed rule is
   a 422 naming the field rather than a 500 later on the availability path.
2. The mirrors are deleted, not left beside it. availability_parse_service._PARAM_VALIDATORS
   is replaced by the shared models, and the frontend AvailabilitySettings.tsx
   validate() is either generated from them or pinned against them by a test that
   fails when they diverge. Three hand-kept copies is the defect, not the symptom.
3. An unknown params key is rejected rather than silently stored — a buffer_after
   carrying `minute` instead of `minutes` must not become a rule that enforces
   nothing.
4. Every RuleType member has a model: working_hours, block_day_of_week,
   block_time_range, block_date_range, block_specific_dates, max_per_day,
   buffer_before, buffer_after, session_defaults. Adding an enum member without a
   model fails a test rather than falling through to Any.
5. Values are range-checked, not just present: day_of_week 0-6, times parse as
   HH:MM, minutes/max non-negative, end after start, dates well-formed.
6. Existing rows are surveyed in dev and prod BEFORE any constraint lands, and
   the counts are recorded on this bead — anything already malformed is named,
   not assumed absent.
7. AvailabilityEngine keeps its bare subscripts. The point is that data reaching
   the engine is trustworthy, not that the engine grows defensive branches.
8. A test covers the LLM path specifically: a proposal from
   availability_parse_service with a key the engine does not read is rejected at
   the boundary, since that is the writer most able to invent one.
notes:
CONSUMER INVENTORY, asked for by Kurt 2026-09-09. It is worse than "add
validation": the rules are already written down THREE times by hand, and the one
door that matters has no check at all.

THE THREE COPIES

1. frontend AvailabilitySettings.tsx `validate()` — the manual form.
2. backend app/services/availability_parse_service.py `_PARAM_VALIDATORS`
   (:310 `_validate_params`) — for LLM-proposed rules.
3. ...and nothing at the create API. `_validate_params`' own docstring says so:
   "Mirrors the frontend's validate() ... so a proposal that would fail the
   manual form's own validation is rejected here instead of being passed
   through -- THE CREATE API DOES NOT VALIDATE PARAMS ITSELF."

So the guarded path is the LLM one, and the unguarded path is the plain API.
Anything posting straight to the create endpoint — a script, a test fixture, a
future client, the SaaS overlay — writes whatever it likes.

THE WRITER THAT WORRIES ME MOST IS THE LLM. availability_parse_service turns a
therapist's sentence ("no appointments on Fridays") into rule_type + params
through a structured model call. It is propose-then-confirm and it does validate
today — but that validation is copy #2 of a schema nobody owns, so the day it
drifts from the engine's expectations the model's output starts producing rules
that store cleanly and enforce nothing.

READERS — all bare subscripts, all in scheduling_engine/services/availability.py:
  :250,:254,:255,:265   working_hours       day_of_week, start, end
  :271                  block_day_of_week   day_of_week
  :285,:286,:294        block_time_range    start, end
  :308,:493             max_per_day         max
  :372,:373,:424        block_date_range    start_date, end_date
  :386,:427             block_specific_dates dates
  :449,:451             buffer_before/after minutes
  :465,:475             session_defaults    duration_minutes, alignment
  :407-439              the free-slot pass re-reads most of the above

  A missing key here is a KeyError at request time, on the availability path,
  surfacing as a 500 — including now on the PATIENT self-booking path
  (routes/patient_booking.py), where the person who gets the error is a client
  trying to book, not the therapist who made the rule.

OTHER READERS:
  routes/scheduling.py:1033,:1038  reads p.params["day_of_week"] on LLM
                                   PROPOSALS with a bare subscript
  routes/scheduling.py:831,:1024   passes params through to responses
  repositories/postgres/availability_rule.py:72,:83  straight through
  models/scheduling.py:192,200,210,237  `params: dict[str, Any]` at the API edge
  scheduling_engine/models/availability.py:53  `data.get("params", {})`

SO THE JOB IS NOT "ADD VALIDATION", IT IS "MAKE ONE AUTHORITY AND DELETE THE
MIRRORS": a Pydantic tagged union discriminated on rule_type, used by the create
API (closing the open door) AND by availability_parse_service in place of
_PARAM_VALIDATORS, with the frontend's validate() either generated from it or
pinned against it by a test. Three hand-kept copies is how the log-incident
parser drifted for months (THERAPY-br0ws) and how booking_policy and
scheduling_policy diverged invisibly — both fixed today, both the same shape.

PROMOTED llama-ok, eng-head pass 2026-09-10 (evening, interactive, Kurt-directed). Six gates: spec unambiguous with verified pointers; done-signal = named tests + CI; blast radius bounded to the named files; self-contained; no collision with in-flight PRs; single target repo. Never-dispatch walk: no PHI handling change, no money/entitlement, no prod infra, no auth/RLS design, no vendor dashboard, no outbound send, not on a claim surface. Scoping note for the worker, also folded into the design: this change adds API-boundary validation only, no DB CHECK, so acceptance item 6 (surveying existing rows on live databases) is NOT the worker's step; it is a separate, credentialed step that precedes any later DB constraint. Record that in the PR.

title: Public booking end-to-end spec on the local harness
description: The anonymous booking link is the only internet-facing write path with no browser coverage. The local harness (docs/design/e2e-harness.md) now runs the whole stack with no cloud, so the spec belongs here.
design: Read frontend/e2e/ (fixtures/auth.ts, scenarios.ts giveBookingLink, playwright.config.ts) and docs/design/public-booking.md. Write frontend/e2e/specs/public-booking.spec.ts: a signed-in clinician creates a booking link (via giveBookingLink) with an all-day availability rule for a fixed weekday; an anonymous browser context opens /book/{slug}, sees the card, picks a date, picks a slot, books with a synthetic name/email, lands on the confirmation page; the confirmation link cancels the booking; assertions: the appointment appears on the clinician's calendar (API check as the clinician), the anonymous surface never returns patient data (network assertion on the slots and card responses), a second booking of the same slot is refused (409), and the cancel link works once. Compose env must have PUBLIC_BOOKING_ENABLED=true on both backend and frontend for this spec only if the harness runs it dark by default; document. DO NOT TOUCH backend behaviour.
acceptance_criteria: 1. Spec green via make e2e on a clean machine. 2. Slot collision refused and asserted. 3. Anonymous responses carry no patient fields (assertion on response bodies). 4. CI e2e workflow green on the PR.
notes: 2026-09-07: shipped in #982 — anonymous booking through the public link, mail confirmation read off the stack, slot contention (409), confirm, clinician-side verification, manage-link cancel, second cancel 404. 25 e2e tests green in CI. Added a fake mail server to the harness (scripts/fake_mail.py) because every booking link is born requiring email confirmation and the booking POST 403s when the sender cannot deliver.
close_reason: Merged: #982. Public booking covered end to end — anonymous booking, mail confirmation read off the stack, slot contention 409, confirm, clinician-side verification, manage-link cancel, second cancel 404. 25 e2e tests green in CI. Added a fake mail server to the harness.

title: make test-all reports success while running none of the integration suite
design:
FOUND 2026-08-27. The target exits 0 having silently skipped every integration
module, which is worse than failing: it is a green signal for work that was
never executed.

Mechanism. `make test-all` runs `pytest tests/ tests_integration/` in one
invocation. tests/conftest.py:28 plants a dummy DATABASE_URL at import time so
settings validation passes for the unit suite. tests_integration/conftest.py's
pytest_configure then sees DATABASE_URL already set, concludes a real database
was supplied by the caller, returns early, and never brings up the container or
sets DATABASE_BACKEND=postgres. Every module in tests_integration/ carries a
skipif on exactly that variable, so all of them skip.

Argument order does not help — both conftests are imported during collection
regardless of the order the paths are given.

Options, roughly in increasing order of how much they fix:

  (a) Make the integration conftest's early return conditional on something the
      unit conftest cannot fake — an explicit opt-out variable, say, rather than
      the mere presence of DATABASE_URL. Smallest change; keeps the historical
      "I brought my own database" workflow working.
  (b) Have the integration conftest fail loudly when it detects the unit
      suite's sentinel value specifically, naming the problem. Cheap, and turns
      a silent skip into an instruction.
  (c) Make `make test-all` run the two suites as separate invocations. Fixes
      the target without touching either conftest, but leaves the trap armed
      for anyone who types the pytest command by hand.

(b) plus (c) is probably right: the target stops lying, and the trap announces
itself for anyone who steps in it another way.

Whatever is chosen, the sentinel is the interesting part — a dummy value that
means "no database" to one suite and "a database is configured" to another is
the actual defect, and it will bite again in a different shape if only the
Makefile is fixed.
acceptance_criteria:
1. `make test-all` runs every integration module, or fails saying why it cannot.
2. Running `pytest tests/ tests_integration/` by hand does not silently skip the
   integration suite — it either works or says what is wrong.
3. The historical workflow of exporting a real DATABASE_URL and running the
   integration suite against it still works.
4. A test covers the failure mode: with the unit suite's sentinel in the
   environment, the integration suite does not report success without running.
notes:
PR pablo#1013 open (2026-09-09).

Adversarial review caught two blocking defects in the first pass; both were
reproduced before fixing.

1. The fix guarded only one of two doors. Every module here is gated by
   skipif(DATABASE_BACKEND != "postgres"), and that variable was set ONLY on the
   testcontainers path — so exporting a real DATABASE_URL (the bring-your-own-
   database workflow the conftest docstring advertises) skipped the entire suite,
   exit 0. That is this bug verbatim on the branch the first pass exempted, and
   it failed acceptance criterion 3.

2. The tests could not see the bug. They used --collect-only, which lists items
   regardless of whether their skipif fires, so "all collected and all will skip"
   and "all collected and all will run" were the same observation — and mass-
   skipping WAS the bug. Deleting the one line whose absence causes it left all
   seven tests passing.

Fixed: the early return now advertises the backend via setdefault, and a new
tests_integration/test_bootstrap_contract.py (deliberately no skipif) asserts
what every other module's skipif requires. The unit-side guard RUNS that module
rather than collecting it and rejects a "skipped" summary. The mutation that
defeated the old tests now fails.

Left alone deliberately: --cov-append starts from nothing if the unit half dies
at collection, making the report look integration-only. Reporting-only, the
target still fails via rc collection. Worth its own bead if it ever bites.

After: ruff + mypy clean, 4226 unit passed, 477 integration passed (main reports
474 for the same scope; the delta is the new contract module).

Worth carrying: any test that shells out to `poetry run` is unreliable from a git
worktree. The alembic idempotency tests do, a worktree has no poetry env, so
poetry falls back to whatever python is ambient and env.py dies importing app.db.
Not a code defect — set VIRTUAL_ENV to the real venv when running from a worktree.
close_reason: Merged as pablo#1013. make test-all ran both suites in one pytest invocation; the unit conftest's placeholder DATABASE_URL read as a real database by the integration conftest, which stood down and let every module skip — exit 0, nothing run. Fixed the shared meaning (a marker only the planting code sets), made the integration conftest refuse rather than skip, and closed the second door where a real DATABASE_URL never got DATABASE_BACKEND=postgres. Adversarial review caught both that second door and the fact the first round of tests used --collect-only and could not tell a running suite from a skipped one; both reproduced and fixed. Integration suite now runs 477 where it previously ran none.

title: Give the token verifiers a typed 'unavailable' error, so a rejection and an outage stop looking alike
design:
FOUND 2026-08-27 reviewing pablo#772. A fix for this was written, merged into the
branch, and REVERTED the same day — the reasoning is preserved here and in
_verify_and_stash_clinician_identity's docstring so the next attempt starts from
the failure rather than repeating it.

The problem. DatabaseSessionMiddleware verifies an inbound credential and, when
it is a clinician's, stashes the identity on request.state. get_patient_context
refuses any request carrying that stash, which is what keeps a clinician's token
from being offered to a patient resolver. But the middleware swallows every
exception, so "nothing stashed" means two different things:

  * every verifier decided this is not a clinician's token — correct, and what a
    genuine patient credential must produce, since the resolver contract requires
    one to be structurally unacceptable to the clinician verifiers; and
  * a verifier could not decide.

The second is real: verify_id_token runs check_revoked=True, a network round
trip. During a provider outage the patient guard reads nothing and hands the
credential to every registered resolver, with only resolver discipline in the
way — the single point of failure the guard exists to remove.

Why the obvious fix failed. VerifierRegistry.verify already distinguishes them:
a 401 means "not my token" and falls through to the next backend, anything else
propagates. Keying a request.state marker off that looks exactly right. It is
not, because verify_firebase_token calls initialize_firebase_app() OUTSIDE its
try block — so a deployment with no credentials configured raises through the
same channel, on every request, permanently. The marker turned "refuse during an
outage" into "patient authentication is impossible here, silently". CI caught it
as fifteen patient tests returning 401. It passed on a developer machine, and
COULD NOT have failed there: with application default credentials present,
Firebase initialises and returns a clean 401, which is the branch that behaves.

So the distinction has to be made where the knowledge is. A verifier knows
whether it is configured; the middleware can only guess from exception shape.
Give the verifier layer an explicit "I am not configured / I could not reach my
provider" error, distinct from "I reject this token", and let the middleware act
on the type rather than on the absence of a stash.

Note that "not configured" should NOT block patient authentication — if no
clinician verifier exists in this deployment, no credential can be a clinician's
and refusing protects nothing. Only "configured but could not decide" should.
That asymmetry is the whole finding.
acceptance_criteria:
1. A verifier can report "not configured" and "could not reach the provider" as
   distinct outcomes from "this token is not mine".
2. A deployment with no verifier configured authenticates patients normally.
3. A deployment whose verifier is configured but failing refuses patient
   resolution rather than falling through to the resolvers.
4. Both cases are covered by tests that do not depend on whether the machine
   running them has credentials — the previous attempt was green locally and
   broken in CI for exactly that reason.
5. initialize_firebase_app()'s failure mode is inside whatever try block decides
   this, not outside it.

title: Retire the comments and code that only exist because the template doubles as a live schema
design:
The prose and the leftovers. Small, and one item is a correctness risk rather
than tidiness, so it is called out first.

COMMENTS THAT GO STALE — and one that goes stale DANGEROUSLY:

  app/auth/patient_context.py:112 (PatientContext docstring)
      "Row-level security backs this up rather than replacing it, and note it
      backs up *nothing* in a single-practice deployment ... so the route shape
      is the primary control, not the fallback."
      Once policies apply everywhere, a reader can invert this: "row-level
      security is a real backstop now, so taking a patient id from the client is
      acceptable." It is not. KEEP THE GUIDANCE, REPLACE THE JUSTIFICATION —
      route shape stays primary for ordinary defence-in-depth reasons, not
      because the backstop is missing. This edit must land WITH the change that
      makes policies universal, not after it, or the window exists in between.

  app/db/__init__.py:852-860 (the PATIENT_READABLE_TABLES preamble)
      The "IMPORTANT — where these policies do and do not apply" block describes
      a deployment shape that will no longer exist. Delete it rather than
      rewriting: with no live data outside a provisioned schema there is no
      longer a place where the policies do not apply, and a hedge about a
      configuration nobody runs invites someone to go looking for it.

  app/db/middleware.py:51 (_verify_and_stash_clinician_identity docstring)
      Argues for unconditional verification by saying that gating it on the flag
      "would silently disarm that guard on every single-tenant install — which is
      the default". The behaviour stays right; the reason cites a setting that
      will not exist. Rewrite to the durable reason: the guard has to run for
      every credential the patient seam can see.

DO NOT DELETE:

  app/db/__init__.py:1049, enable_rls_on_schema's early return for
  DEFAULT_PRACTICE_SCHEMA. It stops being load-bearing and becomes simply
  correct — the template is a template. Removing it would try to apply policies
  to the schema every tenant is cloned from.

LEFTOVERS TO REMOVE:

  app/db/provisioning.py:156          create_practice_schema(DEFAULT_PRACTICE_SCHEMA)
                                      as the live schema
  app/db/provisioning.py:~168-185     the block registering platform.practices

  app/settings.py:281                 the setting itself

  tests_integration/database/test_tenant_isolation.py:12
                                      MULTI_TENANCY_ENABLED stanzas, two of them
                                      set at import time and one in a docstring

VERIFY, DO NOT ASSUME:

  app/db/provisioning.py:326,356      `is_default_template` gates whether
                                      enable_rls_on_schema runs during
                                      provisioning. It is about building the
                                      TEMPLATE, so it probably survives intact —
                                      but confirm, because if it were about the
                                      live-schema special case instead, leaving

1. The PatientContext docstring still tells the reader not to take a patient id
   from the client, and no longer justifies it by the absence of row policies.
   This lands in the same change as universal policies, not a later one.
2. No comment in backend/app/ describes a deployment where row policies do not

3. enable_rls_on_schema still skips the template schema.
4. No test module sets MULTI_TENANCY_ENABLED.
5. The registration of the template as a live practice is gone, and a fresh

6. The role of `is_default_template` is confirmed in writing — kept with a
