title: Sign-out is unreachable when the auth session is stale
description: When the browser's auth session goes stale (expired token that failed to refresh — e.g. a tab left open overnight or a laptop waking from sleep), the app keeps rendering the signed-in shell while every API call returns 401. The UI is inert, and the sign-out control itself depends on an API round-trip, so clicking it does nothing. The user cannot self-rescue: the only ways out are manually clearing cookies or knowing to type the logout URL by hand. Observed 2026-08-18 during local testing; this failure shape is invisible in logs-first triage because nothing errors client-side.
design:
SPEC (spec pass 2026-08-18, drafting agent). Direction decided at triage; this pass verifies mechanism against the code and pins pointers. Two changes, both frontend.

PROBLEM, verified:
A stale session means the auth cookie still verifies (12h maxAge — src/lib/auth-config.ts:9,:53) while the backend rejects the bearer token, so the middleware keeps serving the signed-in shell while every API call 401s. Two client-side gaps keep the user stuck:

(a) DETECTION GAP. The centralized 401 seam already exists: apiClient boots unrecoverable 401s to /login via handleTerminalAuthLogout (src/lib/api/client.ts:315-321; getBlob mirror :425-431; the handler itself :68-85 — provider signOut({wipePersisted:true}) then window.location.assign('/login?reason=…'), re-entry-guarded at :52). But the boot fires ONLY for envelope codes in TERMINAL_AUTH_CODES (:158-163) or IDLE_TIMEOUT. A 401 whose body carries no error envelope — the backend renders a plain-detail HTTPException as FastAPI-default {"detail": …} and logs it as "auth failed: UNKNOWN" (backend/app/api_errors.py:112-124 maps missing envelope code to UNKNOWN, log line :144; e.g. the bare fallback raise in backend/app/auth/providers.py:318) — maps to errorCode "UNKNOWN_ERROR" client-side (client.ts:300) and boots NOTHING. That is exactly the observed failure signature: repeated 401 "auth failed: UNKNOWN" on /api/auth/session while the shell renders inert. (The server-side rescue only covers full RSC loads: app/(dashboard)/layout.tsx:92-98 redirects any 401 to /login?reason=…; a tab already rendered never re-runs it.)

(b) SIGN-OUT CONTROL. Header (src/components/layout/Header.tsx:24-31, wired at :85) awaits getClientAuthProvider().signOut() — for the default firebase provider that is firebaseSignOut (src/lib/auth/firebase/client.ts:284-300): SDK sign-out plus an UNBOUNDED fetch("/api/logout") at :296 (contrast syncAuthTick's /api/login fetch, which IS withTimeout-bounded at :167-175) — then a soft router.push("/login") with no reason param. Failure modes: any hang before the push leaves the click doing nothing; and if the cookie-clear fetch didn't land, the /login push bounces straight back to /dashboard (authenticated-on-/login redirect, src/lib/auth/firebase/middleware.ts:65-67).

KEY FACT — /api/logout is ALREADY reachable with no or invalid session; no public-paths change is needed. proxy.ts:15 routes it into the middleware, and next-firebase-auth-edge short-circuits loginPath/logoutPath BEFORE any token verification (node_modules/next-firebase-auth-edge/lib/next/middleware.js:110-121 -> createAuthMiddlewareResponse :71-87), answering the logout path with removeAuthCookies — a 200 {"success":true} JSON carrying the cookie-removal Set-Cookie headers (lib/next/cookies/index.js:122-132). PUBLIC_PATHS (src/lib/auth/firebase/middleware.ts:17) stays untouched. Consequence: a top-level navigation to /api/logout clears cookies but strands the user on a JSON body — so the middleware must answer NAVIGATIONS to logoutPath with a redirect to /login carrying those same cookie-removal headers.

MECHANISM:
1. Sign-out as navigation to logoutPath.
   a. Middleware (src/lib/auth/firebase/middleware.ts): when the request path is logoutPath AND the request is a top-level navigation (Sec-Fetch-Mode: navigate, with Accept: text/html as fallback), take the library's logout response and return a redirect to /login instead, COPYING its Set-Cookie removal headers verbatim — never re-deriving them (flags and enableMultipleCookies behavior, auth-config.ts:48-56, must be byte-identical; cookie flags are a closed decision). fetch() callers (firebase/client.ts:122,:143,:296 — cors mode) keep today's 200 JSON. Forward a whitelisted reason query param (only values in FORCED_LOGOUT_REASONS, src/lib/auth/forced-logout.ts:16) from the logout URL onto the /login redirect. Also handle the DEV_MODE branch (middleware.ts:49-51 currently skips everything): redirect logoutPath navigations to /login there too — no app route exists for /api/logout (frontend/app/api has only auth/ and config/), so today a dev-mode navigation would 404.
   b. Header.tsx handleSignOut: bound the provider sign-out (best-effort; withTimeout already exists, firebase/client.ts:100-106) and pass {wipePersisted:true} (same bfcache rationale as client.ts:72-79), then HARD-navigate window.location.assign(logoutPath) (imported from @/lib/auth-config) instead of router.push. One navigation clears cookies and lands on /login in the same response — nothing to bounce, nothing for a dead session to block. PROVIDER CAUTION: oidcSignOut self-navigates to the IdP end-session URL (src/lib/auth/oidc/client.ts:163) and must keep owning its navigation — gate the Header's logoutPath assign so it never stomps that redirect (e.g. only for the firebase provider, or let the provider contract own the terminal navigation).
2. Unclassifiable 401 = terminal. In apiClient's 401 branch (client.ts:315-321) and getBlob's (:425-431): for client-managed-token requests (!token), a 401 whose body yields no recognized envelope code (errorCode UNKNOWN_ERROR — i.e. not MFA_REQUIRED, not IDLE_TIMEOUT, not in TERMINAL_AUTH_CODES) is treated as terminal -> handleTerminalAuthLogout("session_expired"). The refresh-retry gate (:248-253) is NOT widened — closed decision. MFA_REQUIRED stays excluded; IDLE_TIMEOUT keeps its own reason; the re-entry guard is unchanged. This makes the inert shell self-resolving: the first 401 from any call — including the IdleTimeout session peek (src/lib/api/session.ts:24-26, fired from src/components/IdleTimeout.tsx:102) — lands on /login?reason=session_expired, which the middleware lets render (isForcedLogoutArrival, forced-logout.ts:18-20, consumed at firebase/middleware.ts:65) and where LoginScreen clears the stale client session itself (src/lib/auth/firebase/LoginScreen.tsx:52-75 -> clearStaleSession, firebase/client.ts:114-126). If routing the terminal flow itself through logoutPath (assign logoutPath?reason=… so the cookie clear and the landing are one response) proves clean with 1a's reason forwarding, prefer it; otherwise handleTerminalAuthLogout's existing /login?reason=… landing stands.

DECISIONS CLOSED — do not re-litigate: sign-out must work without a working API session; the redirect target is the existing logoutPath, not a new route; middleware auth semantics, cookie flags, and Secure-cookie behavior unchanged (the navigation answer copies the library's cookie-removal headers verbatim and changes no verification outcome on any path); do not touch token refresh logic (the :248-253 retry gate stays as-is), the login flow (LoginScreen untouched), or the public-paths list (verified unnecessary — logoutPath is handled pre-verification, pointers above).

OUT OF SCOPE: backend error envelopes (giving providers.py:318 a proper code is a separate bead — the client must tolerate unclassifiable 401s regardless, since any proxy or edge layer can also produce one); LoginScreen / forced-logout reason set; OIDC logout redesign (its self-navigation just must not regress); idle-timeout semantics; any new route.

SEQUENCING: siblings PABLO-bhz and PABLO-mep live in settings/calendar/availability surfaces (dashboard settings page, src/components/settings/, src/components/calendar/, scheduling engine) — checked against this bead's file set below: ZERO overlap, safe to run in parallel with both.

FILES: src/components/layout/Header.tsx, src/lib/api/client.ts, src/lib/auth/firebase/middleware.ts, src/lib/auth/firebase/client.ts (only if the timeout bound / navigation ownership lands there), plus tests: src/lib/api/__tests__/client.test.ts, new src/components/layout/__tests__/Header.test.tsx, new middleware coverage (see acceptance).

DONE SIGNAL: the unclassifiable-401 test is red on current main and green with the change (state red-then-green in the PR body); frontend vitest + lint green; exactly one PR.
acceptance_criteria:
Runner: vitest (frontend/package.json:11 "test": "vitest", vitest ^4.1.10 at :66; happy-dom environment, vitest.config.ts:8).

1. RED-THEN-GREEN, unclassifiable 401: extend the existing "apiClient terminal-auth handling" suite (src/lib/api/__tests__/client.test.ts, describe :62; err401 envelope helper :21) with a 401 whose JSON body is FastAPI-default {"detail": "..."} (NO error.code envelope): on a client-managed request it calls provider signOut({wipePersisted:true}) and navigates to the session_expired landing (mirror the TOKEN_REVOKED assertions at :139-152). This test must FAIL on current main. Also assert: a bare-body 401 with a caller-supplied token does NOT boot (pattern :128-137); MFA_REQUIRED still does not boot (existing :118 stays green); a burst of bare-body 401s fires exactly one boot (pattern :139-152). Mirror the bare-body case in the getBlob describe (:154).
2. NEW src/components/layout/__tests__/Header.test.tsx (provider-mock pattern: src/components/__tests__/IdleTimeout.test.tsx:12-42): clicking "Sign out" (a) calls the provider signOut; (b) hard-navigates to "/api/logout" (assert on a stubbed window.location.assign); (c) still navigates when signOut rejects; (d) still navigates when signOut never settles (fake timers advanced past the bound). (c) and (d) pin the bug: today the handler ends in router.push and (d) never navigates at all.
3. Middleware logout-navigation behavior: a request for /api/logout with Sec-Fetch-Mode: navigate yields a redirect to /login whose response carries the library's cookie-removal Set-Cookie headers unchanged (including the multiple-cookie shape, auth-config.ts:56); a cors-mode request still gets today's 200 JSON; a whitelisted reason param is forwarded onto /login, any other value dropped. Test as src/lib/auth/firebase/__tests__/middleware.test.ts if the edge runtime mocks are workable in vitest; otherwise extract the navigation-answer into a pure helper, unit-test THAT, and keep it the middleware's single code path (precedent: src/lib/auth/__tests__/public-paths.test.ts tests the extracted helper).
4. No regressions: existing client.test.ts terminal-auth cases, src/components/__tests__/IdleTimeout.test.tsx (idle boot unchanged), and src/lib/auth/firebase/__tests__/client.test.ts stay green. No diff to PUBLIC_PATHS (src/lib/auth/firebase/middleware.ts:17), cookieSerializeOptions (src/lib/auth-config.ts:48-54), the refresh-retry gate (src/lib/api/client.ts:248-253), or src/lib/auth/oidc/client.ts.
5. Manual verification recorded in the PR body: with a healthy signed-in session, sign-out lands on /login signed out (normal path unchanged); with a stale session (expired token that cannot refresh), both the sign-out click and the next API 401 land on /login with session cookies cleared.
6. Exactly one PR; frontend vitest + lint green.
notes: LANE: never-dispatch, Kurt-paired; no llama-ok — trigger walk (all seven): (1) PHI/HIPAA: NO — auth-session navigation and 401 classification; no patient data, no new logging. (2) Money/entitlement: NO — no money movement; sign-out only removes access artifacts (cookies), grants nothing. (3) Prod infra/destructive ops: NO — frontend code only; no migrations, no infra, no data deletion. (4) Auth design: FIRES — the closed decisions pin auth SEMANTICS as unchanged (no verification-outcome, cookie-flag, or public-paths change; the logout path is already handled pre-verification per next-firebase-auth-edge middleware.js:110-121), and the 401-widening is fail-toward-signed-out, so authenticated reach never grows — but the diff necessarily lands INSIDE the route-protection middleware (src/lib/auth/firebase/middleware.ts) and the terminal-session classification (src/lib/api/client.ts:315-321), where a wrong Set-Cookie copy or matcher condition is an auth-surface incident despite unchanged intended semantics. Supervised implementation. (5) Vendor dashboards: NO — none involved. (6) Patent-adjacent (assessed in full; OSS is world-readable): NO — a sign-out/401-redirect fix touches no claim territory (no learning loop, no scoring, no placeholder construct, no runtime governance). (7) Outbound communication: NO — nothing is sent to anyone. Overall: sole firing trigger is the auth surface (4) — spec-ready applied; llama-ok deliberately NOT applied (dispatch authorization is a separate gate and not the drafting agent's to give).

title: Appointment dialog can only book the first 20 patients
description:
## Problem

`AppointmentModal.tsx` calls `usePatientList()` with no params. The backend default is `page_size=20` (`backend/app/routes/patients.py`), so the New appointment dialog's patient `Select` renders only the first 20 patients — `patients.map()` over one unpaginated page, with no search input.

Patients sort by `last_name, first_name`, so which 20 you get is alphabetical. A clinician with more than 20 patients simply cannot book an appointment for anyone outside that window: the option is not in the DOM, and there is no way to search for it from the dialog.

## Why it matters

21+ patients is an ordinary caseload for an established practice. For those users the calendar's primary create path is broken for most of their roster, with no workaround and no error message — the patient just isn't in the list.

## Related

PABLO-y93 fixed exactly this class of bug for the patient LIST (page_size=100 + 'showing N of M'), but the appointment dialog was not part of that change and still has the original default.
design:
## DECISIONS CLOSED — do not re-litigate

**Build the searchable typeahead. Do not simply raise page_size.** `GET /api/patients` already accepts a `search` param; query it server-side as the user types so roster size stops mattering. Raising `page_size` to 100 only moves the ceiling (the endpoint caps at 100) and would not satisfy the acceptance criteria, which require a practice above 100 patients to work.

**Debounce input ~250ms** and keep the currently-selected patient rendered even when it falls outside the active result set, so an edit-existing-appointment open does not blank the field.

**Keep the empty query working:** with no text typed, show the first page as today, so the common small-practice case is unchanged and needs no typing.

## Where

- `frontend/src/components/calendar/AppointmentModal.tsx` — the patient control is a plain shadcn `Select` today (`patients.map()` over `usePatientList()`); swap it for a `Command`/combobox that accepts input.
- `frontend/src/hooks/usePatients.ts` — `usePatientList` already takes params; pass `search` through. Do not change its signature for other callers.

## Do NOT touch

- `PatientTable.tsx` and the patient-list pagination — that surface was already fixed under PABLO-y93 and is out of scope here. Changing it widens the diff into a file this bead does not own.
- The backend route, its response model, or the appointment POST payload. This is a frontend-only change; the API already has everything needed.

## Tests

`frontend/src/components/calendar/__tests__/AppointmentModal.test.tsx` — add a case for selecting a patient that is NOT in the first page of results (i.e. only reachable via search).
acceptance_criteria:
- A practice with more than 100 patients can find and book any patient from the New appointment dialog.
- Selecting a patient still books correctly (POST /api/appointments unchanged).
- The dialog's existing unit tests pass, with a new case covering a patient outside the first page.
- No change to the appointment payload or backend route signature.
notes:
EVIDENCE STRENGTHENED 2026-08-15: this is not only a UX ceiling, it is actively breaking the deployed e2e gate, and the breakage is progressive rather than a clean pass/fail.

Measured against the shared test tenant: soft-deleting every patient made the scheduling e2e pass immediately; an hour of runs re-accumulated patients (~2 per run) and the same spec degraded in lockstep with the count — passed at 0 active patients, intermittent around 20-30 (a new patient sometimes still fell inside the first page, because patients sort by last_name,first_name so inclusion is alphabetical luck), and failed on every run at 44.

The user-visible consequence at >20 patients is worse than 'cannot find the patient': the picker silently offers no matching option, and an appointment can end up booked against the wrong patient or none at all rather than failing loudly. That is the part worth fixing carefully.

Practical note for whoever takes this: raising page_size is not enough even as a stopgap, because the ceiling just moves to 100 and the same silent-wrong-selection behaviour returns. The search-backed typeahead in the design section removes the ceiling entirely.

title: Give the free-slots route its first consumer: a 'find a time' affordance in the appointment flow
description:
Nothing calls GET /api/availability/slots. The settings surface added recently
lets a therapist author availability rules, and the engine evaluates them
correctly, but no part of the product ever asks the engine what is free - so a
therapist configures rules and sees no effect anywhere.

Add a "find a time" affordance to the appointment creation flow that pulls real
open slots for a date instead of asking the user to type a time and hope.
design:
FRONTEND, plus whatever thin client code the call needs.

  frontend/src/lib/api/availability.ts   - today exports only the four rules
                                           CRUD calls; add the free-slots read
  frontend/src/hooks/useAvailability.ts  - follow the existing hook pattern
  the appointment create surface         - add the affordance alongside the
                                           existing manual time entry, do not
                                           replace it

TWO EMPTY STATES, RENDERED DIFFERENTLY. This is the whole reason the sibling
bead about unconfigured-vs-no-openings exists: "you have not set up your
availability yet" is an onboarding prompt pointing at the settings surface,
and "no openings that day" is a real answer. Never render the first as the
second. Depends on that distinction being available from the engine.

KEEP MANUAL ENTRY. A therapist must still be able to book a time the rules do
not offer - overriding your own availability is a normal thing to do. This
affordance is a convenience, not a gate.

Mirror the test style of the settings surface's existing component tests.
acceptance_criteria:
1. The appointment create flow can list real open slots for a chosen date,
   sourced from the free-slots route.
2. Selecting a slot fills the appointment time; manual entry still works and
   is not gated by the rules.
3. "Not configured" and "no openings" render as visibly different states, and
   the first links to the availability settings surface.
4. Component tests cover: slots listed, slot selected, no openings, not
   configured.

title: Refuse double-booking on the appointment write path — create, update and recurring
design:
DOUBLE-BOOKING IS CURRENTLY ACCEPTED WITH A 201. Two appointments for the same
clinician at the same time are both created. Rules are policy; collisions are
physics, and this bead is only about the physics.

PROVEN 2026-08-02, not inferred:
  backend/app/routes/scheduling.py:193  create_appointment
    -> backend/app/scheduling_engine/services/scheduling.py:42
  which validates ONLY (lines 53-62): patient_id non-empty; start_at and end_at
  present; duration_minutes is a positive int. Then it constructs the
  Appointment and calls repo.create (:92). There is no overlap check, no
  end > start check, no past-date check. SchedulingService never imports
  AvailabilityEngine.
  AppointmentConflictError already exists at
  backend/app/scheduling_engine/exceptions.py:25 and is raised NOWHERE - the
  only reference in the repo is its own definition.

DO NOT REUSE check_conflicts FOR THIS. AvailabilityEngine.check_conflicts
(backend/app/scheduling_engine/services/availability.py:48) is RULES-ONLY: it
iterates the user's rules and returns [] when there are none, so a user with no
rules gets an empty conflict list for a time that exactly double-books. Wiring
it in and calling this bead done would leave the default case broken. Appointment
subtraction lives only in get_free_slots (:79-85), a different method with a
different signature. Use the repository primitive instead.

DEPENDS ON the list_overlapping primitive bead. Do not hand-roll a second
overlap predicate here.

WHERE TO ENFORCE - service layer, not the route. The route-level shortcut leaves
two holes: backend/app/services/ical_sync_service.py:321 writes straight to the
repo, and there is more than one write route. Put it in SchedulingService so
every caller inherits it.

  1. SchedulingService.__init__ (services/scheduling.py:39) currently takes only
     appointment_repo. Keep the signature backward-compatible for the many
     tests that construct SchedulingService(repo) directly.
  2. create_appointment (:42): after the existing validation, before constructing
     the Appointment, ask the repo for overlaps and raise
     AppointmentConflictError when any are returned.
  3. update_appointment (:105): the mutable allow-list includes start_at, end_at
     and duration_minutes (:114-129), so a legal booking can currently be MOVED
     on top of another one. Check there too, passing
     exclude_appointment_id=appointment_id so an appointment never collides with
     itself. CAREFUL: update_appointment is also called internally at
     routes/scheduling.py:414 to attach session_id during start-session. That
     call passes no times. Only run the check when a time field is actually

title: Extract the shared sign-in credential block used by /login and /native-auth
description:
The web sign-in screen and the desktop-app sign-in handoff now carry near-identical credential blocks: Google button, passkey button + recovery-code link, email/password form, forgot-password, sign-up toggle, MFA challenge and verify-email steps. The two differ only in what happens after a credential resolves — one seeds a session cookie and routes to the dashboard, the other exchanges for a one-time code and hands back to the native app.

Every new factor has to be added twice, and the passkey gap on the handoff page (PABLO-bqz) is exactly what that costs: passkeys shipped on one surface and silently missed the other.

Proposal: extract a presentational credential block that takes an onCredential(credential, method) callback plus a few flags (allow sign-up, show 'last used' hints), and have both screens render it with their own completion handler. Keep the post-credential behaviour in each screen — that's the real difference.

Follow-up to PABLO-bqz.
design:
The web sign-in screen (`frontend/src/lib/auth/firebase/LoginScreen.tsx`) and the
desktop-app sign-in handoff (`frontend/src/lib/auth/firebase/NativeAuthScreen.tsx`)
carry near-identical credential blocks. They differ only in what happens AFTER a
credential resolves: LoginScreen seeds a session cookie and routes to /dashboard;
NativeAuthScreen exchanges the ID token for a one-time code and hands back to the
native app's redirect_uri.

That duplication has already cost us once — passkeys shipped on /login and silently
missed /native-auth (PABLO-bqz).

SEAM
Add `frontend/src/components/auth/CredentialBlock.tsx`, a presentational component
that owns credential acquisition and NOTHING about what follows. Export it from
`frontend/src/components/auth/index.ts`.

    type AuthMethod = "google" | "email" | "passkey"

    interface CredentialBlockProps {
      // Called exactly once, when a credential is fully resolved — including
      // after an MFA challenge or a recovery-code redemption. The host decides
      // what happens next. May be async; the block stays in its loading state
      // until it settles.
      onCredential: (credential: UserCredential, method: AuthMethod) => Promise<void>
      email: string
      onEmailChange: (email: string) => void
      // Show the "Create account" toggle and the sign-up form (default true).
      allowSignUp?: boolean
      // Show the "Last used" pill on the method this device last used (default false).
      showLastUsed?: boolean
      // Show the "Having trouble signing in?" storage-reset link (default false).
      showAuthReset?: boolean
      // Host-supplied message rendered in the block's error slot (e.g. the
      // forced-logout notice). The block may overwrite it with its own errors.
      notice?: string
    }

The block owns these internal steps and renders each in place of the sign-in form:
`sign-in` | `mfa` | `recovery-code` | `verify-email`. It keeps the existing
`MfaChallengeScreen`, `RecoveryCodeScreen` and `VerifyEmailScreen` components as-is —
this is a move, not a redesign.

It also owns: the Google button, the passkey button + "Lost your passkey?" link
(gated on `useConfig().passkeysEnabled && browserSupportsWebAuthn()`, resolved in a
post-mount effect to avoid an SSR mismatch), the email/password form, forgot-password,
the sign-up toggle, the `pablo:lastAuthMethod` localStorage hint, and the Terms /
Privacy footer text.

Take the RICHER of the two implementations wherever they differ. Specifically:
  - VerifyEmailScreen: LoginScreen's version (resend button + its own error state)
    wins over NativeAuthScreen's bare one.
  - Password autoComplete, minLength (15 on sign-up) and placeholder copy: LoginScreen's.
  - Layout order: Google, then passkey, then divider, then the email form — LoginScreen's
    order, applied to both.

WHAT STAYS IN EACH HOST
LoginScreen keeps: the brand panel + ThemeSwitcher, the mobile logo header, the
already-authenticated -> /dashboard effect, the forced-logout `?reason=` handling
(passed down via `notice`), `installAuthRecovery` / `consumeRecoveryNotice`, the
`?setup=` token prefill, and `finishLogin` (POST /api/login, then route to /dashboard).
It renders `<CredentialBlock showLastUsed showAuthReset ... />`.

NativeAuthScreen keeps: `redirect_uri` + `state` validation and its "Invalid Request"
screen, the "Sign-in complete" redirecting screen, and `redirectToApp` — including the
403 MFA_REQUIRED bounce to /mfa-enrollment. It renders
`<CredentialBlock allowSignUp ... />` with `onCredential={(c) => redirectToApp(c.user)}`.

CONSTRAINTS
- No behaviour change on either surface. This is a pure extraction; a user should
  not be able to tell the difference.
- Do not touch the backend, the OIDC surfaces, or any of the Auth* primitives in
  `frontend/src/components/auth/`.
- `AuthMethod` and the `pablo:lastAuthMethod` key move into CredentialBlock; nothing
  else should still reference them.
acceptance_criteria:
1. `frontend/src/components/auth/CredentialBlock.tsx` exists, is exported from
   `frontend/src/components/auth/index.ts`, and neither LoginScreen.tsx nor
   NativeAuthScreen.tsx still contains its own Google button, passkey button,
   email/password form, MFA-resolver branch, or verify-email branch. Both files
   get materially shorter.

2. New vitest component tests at
   `frontend/src/components/auth/__tests__/CredentialBlock.test.tsx` (mock
   `firebase/auth`, `@/lib/config`, `@/lib/api/passkey` and `@simplewebauthn/browser`
   the way `frontend/src/lib/auth/firebase/__tests__/client.test.ts` mocks its
   dependencies). They assert:
   a. With passkeysEnabled true and WebAuthn supported, a "Sign in with a passkey"
      button and a "Lost your passkey? Use a recovery code" link render.
   b. With passkeysEnabled false, neither renders.
   c. A successful email/password sign-in calls `onCredential` exactly once with
      method "email".
   d. A successful passkey ceremony calls `onCredential` exactly once with method

   e. `allowSignUp={false}` hides the "Create account" toggle.

3. `cd frontend && npx tsc --noEmit` exits clean.

title: Idle session can be silently revived via refresh-token swap
description:
The server-side idle timeout (backend/app/auth/idle_session.py, wired via auth/service.py::enforce_idle_session) should 401 any request whose session has been inactive past settings.idle_timeout_seconds, forcing re-auth. Two independent bugs let an idle session silently re-arm itself.

Bug A — get_current_user_no_mfa skips the idle check entirely. It verifies the Firebase token and resolves the user but never calls idle_session.check_and_touch, so every endpoint depending on it (including GET /api/users/me/status, the SPA cold-load call) bypasses the idle gate. The _no_mfa dependency exists for pre-MFA-enrollment flows; the idle check only reads uid/auth_time and has no MFA dependency, so _no_mfa should not also mean _no_idle.

Bug B — 'marker missing' is conflated with 'first request of a new session'. check_and_touch has three branches: marker+activity present -> refresh activity; marker present, activity absent -> burn marker + 401 IDLE_TIMEOUT; marker absent -> seed both keys + allow (treated as fresh sign-in). The third branch cannot distinguish a brand-new sign-in from a marker that was burned minutes ago on idle-out. Refresh-token swaps reuse the same auth_time, so a previously-timed-out session resurrects on the next request from any other live session.

Fix:
- Bug A: call idle_session.check_and_touch(decoded_token) inside get_current_user_no_mfa, after verify_firebase_token and before _resolve_user. Use a lazy import, mirroring enforce_idle_session.
- Bug B: add a tombstone key idle:revoked:{uid}:{auth_time} with TTL = _SESSION_MARKER_TTL_SECONDS. Before the marker check, redis.exists(revoked_key) -> if present, raise 401 IDLE_TIMEOUT immediately without touching marker/activity. When the burn-marker branch fires, SET the tombstone in the same pipeline as the marker delete so both land atomically. Tombstone TTL matches marker TTL because the only way a timed-out auth_time returns is via the same refresh token, itself capped by Firebase's inactivity window.

Tests (backend/tests/test_idle_session.py):
1. Tombstone set on idle expiry — extend the burn-marker test to assert redis.exists(revoked key) and TTL ~ _SESSION_MARKER_TTL_SECONDS.
2. Tombstone short-circuits later requests — pre-seed the revoked key with no marker/activity, assert 401 IDLE_TIMEOUT and that marker/activity are NOT created (regression for Bug B).
3. No-MFA path enforces idle — call get_current_user_no_mfa with Redis state matching 'marker present, activity expired', assert 401 IDLE_TIMEOUT (regression for Bug A).

Acceptance: make check passes (lint + mypy + pytest); the three tests above are present and passing.

title: New-chat first message lost — panel remounts on lazy conversation create
description:
## Symptom (user-reproduced)

Open a new chat (click "New", or just start typing on a brand-new patient), type the FIRST message, submit → the chat window flashes "Loading conversation…", the message is LOST, and the panel resets. Typing again works. Intermittent-feeling but deterministic given the code path.

## Root cause

`frontend/src/components/chat/ChatPanelWithHistory.tsx:95` keys the ChatPanel on the conversation id:

    key={`${activeConversationId ?? "new"}::${panelMountId}`}

The first send lazily creates the conversation: `ChatPanel.performSend` calls `onConversationCreated(id)` (`ChatPanel.tsx:239`) BEFORE it runs `streamChatMessages` (`ChatPanel.tsx:257`). The parent handler then sets `activeConversationId = id` (`ChatPanelWithHistory.tsx:107`), which changes the key from `new::N` to `<id>::N`. React unmounts the in-flight panel and mounts a fresh one with `conversationId={id}` → `hydrating = Boolean(initialConversationId) = true` → renders "Loading conversation…" (`ChatPanel.tsx:445`) and runs the hydrate effect, which `getConversation`s the just-created, still-EMPTY conversation. The optimistic user/assistant bubbles and the SSE stream belonged to the now-unmounted instance → first message + its response are lost. Second attempt works because `activeConversationId` is already set, so no key change, no remount.

"Brand-new patient, type without clicking New" is the same path: the panel starts at `conversationId=null`, first send creates → remount → loss.

## Fix

Decouple the panel's React `key` (mount identity) from `activeConversationId`:
- Key the ChatPanel on `panelMountId` ONLY. It is already bumped by the user-driven `handleSelect` / `handleNew` — the only moments a true remount is desired.
- `onConversationCreated` should update sidebar highlight (`activeConversationId`) + `listVersion`, but NOT anything in the mount key.
- Guard the hydrate path too: the `conversationId` prop passed to ChatPanel must not flip undefined→id on the LIVE instance, or the `[initialConversationId]` effect (`ChatPanel.tsx:130-165`) re-fires and clobbers in-flight messages via the prop path instead of the key path. Cleanest: track a separate `mountedConversationId` (set only by select/new) for the hydrate prop + key, leaving `activeConversationId` purely for sidebar highlighting.

## Why CI never caught it

The chat E2E (pablo-saas THERAPY-hd4h) is API-only — it hits `/api/chat/*` directly with no browser, so a React remount race is invisible to it. THERAPY-z3a5 (the known flaky chat E2E) is a DIFFERENT race (empty assistant message on SSE timeout in save-as-note), not this.

## Acceptance

- [ ] First message in a new chat persists and streams a response — no "Loading conversation…" flash, no loss
- [ ] Same for "type on brand-new patient without clicking New"
- [ ] Switching to an existing conversation via the sidebar still remounts cleanly (no stale stream)
- [ ] Browser-level regression test added (see related E2E coverage note) — API-only won't catch this
close_reason: Decoupled ChatPanel mount key/hydrate prop from sidebar-highlight state (mountedConversationId vs activeConversationId). Added jsdom+RTL regression test (verified fail-on-bug). Closing with the PR.

title: Document download 401s — <a href> can't send bearer token
description: ## Symptom Clicking a document in the patient Documents list to download it returns **401 (not authenticated)**. No document can be downloaded. ## Root cause \`frontend/src/components/patients/PatientDocuments.tsx:250\` renders the download as a plain anchor: \`\`\`tsx Download \`\`\` which points at \`/api/documents/{id}/file\` (\`frontend/src/lib/api/patientDocuments.ts:107\`). That backend route (\`backend/app/routes/patient_documents.py:405\`, \`download_document_file\`) is gated by \`Depends(require_baa_acceptance)\` — it needs the Firebase **bearer token** in the \`Authorization\` header. A raw \`\` navigation only sends cookies, never custom headers, and Pablo auth is bearer-token (not cookie-session). So the request arrives unauthenticated and 401s before the route can mint the signed GCS URL and 302 to it. The signed-URL design implicitly assumed the browser would hit \`/file\` authenticated; with header-based auth, link navigation can't. ## Fix options 1. **Return the signed URL as JSON, open it client-side (recommended).** Add/adjust the route to return \`{ url: }\` with 200 (or keep the 302 and add a JSON sibling). Frontend calls it through the authenticated fetch client (bearer token attached), then \`window.open(url)\` / \`location.assign(url)\` to the GCS signed URL directly. The signed URL itself needs no auth header — GCS authorizes via the signature — so this cleanly separates app-auth from object-auth. Audit event still fires server-side when the URL is minted. 2. Fetch \`/file\` with \`redirect: \"manual\"\`, read the \`Location\` header, then navigate. Riskier: forwarding the Authorization header into a cross-origin GCS redirect can make GCS reject the request; manual redirect handling across origins is fiddly. 3. Cookie-session auth for this one endpoint — rejected, diverges from the app's bearer-token model. Recommend option 1. ## Relationship to patient-ux-refactor epic The planned \`DocumentViewerSheet\` (design/patient-ux-refactor.md, Phase 1) loads the same signed-URL path to render PDFs/images inline. It MUST use the authenticated-fetch-then-open pattern from option 1, not a raw URL. **This bead is effectively a prerequisite for the viewer bead** — fix the download contract first, then the viewer reuses it. ## Acceptance - [ ] Clicking Download on a document returns the file, not a 401 - [ ] Works for all three categories (chart, therapist_private, psychotherapy_notes) - [ ] The patient-document-access audit event still fires server-side - [ ] Frontend obtains the signed URL via the authenticated API client (bearer token), then navigates to GCS - [ ] No token ever placed in a URL/query string

title: Per-tenant alembic fan-out is not thread-safe — default to serial
description:
`backend/app/db/migrate_tenants.fan_out` parallelizes `command.upgrade` calls across N tenant schemas using a ThreadPoolExecutor (default 8 workers). Alembic's EnvironmentContext is a process-global singleton, so concurrent calls into `command.upgrade` race on it — the second thread to call `context.configure` corrupts the first's state.

Symptom: no-op fan-out runs (every tenant already at head) pass cleanly, hiding the bug indefinitely. The first multi-tenant DDL after the parallelism was enabled fails on every tenant at once — observed today against ~19 schemas during the patient_documents OCR column migration. Serializing with `PABLO_MIGRATE_MAX_WORKERS=1` makes it pass.

Compounding the diagnosis: alembic's env.py calls `fileConfig()` at import, which wipes the root logger's handlers each time it runs. The per-tenant `logger.info`/`logger.exception` output never made it to Cloud Logging — only stdout `print()` calls did. Whatever path eventually re-enables parallelism should also fix this so the next failure is diagnosable on first occurrence.

Default flipped to 1 in the meantime. To re-enable parallelism safely, options worth exploring:
- Subprocess-per-tenant (each child has its own EnvironmentContext)
- Run alembic offline (`--sql`) per tenant and apply DDL ourselves
- Replace alembic at the fan-out layer with a thinner runner that drives migration scripts directly without context globals

Acceptance: fan-out can run with > 1 worker against multiple tenants with real DDL without context corruption. Per-tenant tracebacks surface in Cloud Logging on failure.

title: A claim adjudicated by webhook never bills the client
description:
A claim adjudicated through the clearinghouse webhook never bills the client.

`app/claims/fanout.py::_apply_remittance` calls `apply_posting` with no
`charges`, so the posting moves the claim and records the receipt but writes
no `patient_resp` row. The periodic pass is what passes `charges` — and it
reads `list_by_state(AWAITING_STATES)`, where AWAITING_STATES is
`("submitted", "ch_accepted", "payer_accepted", "stalled")`. The webhook has
already moved the claim to `partial` or `paid`, so it is never read again.

Net effect: the fast path posts the payer's money and silently drops the
client's share. The slow path would write it, and never gets the chance.

Found by the e2e added in pablo#1106 — "an ordinary remittance bills the
client without asking anybody" fails because no ledger row ever appears. The
hold half of that spec passes, so this is specifically the ordinary,
everything-agrees case that is broken.

Scope note: this predates the remittance-hold work. The ledger write itself
was only wired into the periodic pass recently (pablo#1092); before that
neither path wrote the row, so nothing regressed — this is the second half
of the same gap.
design: Give the webhook path a charge ledger, the same way the periodic pass has one: _pipeline_for in fanout.py builds the ClaimPipeline, so the charge repository can be constructed on the same tenant session and passed through apply_remittance to apply_posting. Alternative worth weighing first: have the periodic pass also re-read recently-adjudicated claims, which fixes this and any other post-adjudication work the webhook skips — but it re-opens the idempotency question the receipt ledger currently answers per event key. Whichever way, the e2e that is marked fixme in pablo#1106 is the acceptance test: un-mark it.
acceptance_criteria: 1. A remittance delivered by webhook writes the client's patient_resp ledger row. 2. The row is written once, not once per delivery. 3. A remittance that contradicts itself still writes no row and still raises a hold. 4. The e2e 'an ordinary remittance bills the client without asking anybody' is un-fixmed and passes. 5. make check and the compose e2e green.

title: The unit suite cannot finish locally: a PDF extraction test hangs forever
description:
`tests/test_note_import_service.py::test_extract_real_sample_pdf` never
returns on a developer Mac. The process sits at 0% CPU with ~44MB RSS and no
open network sockets, so it is blocked rather than working, and it blocks
forever — there is no per-test timeout in this suite to cut it short.

The consequence is that `make check` cannot complete locally. Anyone running
the full suite on a Mac watches it stall silently at roughly 45% and either
waits indefinitely or kills it, and a killed run tells you nothing about
whether your change was green.

Reproduced 2026-09-11 on clean `main` (6d75beca), in isolation:

    cd backend && python -m pytest -o addopts="" -q -p no:randomly \
      tests/test_note_import_service.py
    # 22 tests pass, then stops at test_extract_real_sample_pdf

Also reproduced twice inside a full-suite run, on two different branches and
two different orderings — which is how it was first noticed, and why it was
initially mistaken for a regression in the branch under test.
design:
Two separate things to fix, and the second matters more than the first.

1. THE HANG ITSELF. The test extracts text from a real sample PDF, so the
   suspects are the extraction backend blocking on something it expects to
   find locally — an OCR binary, a model file, a font cache — rather than
   failing fast when it is absent. Find what it blocks on before deciding
   whether the fix is to make the dependency explicit, skip the test when
   the dependency is missing, or stop shelling out at all. A `skip` with no
   diagnosis just moves the silence.

   Worth checking whether CI passes this test, and if so what CI has that a
   laptop does not. If CI passes and laptops hang, the coverage is real but
   only reachable in one place, which is its own problem.

2. NO PER-TEST TIMEOUT. This is the part that turned a slow test into a
   half-hour diagnosis. The suite has no `pytest-timeout`, so a blocked
   test is indistinguishable from a slow one and the run never ends. Add
   `pytest-timeout` with a generous default (60s, say) in the pytest config
   so a future hang fails with a traceback naming the test.

   `-o faulthandler_timeout=N` is NOT a substitute: it dumps a traceback but
   does not fail or kill the test, so the run still hangs. That was tried
   here first and produced nothing.

Found while building the remittance-hold work (PABLO-4aaq / PABLO-4ni2);
unrelated to it, and filed separately so it is not carried by a claims PR.
acceptance_criteria: 1. tests/test_note_import_service.py completes on a developer Mac without hanging. 2. The suite carries a per-test timeout so a future hang fails loudly instead of stalling. 3. make check completes locally.

title: e2e: a client books, reschedules and cancels through the portal in a browser
design: The patient self-booking routes have 39 integration tests against a real Postgres (backend/tests_integration/api/test_patient_booking_routes.py: practice gate, request vs auto mode, holds, cross-patient RLS, notice and horizon windows, a smuggled patient id) and no browser test at all. Write one Playwright spec in frontend/e2e/specs/ that drives the portal the way a client would, on the compose stack (docs/design/e2e-harness.md). Mirror the shape of frontend/e2e/specs/public-booking.spec.ts: serial tests sharing one fixture, response-field allowlists on every anonymous or patient-scoped payload, and the mail fixture (e2e/fixtures/mail.ts) for any email the flow sends. SETUP via fixtures in e2e/fixtures/scenarios.ts: a practice with working hours (giveWorkingHours), a self-bookable appointment type (giveBookableType), the practice switch on (letNewClientsSelfBook / self_book_existing as the flow needs), a patient with a portal identity (add a givePortalPatient helper if none exists; check e2e/fixtures/auth.ts for how a patient principal signs in against the auth emulator). TESTS, in order: (1) the client sees only their own upcoming appointments; (2) the client books a free slot and it lands PENDING in request mode and CONFIRMED in auto mode, on the clinician's calendar, with the type's duration; (3) a slot another client holds is absent from the list and refused on POST; (4) reschedule moves the appointment and frees the old slot; (5) cancel inside and outside the cutoff behaves per policy. Keep every assertion on what the browser shows plus one API read-back per step; never assert on internal ids. OUT OF SCOPE: the clinician-side portal settings page; SMS; anything behind a flag the compose stack does not set (say so in a comment if a step needs one).
acceptance_criteria: 1. frontend/e2e/specs/patient-portal-booking.spec.ts exists and passes on the compose stack (make e2e-up && make e2e). 2. It covers view, book (both modes), held-slot refusal, reschedule and cancel, each as its own test in one serial describe. 3. Every patient-facing payload it reads is checked against a field allowlist, mirroring public-booking.spec.ts. 4. Fixtures it needs live in e2e/fixtures/scenarios.ts, not inline in the spec. 5. e2e typecheck and eslint green; the spec is registered wherever the harness lists specs, if it does.

title: Seed a default consultation appointment type so a new practice starts with something bookable
design:
Defaults are the product: most solo practices never open a settings page, so what a brand-new practice gets with zero configuration matters more than what the settings page can express. Today a new practice has no appointment types and no availability rules, so every scheduling capability is dark until someone goes looking.

Seed ONE appointment type at practice provisioning: "Free consultation", 15 minutes, audience "new", offerable true, no fee. It is the shape the profession already uses to screen a prospective client, it is the one appointment that is genuinely safe to auto-book (short, low-commitment, capped), and it makes "what can a new client book?" a confirmation rather than a decision.

SELF_BOOKABLE STAYS FALSE ON THE SEED. Seeding the type is a convenience; turning on public self-booking is a decision, and every gate in scheduling_policy deliberately defaults closed so that a practice upgrading into this code cannot discover that patients can suddenly book it. The seed makes the choice EASY, it does not make it FOR them.

Deletable and editable like any other type. A practice that deletes it must not have it reappear on next provisioning-touch or restart.

WHERE THE ROW IS CREATED (decided, do not guess). Appointment types live in backend/app/repositories/postgres/appointment_type.py, with the table in backend/app/db/models.py and captured in backend/app/db/tenant_template.sql. Provisioning applies the TENANT TEMPLATE, so there are two candidate homes for a seeded ROW: (a) an INSERT in tenant_template.sql, which is a captured artifact where a data INSERT beside DDL is easy to lose on the next regen; (b) code in provisioning.py after the template is applied, which is explicit, testable, and created by the same path that creates the schema. Use (b), and say so in the PR.

DO NOT retro-seed existing practices, and do not add a startup path that recreates the row. A deleted seed staying deleted is the criterion most likely to be broken by an over-eager "ensure defaults exist on boot" helper. There must be no such helper.

Commit and PR text: plain and human-toned; no tracker ids.
acceptance_criteria: 1. A newly provisioned practice has exactly one appointment type: Free consultation, 15 minutes, audience new, offerable true, self_bookable FALSE, no fee. 2. It is fully editable and deletable. 3. Deleting it is durable: no later provisioning or startup path recreates it, covered by a test. 4. Existing practices are not retro-seeded. 5. Where a settings surface asks which type a new client may book, it pre-fills from this type when present and degrades gracefully when it has been deleted; if no such surface exists yet, say so in the PR. 6. make check green.

title: Teach the availability parser about appointment types, weekly caps and exclusivity
design:
The availability parser (backend/app/services/availability_parse_service.py) is the surface a practice actually uses to state its rules: a therapist is far likelier to type "only two intakes a week, Tuesdays and Thursdays" than to assemble rules in a form. Its rule vocabulary is closed (rule_type + params + enforcement, validated per type) and carries NO appointment-type concept: appointment_type does not appear in the parser at all. So the type-scoping work adds capabilities the primary input surface cannot express. Without this change a practice can only reach them through the API, and the parser will either drop the intake half of the sentence or refuse it.

SCOPE
- Teach the parser appointment types: resolve a named type from the sentence ("intakes", "consultations") against the practice's OWN AppointmentType rows, and bind appointment_type_id on the emitted rule. Never invent a type that does not exist: an unresolvable name is a clarification, not a guess.
- Extend the vocabulary to MAX_PER_WEEK, with the same params validator shape as max_per_day.
- Teach it the exclusivity flag, so "Tuesday afternoons are for intakes only" produces a narrowed rule with allow_other_types false rather than a plain narrowing.
- Keep the existing enforcement default: rules parse as "hard" unless the sentence clearly says otherwise, per the current prompt.

AMBIGUITY IS THE HARD PART, not extraction. "Two intakes a week on Tuesdays" is one rule or two depending on reading, and "I only do intakes on Tuesdays" may mean intakes are restricted to Tuesdays, or that Tuesdays are for intakes only, which are DIFFERENT rules (a narrowing versus an exclusivity). The parser must not silently pick. Where the reading changes what gets stored, return the confidence signal the schema already carries and let the surface confirm, rather than guessing and writing.

Evals belong here: a fixture set of real-sounding sentences with expected rule output, including the ambiguous pairs above, so a prompt change cannot quietly regress the binding.

Commit and PR text: plain and human-toned; no tracker ids.
acceptance_criteria: 1. The parser can bind appointment_type_id on emitted rules, resolved only against the practice's existing AppointmentType rows; an unresolvable type name never silently produces a global rule. 2. max_per_week is in the vocabulary with a params validator mirroring max_per_day. 3. The narrowing-versus-exclusivity ambiguity is surfaced for confirmation rather than guessed, with a test for each reading. 4. Sentences that name no type still produce global rules exactly as today, pinned by existing tests. 5. An eval fixture set covers type-bound, weekly-cap and ambiguous sentences. 6. make check green.

title: Let a type-scoped window exclude other appointment types, which is reserved capacity without a reservation
design:
Follow-up to type-scoped availability rules: when a practice narrows an appointment type like intakes to a window, a simple flag decides whether other appointment types may still use that window.

WHY THIS IS THE CLEVER PART. Reserved capacity was previously scoped as a FLOOR (hold N slots free for intakes), which is alien to this engine, where every one of the nine rule types SUBTRACTS availability. An exclusivity flag inverts it into an EXCLUSION: a type-scoped window that other types may not use. Intakes then hold that window by subtraction, in the grain the engine already works in, with no reserved-but-unbooked slot concept and no new storage shape.

DESIGN: a type-scoped rule that defines a window carries allow_other_types: bool (default TRUE, i.e. today's behaviour: narrowing a type does not, by itself, exclude anything). When FALSE, that window is unavailable to every other appointment type.

COMPOSES WITH ENFORCEMENT: a SOFT exclusive window means "prefer intakes here, the practice can still override"; HARD means "nothing else, ever". Both readings come free from the enforcement level already on every rule. Do not invent a second severity concept.

EDGE CASES THAT MUST BE SETTLED, NOT DISCOVERED:
- Two types claiming overlapping exclusive windows. Pick a deterministic resolution and document it; do not leave it to rule ordering.
- An exclusive window that swallows all working hours, leaving every other type with nothing. Warn at rule-creation time; never silently lock a practice out of its own calendar.
- Appointments already booked in a window that later becomes exclusive are untouched. The rule governs future listing, never retroactive cancellation.
- Exclusivity applies to the listing path. It must NOT prevent a practice from deliberately booking whatever it wants directly; that is what SOFT is for.

Commit and PR text: plain and human-toned; no tracker ids.
acceptance_criteria: 1. A type-scoped window rule carries allow_other_types, defaulting True so existing rules are unchanged. 2. With it False, get_free_slots offers that window only for the named type and nothing there for any other type. 3. HARD vs SOFT exclusivity reuse the existing enforcement level rather than a new severity field. 4. Overlapping exclusive windows resolve deterministically, documented and tested. 5. Creating a rule that would leave other types no availability at all produces a warning. 6. Appointments booked before the rule existed are never retroactively invalidated, with a test. 7. make check green.

title: Scope an availability rule to an appointment type: per-type daily caps and exclusive windows
design:
Depends on the link-to-type work landing first: the engine cannot apply a type-scoped rule until it knows which appointment type it is listing for.

PART 1: SCOPE A RULE TO A TYPE. Add an optional appointment_type_id: str | None = None to AvailabilityRule (models/availability.py), carried through from_dict/to_dict and the Postgres row. None means "applies to every type", which is exactly today's behaviour, so every existing rule keeps working untouched. Availability rules ARE in production and practices have real working_hours rules today, so the optional column with None meaning "every type" is correct and necessary here. Do not make it required.

Thread the type through the listing path: get_free_slots currently takes (user_id, date_str, duration_minutes, tz=) and has no idea what kind of appointment it is listing. It needs an optional appointment_type_id. Every call site must be updated deliberately, NOT defaulted and forgotten: routes/public_booking.py (:324, :576, :797), routes/scheduling.py (:851), and the remaining engine callers (grep for get_free_slots and list them in the PR). Passing None must preserve today's behaviour exactly.

Rule selection becomes: a rule applies if its appointment_type_id is None, OR it equals the type being listed. State explicitly what happens when a global rule and a type-scoped rule of the same rule_type both apply: for working_hours the intersection is the defensible answer (a type cannot be offered outside the practice's own hours), and for buffers the larger wins. Write that down in the docstring; a reader must not have to infer it.

PART 2: MAX_PER_DAY PER TYPE. THIS IS THE HEADLINE. A practice saying "at most 2 intakes a day" is the ordinary case; the window-narrowing and exclusivity work is the long tail. Build and present this as the primary capability. This needs NO new rule type: a MAX_PER_DAY rule with an appointment_type_id is "at most N intakes a day". The counting rule is the part to get right: a type-scoped cap counts only that type's active appointments, while a global cap keeps counting ALL of them, and both apply independently. An intake still consumes global capacity; the two caps are not alternatives. Soft max-per-day enforcement in the listing path already exists (#895): "max 2 intakes a day, soft" must behave per that enforcement so there is one enforcement story, not two.

PART 3: THE EXCLUSIVITY FLAG (folded in here so the two land as one change). A type-scoped rule that defines a window carries allow_other_types: bool, default TRUE, meaning today's behaviour: narrowing a type does not, by itself, exclude anything. When FALSE, that window is unavailable to every other appointment type.

Why this is the clever part: reserved capacity was previously scoped as a FLOOR (hold N slots free for intakes), which is alien to this engine, where every rule type SUBTRACTS availability. The flag inverts it into an EXCLUSION, a type-scoped window that other types may not use, so intakes hold that window by subtraction, in the grain the engine already works in, with no reserved-but-unbooked slot concept and no new storage shape.

Composes with enforcement: a SOFT exclusive window means "prefer intakes here, the practice can still override"; HARD means "nothing else, ever". Both readings come free from the enforcement level already on every rule. Do not invent a second severity concept.

Edge cases that must be settled, not discovered:
- Two types claiming overlapping exclusive windows: pick a deterministic resolution and document it; do not leave it to rule ordering.
- An exclusive window that swallows all working hours, leaving every other type with nothing: warn at rule-creation time; never silently lock a practice out of its own calendar.
- Appointments already booked in a window that later becomes exclusive are untouched. The rule governs future listing, never retroactive cancellation.
- Exclusivity applies to the listing path. It must NOT prevent a practice from deliberately booking whatever it wants directly; that is what SOFT is for.

FILES: backend/app/scheduling_engine/models/availability.py, backend/app/scheduling_engine/services/availability.py, backend/app/repositories/postgres/ (rule row + two columns), backend/app/db/models.py plus tenant template migration (one Alembic revision covering both columns), the rule CRUD routes in backend/app/routes/scheduling.py, and tests.

AvailabilityRule carries an optional appointment_type_id; None means every type and is byte-identical to today. 2. get_free_slots accepts an optional appointment_type_id and passing None preserves current behaviour; every call site is updated deliberately and listed in the PR. 3. A MAX_PER_DAY rule scoped to a type caps only that type, counting only that type's active appointments, while a global MAX_PER_DAY still counts all; both apply, with a test for each and one for both together. 4. A type-scoped soft cap behaves per the existing soft max-per-day listing enforcement. 6. With allow_other_types False, get_free_slots offers that window only for the named type and nothing there for any other type; HARD vs SOFT reuse the existing enforcement level. 8. title: Book a link through an appointment type, and drop the duplicate and unused switches
design:
Connect a booking link to an appointment type and enforce who may book it. Public booking has never been enabled in any production deployment, so there is no installed base and no back-compat path to preserve. Everything below takes that freedom.

1. REQUIRED TYPE. BookingLink gains a REQUIRED appointment_type_id. Not nullable, no "untyped link behaves as today" branch: a nullable FK would mean the enforcement this change exists for is always bypassable by a link with no type. A real Alembic revision plus tenant template change is still needed; there is simply no backfill and no legacy branch. Any dev links that exist are disposable; recreate them.

2. DELETE BookingLink.session_type. It is a free-text string describing what kind of appointment the link is for, which is exactly what appointment_type_id expresses with a real row behind it. Keeping both lets a link say "Intake" while pointing at a 50-minute follow-up type, with nothing to reconcile them.

3. DURATION COMES FROM THE TYPE. Remove duration_minutes from BookingLink; AppointmentType.duration_minutes is the single source. Two fields answering one question is the class of bug being removed elsewhere in settings; do not create a fresh instance of it.

4. DELETE scheduling_policy.self_book_mode ("request" | "auto"). Never shipped, never enforced, and the wrong shape twice over. It is practice-wide, but the decision is naturally per TYPE (a short consult is safe to auto-book, a full intake is not), and per-type is where self_bookable already lives. Do not build a "request mode" where a therapist approves a proposed time before it is confirmed: that is a second approve-a-time mechanism. The resulting model: a self-bookable type is booked instantly, bounded by type + availability rules + per-type caps + min_notice_hours. Anything not self-bookable is not offered for self-booking at all. There is no third state.

5. WIRE THE DORMANT SWITCHES. AppointmentType.audience ("new" | "existing" | "both"), self_bookable, offerable and scheduling_policy.may_self_book are defined, persisted and consumed by NOTHING: may_self_book has zero production call sites (only backend/tests/test_scheduling_policy.py), and db/models.py:731 says outright "Storing policy is all this does. Enforcing it at booking time is separate and not yet built." Keep the documented two-switch rule (db/models.py:726-729): the practice-level gate says self-booking is allowed at all, the per-type flag says this type in particular. Both must be true. Gates keep their closed defaults, so no practice is surprised.

6. ONE VISIBLE SWITCH, THREE FIELDS. The two-switch model is right and stays; what must NOT reach the practice is three switches across two screens (self_book_new x self_bookable x audience). Turning on "new clients can book with you directly" sets all three together for the chosen type. The settings surface for that is separate work; this change lands the model and enforcement.

7. FAIL CLOSED, QUIETLY. A link whose type excludes the booker, or is not self_bookable, or whose practice gate is off, refuses without disclosing whether the type exists. But the OWNER-facing view of that link must say plainly why it is not bookable, otherwise the most likely outcome is a therapist sending a dead link and never learning why.

VERIFIED ON MAIN 2026-09-10: backend/app/models/booking_link.py still carries duration_minutes (:62, :95, :103, :113, :147, :180, :200) and session_type (:63, :96, :114). The soft max-per-day enforcement in the free-slot listing has already landed (#895), so this change builds on that enforcement story rather than beside it.

FILES: backend/app/models/booking_link.py, backend/app/routes/public_booking.py, backend/app/scheduling_engine/services/scheduling_policy.py, backend/app/db/models.py plus tenant template plus Alembic revision, and tests.

Commit and PR text: plain and human-toned; no tracker ids.
acceptance_criteria: 1. BookingLink carries a REQUIRED appointment_type_id; a link cannot be created without one. 2. BookingLink.session_type is deleted. 3. BookingLink.duration_minutes is deleted; duration comes from AppointmentType. 4. scheduling_policy.self_book_mode is deleted with its column, model field and API surface; no request-vs-auto branch is built. 5. audience, self_bookable and offerable are enforced on the public booking path, and may_self_book gains a real production call site. 6. Practice-level AND per-type switches must both be true, with a test covering each being off independently; all gates keep their closed defaults. 7. A link whose type excludes the booker fails closed without disclosing whether the type exists, while the owner-facing view states plainly why it is not bookable. 8. A same-commit Alembic revision plus tenant template change covers the added and removed columns. 9. make check green.

Filed by the eng-head pass 2026-09-10 (evening, interactive, Kurt-directed) from the SaaS board's spec, rehomed here because the work lands in this repo. Six gates: spec unambiguous with verified pointers; done-signal = named tests + CI; blast radius bounded to the named files; self-contained; no collision with in-flight PRs; single target repo. Never-dispatch walk: no PHI handling change, no money/entitlement, no prod infra, no auth/RLS design, no vendor dashboard, no outbound send, not on a claim surface. Chain order for the booking set: link-to-type -> type-scoped rules -> exclusivity -> parser; the dependency edges enforce it.

Everything in the spec landed except item 4: scheduling_policy.self_book_mode is READ by patient self-booking (routes/patient_booking.py, request vs auto), so it is not the dead switch the 2026-09-04 read found and it stays. title: A pipeline failure after filing rolls the filing back and reconciles forever
description:
A claim filed by the pipeline can lose its state transition and then reconcile
forever, because the transition is written in a session that a LATER stage of
the same run can roll back.

Observed on a deployment every five minutes, indefinitely, with IDENTICAL
counters on each run — which is the tell that work is redone and discarded
rather than making progress:

    claims_pipeline_done ... submit_reconciled=1 submit_submitted=0 status_moved=2
    claims_pipeline_clinician_failed schema=<practice> user_id=<clinician>
      psycopg2.errors.LockNotAvailable: canceling statement due to lock timeout
      CONTEXT: while updating tuple (0,8) in relation "claims"
        poll_acknowledgments -> _apply_feed -> apply_fetched

Mechanism:

1. `submit_pending` mints the idempotency marker and COMMITS it — deliberately;
   the marker must be durable before the vendor call.
2. `_attempt` calls `move()`, which updates the claim's state in the session but
   does not commit. The session-owning caller commits at the end of the run.
3. `poll_acknowledgments` runs later in that SAME session and raises.
4. `for_each_clinician` catches it and the session rolls back.

The marker survives (step 1 committed). The state transition does not (step 3
discarded it). So the next run finds a claim carrying a pending marker,
reconciles it out of the feed, moves it again, and loses it again.

Effect: the practice cannot file anything at all. A claim created after the
wedge sits in `validated` indefinitely — which is how this surfaced, as a
ten-minute poll timeout in the insurance-claim-lifecycle e2e.

The lock timeout is the trigger, not the defect: ANY exception raised by a
later stage produces the same loop. What holds the row lock persistently is a
second question worth answering separately.
design:
DECISIONS CLOSED — do not re-litigate:

- Do NOT fix this by removing the commit in `submit_pending`. The marker must be
  durable before the vendor call; that is the outbox pattern, and it is what
  keeps a crashed submission from being filed twice.
- Do NOT fix it by widening the lock timeout. That hides a wedge behind a
  longer wait.

The defect is that one clinician's run is a single transaction spanning stages
that are otherwise independent. A failure in the polling stage must not be able
to discard a filing that already happened — the claim is with the payer by
then, and the database says otherwise.

Two candidate shapes. Pick one and say why in the PR:

(a) Commit at the stage boundary. Each stage — submit, status, remit, watchdog
    — commits its own work before the next begins, so a later failure cannot
    roll back an earlier stage's durable facts. Smallest change; the stages are
    already sequential and independent in `run_practice`.

(b) Give each stage its own session. Stronger isolation, larger diff, and it
    changes how `for_each_clinician` hands out `TenantRun`.

Separately worth investigating: what holds the row lock persistently. Two
candidates — an idle-in-transaction session, or two clinician runs contending
because `practice_user_ids` fell back to "every platform user" for a practice
with no email-mapping rows. `pg_stat_activity` on the affected deployment will
say which.

Do NOT touch `app/claims/routing.py` or the webhook routing path. That work
just landed and is unrelated to this.
acceptance_criteria:
1. A claim whose submit stage succeeded keeps its state transition even when a
   later stage of the same run raises. Proven by a test that makes the polling
   stage raise, then asserts the claim is still `submitted` afterwards.
2. A second run of the pipeline over the same data does not repeat the same
   reconcile — the marker and the state can no longer disagree in a way that
   loops.
3. An integration test covers the sequence on real Postgres: submit commits,
   the next stage raises, the claim's state survives.
4. The wedged practice files again: `submit_submitted` rises above zero and the
   stuck claim leaves `validated`.
5. Webhook routing behaviour is unchanged and the claim webhook tests stay green.
close_reason: Fixed in pablo#1083 — each pipeline stage now commits before the next begins, so a later stage's failure cannot roll back a filing that already happened. Test verified to fail without the fix. The persistent row lock that triggered it on dev remains open as a separate question, noted in the PR.

title: The claim review dialog can stick on "Filing…" forever with no error
description:
Observed on deployed dev 2026-09-10 while writing the claims e2e: the claim
review dialog sat with its button DISABLED and labelled "Filing…" for the full
30 seconds the test waited (34 retries), showing the user no error and
offering no way forward.

"Filing…" is exactly `validate.isPending` — ClaimReviewDialog.tsx:224 — and
that flag is set by `validate.mutateAsync({ claimId })` inside handleFile
(:119), which runs only from the button's own onClick. So the mutation was
started and its promise never settled.

Corroborating evidence from dev's access logs over the same two hours:

    3 x POST /api/claims/from-session/{appointment_id}   201    (3 dialogs opened)
    2 x GET  /api/claims/{claim_id}                      200
    1 x POST /api/claims/{claim_id}/validate             200

Access logs record COMPLETED requests, so a request that never returns leaves
no line. Three dialogs produced one validate completion. Every completed claims
request in that window finished in about 200ms, so this is not slowness.

THE PRODUCT DEFECT IS NOT THE HANG ITSELF — it is that the UI has no answer for
one. handleFile awaits the mutation and catches a REJECTION; a promise that
simply never settles hits neither branch. There is no timeout, no error copy,
no re-enable. The therapist is left looking at "Filing…" on a claim that may or
may not have been filed, and the only exit is a reload — after which the claim
may exist, or not, with nothing on screen having said which.

Why that matters more than an ordinary hang: this is the first irreversible
step in billing a client's insurance. "Did that go through?" is precisely the
question the interface must never leave open.
design:
Two parts. The second is the one that must happen.

1. FIND THE HANG. Reproduce POST /api/claims/{claim_id}/validate against dev
   and find out why some calls never return while others answer in 200ms.
   Start by checking whether the request reaches the backend at all (no access
   log line means either a hang inside the handler or a connection that never
   got there). The claims pipeline holds tenant sessions and talks to the
   clearinghouse; either is a place a request can wait forever.

2. GIVE THE UI AN ANSWER FOR IT, whatever the cause. A never-settling promise
   must not be able to strand this dialog:
   - put a timeout on the validate call, and
   - on timeout, re-enable the button and say plainly that the claim's status
     is unknown and to check the claims tracker before filing again — NOT
     "try again", which invites a double-file on a claim that may have gone
     through.
   The second half of that sentence is the important half: the safe action
   after an unknown filing is to LOOK, not to retry.

DECISIONS CLOSED:
- Do not make the button optimistically re-enable without saying anything.
  Silent recovery on a money path is how a claim gets filed twice.
- The fix belongs in the engine's own component (frontend/src/components/
  billing/claims/ClaimReviewDialog.tsx), not in the overlay: a self-hoster's
  dialog can hang the same way.

FOUND BY: the deployed claims e2e (pablo-saas#3145). Worth noting that the OSS
local-stack spec cannot see this — its clearinghouse and its database are on
the same machine and answer instantly.
acceptance_criteria: 1. A validate call that never settles leaves the dialog usable rather than stuck: the button re-enables and the copy says the outcome is unknown. 2. The copy directs the user to check the claims tracker, not to retry. 3. The underlying hang is either fixed or characterised on this bead with evidence. 4. A test covers the never-settles case (not merely the rejection case). 5. make check passes.

title: Walk the whole hold loop in a browser, against the fake clearinghouse
description:
Nothing drives the hold loop end to end. The unit tests will cover the check
and the repositories, but the path a therapist actually walks — a payer's
numbers disagree, the client is not billed, the disagreement appears as work,
the therapist settles it — crosses the pipeline, the database, the row policy
and the browser, and only a browser test crosses all four at once.

This is also the cheapest place it can ever be tested: the local stack already
runs a fake clearinghouse that manufactures remittances by control-number
prefix, so a self-contradicting 835 is a few lines rather than a deployment.
design:
Two pieces.

1. Teach scripts/fake_clearinghouse.py a new control-number prefix that
   produces an 835 whose claim-level patient-responsibility total DISAGREES
   with the same figure itemised across the service lines. Follow the existing
   prefix pattern (REJ-/PART-/DENY-) rather than inventing a second mechanism,
   and build it by editing the recorded remittance's amounts the way the other
   rules already do, so the document keeps the captured shape.

   Note the latent trap in the sibling fake used by unit tests
   (tests/claims_pipeline_fakes.py remittance_report): it overrides
   claim-level amounts but NOT line-level ones, so any caller passing a paid
   amount other than the recorded one already gets a self-inconsistent
   remittance by accident. Deliberate disagreement here must be built on
   purpose and be obvious in the code, not be mistakable for that bug.

2. A browser spec that walks the loop: a visit ready to bill, a claim filed
   with the disagreeing prefix, then assert (a) the claim shows the payer's
   payment, (b) the client's ledger carries NO new row, (c) the disagreement
   appears as work for the clinician, and (d) settling it as "bill as stated"
   writes exactly the withheld row.

DECISIONS CLOSED:
- Mirror frontend/e2e/specs/claims.spec.ts; it is the sibling that already
  drives a claim to the clearinghouse and knows the traps.
- The claims pipeline runs on an interval; the e2e compose already sets it to
  one minute for exactly this reason. Do not add sleeps in the spec.
- Resetting the fake cancels queued receipts, so a spec that resets will cancel
  another spec's acknowledgement. claims.spec.ts is describe.serial and says
  so; follow it.
- A visit is billable only with a session linked to the appointment AND a
  FINALIZED note. giveVisitReadyToBill in the fixtures encodes this.

DO NOT touch: the hold model or the therapist surface (sibling beads own them).
This bead is the harness rule plus the spec.
acceptance_criteria:
1. A claim filed with the disagreeing prefix produces an 835 whose stated
   patient-responsibility total differs from the itemised total.
2. A browser test drives that claim and asserts the payer payment posted.
3. The same test asserts the client's ledger gained no row.
4. The same test asserts the disagreement is visible to the owning clinician
   as work.
5. The same test settles it as "bill as stated" and asserts the previously
   withheld ledger row now exists, once.
6. The suite passes repeatedly without sleeps and without cancelling a sibling
   spec's queued receipts.
7. make check passes.

title: A seam that hands a hold to whoever is going to investigate it
description:
A hold says the engine refused to guess. It does not say why the payer's two
statements disagreed, and answering that is not the engine's job — it needs
someone to read the remittance, compare it against what the parser believed,
and reach a conclusion.

Different deployments will answer that differently. Some will want the
remittance kept for later study, some will want it raised to whoever runs the
deployment, some will want nothing beyond what the practice already sees. The
engine should not pick.

So the engine offers a seam: a hold, and the remittance behind it, handed to
whatever a deployment registered to receive it.
design:
Define a protocol the engine calls when a hold is raised, and ship a default
that does nothing. Mirror the pattern app/claims/credentials.py already uses
for the clearinghouse credential provider: the engine states an interface and
asks for it; a deployment registers an implementation at start-up; the engine
never imports the implementation.

DECISIONS CLOSED:
- The engine's own behaviour NEVER depends on the answer. A registered
  receiver that raises, hangs, or is absent must not change what the practice
  sees, must not release the hold, and must not delay the posting path. Wrap
  the call and swallow failures with a log line.
- What it is handed: the hold (id, state, timestamps, both totals and the
  delta, the CARC/group codes, line count, payer) plus enough provenance to
  find the source document again — the vendor transaction the remittance
  arrived on — and what the parse believed.
- The DEFAULT is a no-op. A deployment that registers nothing behaves exactly
  as it does today; the practice still sees the hold and can still settle it.
  This is not a degraded mode, it is the ordinary one.
- The seam is called on the hold's transitions too, not only on creation, so a
  receiver can follow a hold to resolution without polling.
- The engine does not retain a second copy of the remittance for this purpose.
  Retention beyond what the engine already keeps is the receiver's business.
- No PHI decision is delegated: the seam hands over data that is already
  inside the deployment's boundary, to code running inside that same boundary.
  What a receiver then does with it is the receiver's responsibility, and the
  interface documentation should say so plainly.

DO NOT build here: any particular receiver, any storage of remittances beyond
what already exists, any outbound call.
acceptance_criteria:
1. Raising a hold calls the registered receiver once, with the hold and the
