async DB driver, which is far out of scope.

THE DESIGN INSTEAD - a sync facade over an owned loop:

Keep `ClearinghouseClient` SYNCHRONOUS, exactly as it is. The SDK-backed
implementation owns ONE long-lived event loop on a background thread and
marshals each call to it with `asyncio.run_coroutine_threadsafe`, blocking on
`future.result(timeout=...)`.

What that buys, and why it beats the async Protocol:
* ZERO call sites change. No routes, workers, jobs, or the 32 errors above.
* ZERO test fakes change. That churn was most of the diff and most of the risk
  to the integration and end-to-end suites.
* Loop affinity is solved BY CONSTRUCTION. One loop for the client life, callable
  from any thread, so both `asyncio.to_thread(run_pipeline)`
  (`backend/app/jobs/claims_pipeline.py:135`) and the threadpool routes work
  unchanged. See the loop-affinity note below, which this design retires.
* A hard per-call timeout comes free from `future.result(timeout=...)`.

Cost: one background loop thread per process, and a thread hop per call -
microseconds against a network round trip.

Build:
1. A small loop-owner: start a daemon thread running `asyncio.new_event_loop()`,
   expose `run(coro, timeout)`, and stop it cleanly on application shutdown.
2. The SDK client is created ON that loop (a Config cannot be built off-loop at
   all - see PABLO-zz6p.1) and cached keyed on `(api_key, base_url)`, NOT as a
   bare singleton: `SettingsClearinghouseCredentialProvider` deliberately
   re-reads settings each call so a redeployed key takes effect without a code
   change, and a naive singleton would pin the old key forever.
3. Translate SDK exceptions into the existing `Clearinghouse*Error` taxonomy so
   callers see no difference.

DO NOT change the Protocol signature. DO NOT convert routes, workers or jobs.
acceptance_criteria:
1. `ClearinghouseClient` is unchanged and still synchronous; `git diff` touches no route, worker or job.
2. A loop-owner exists, is started once, and is shut down cleanly on application shutdown (no "Unclosed client session" warning in the test run).
3. The SDK client is cached keyed on `(api_key, base_url)`; a test proves that changing the configured key yields a different client rather than the stale one.
4. A test proves a call made from a non-main thread (as `asyncio.to_thread(run_pipeline)` does) succeeds against the same cached client.
5. A per-call timeout is enforced and surfaces as `ClearinghouseUnavailableError`.
6. `make check` passes.

title: Point the SDK at a configurable origin so the e2e fake clearinghouse keeps working
description: `ClearinghouseCredentials.base_url` (added in #989) points all four vendor hosts at one origin. The SDK exposes no base-URL override and no client or transport injection, so SDK-backed methods cannot honour it. Before the migration starts we need to know whether that field can go.
design:
The premise this bead was filed on was WRONG and is now settled by evidence.

PROBED against the installed package (`stedi` 1.0.0, Python 3.13). The SDK is
Smithy-generated and `stedi.Config` accepts:

  endpoint_uri: str | URI | None          <- base URL override, first class
  endpoint_resolver: EndpointResolver     <- plus StaticEndpointResolver
  transport: ClientTransport | None       <- AIOHTTPClient / SharedAIOHTTPClient
  interceptors: list[Interceptor[...]]    <- per-operation request/response hooks
  http_request_config, retry_strategy, protocol

So the SDK CAN be pointed at another origin, CAN have its transport replaced,
and CAN be intercepted. The PyPI README says none of this; do not trust it.

DECISION (closed): `CLEARINGHOUSE_BASE_URL` STAYS. Map it to `Config.endpoint_uri`
for SDK-backed operations. The containerised fake clearinghouse
(`scripts/fake_clearinghouse.py`, wired at `docker-compose.e2e.yml:90`) keeps
working unchanged, and the end-to-end harness keeps exercising real
serialisation through the SDK rather than bypassing it. Do NOT replace the fake
with an in-process Protocol implementation - that would stop the e2e layer
testing the thing we are migrating.

Scope of THIS bead, now that the decision is made:
1. Confirm `endpoint_uri` forces every SDK operation to that origin and that
   version path prefixes (e.g. `/2024-04-01/...`) are preserved, so one fake can
   still answer for all hosts. Prove it against `scripts/fake_clearinghouse.py`.
2. Keep `ApiBases.resolve` for the httpx-retained methods (payer search, the
   three enrollment methods). It shrinks; it does not die.
3. Record in the notes that `interceptors` gives us a wire-level capture seam if
   we ever want one - fixtures are still captured at the SDK boundary by
   default, because that is the seam our parser actually consumes.

NOTE the transport is aiohttp, not httpx. Adding the SDK adds an aiohttp
dependency alongside our existing httpx. Flag it; do not try to force httpx.

Do NOT migrate any endpoint in this bead.
acceptance_criteria:
1. A test proves `Config(endpoint_uri=...)` routes an SDK operation to that origin with its version path intact, against the existing fake clearinghouse.
2. `CLEARINGHOUSE_BASE_URL`, `settings.clearinghouse_base_url` and `ClearinghouseCredentials.base_url` still exist and are documented as applying to both SDK and httpx paths.
3. `docker-compose.e2e.yml` needs no change to keep pointing at the fake.
4. The bead notes record the aiohttp dependency and the `interceptors` capture seam.
5. `make check` passes.
notes:
INTERCEPTORS AS A CAPTURE SEAM (scope item 3, recorded here as the design asked).

stedi.Config accepts interceptors: list[Interceptor[...]], per-operation
request/response hooks. That is a wire-level capture seam if we ever want one:
it sees the serialised request and the raw response, before and after the
SDK's own modelling.

We are NOT using it, and the default should stay as it is. Fixtures are
captured at the SDK BOUNDARY — the deserialised output — because that is the
seam our parsers actually consume. A wire-level capture would record bytes
nothing in this codebase reads, and would drift from the models without
anything noticing.

The one case that would justify reaching for it: proving the SDK itself
serialises a request the way the vendor documents, which is a question about
the SDK rather than about us, and is better answered by capturing the vendor's
own answer to a real call.

ALSO WORTH KNOWING, from the same probe: the SDK's transport is aiohttp, not
httpx, so the SDK adds an aiohttp dependency alongside the existing httpx.
Flagged as the design said; do not try to force httpx onto it.
close_reason:
Verified done 2026-09-10 against all three acceptance criteria, each checked rather than assumed.

1. A TEST PROVES endpoint_uri ROUTES AN SDK OPERATION, VERSION PATH INTACT.
   backend/tests/test_clearinghouse_base_url.py::TestConfiguredBaseUrlReachesTheSdk
   ::test_an_sdk_call_lands_on_the_origin_keeping_its_version_path runs a real
   list_claims against a recording server and asserts the origin was replaced
   while /2025-03-07 — the claim-lifecycle API's own version path, which no
   code supplies — was not. 8 tests in the file, all passing.

2. THE THREE NAMES EXIST AND ARE DOCUMENTED FOR BOTH PATHS.
   settings.clearinghouse_base_url (settings.py:1246),
   ClearinghouseCredentials.base_url (credentials.py:64), CLEARINGHOUSE_BASE_URL
   read at credentials.py:103. stedi_sdk.py's module docstring states the
   equivalence outright — 'both clients honour it', the SDK spells it
   endpoint_uri, and like ApiBases.resolve it replaces the origin only — and
   names the test that pins it.

3. docker-compose.e2e.yml NEEDED NO CHANGE.
   CLEARINGHOUSE_BASE_URL=http://fake-clearinghouse:8080 is untouched since
   #989. (The file did change today for unrelated reasons — a browser-facing
   URL for the fake and a one-minute claims-pipeline interval — but not that
   line and not that mechanism.)

Scope item 2 also holds: ApiBases.resolve is alive and used at nine call sites
in stedi.py for the httpx-retained methods. It shrank; it did not die.

INDEPENDENT EVIDENCE beyond the unit tests: the browser test added in pablo#1056
(frontend/e2e/specs/claims.spec.ts) files a claim through the SDK against the
containerised fake and asserts it lands on /2025-03-07/professional-claim-submissions.
That is the decision in this bead working end to end, in the harness it was
made to protect.

Scope item 3 recorded in the notes above. No endpoint was migrated here, as
instructed.

title: Move the clearinghouse adapter onto the vendor SDK and native API surface
description: Our clearinghouse adapter is hand-rolled httpx against the vendor's legacy compatibility endpoints. The vendor now ships an official Python SDK and a native surface that does work we currently do ourselves. Move to both, behind the existing protocol.
design:
Stedi now publishes an official Python SDK (PyPI `stedi`) generated from its
internal API models, and a native API surface our adapter does not use.
`backend/app/claims/stedi.py` is built entirely on the legacy
Change-Healthcare-compatibility endpoints (`/change/medicalnetwork/...`) plus a
transaction-polling host.

The native surface does work we currently hand-roll: a typed eligibility
response instead of raw EB01 codes, and a per-claim timeline carrying
submissions, 277CA acknowledgments and 835 payment information already matched
to the claim.

DECISIONS CLOSED - do not re-litigate:
1. The `ClearinghouseClient` Protocol STAYS as the seam. Swap the implementation
   behind it; do not scatter SDK calls through callers.
2. The Protocol MAY change shape. It becomes async, and its transaction-feed
   methods are replaced by claim-lifecycle methods.
3. The SDK covers eligibility, professional claims, claim lifecycle and event
   destinations ONLY. Payer search and the three enrollment methods stay on
   httpx. Do not wait for SDK coverage of those.
4. Adoption is phased BY IDEMPOTENCY CLASS. Safe reads first; the keyed claim
   submission last, and only if the SDK can set `Idempotency-Key`.
transport injection. Raw X12 is
   still available in-band (the `x12` response field)./5. Fixtures are captured at the SDK boundary by default, because that is the
   seam our parser consumes. The SDK DOES expose endpoint_uri, transport and
   interceptors (verified against stedi 1.0.0), so wire-level capture stays
   available if we want it. Raw X12 is also in-band (the `x12` response field)./transport injection. Raw X12 is
   still available in-band (the `x12` response field).
6. Acceptance for the epic is the existing live lane
   (`.github/workflows/clearinghouse-live.yml` ->
   `backend/tests_integration/clearinghouse_live/`) run against both
   implementations and diffed at the parsed-model level.

Children are deliberately SERIAL - they all touch `backend/app/claims/stedi.py`
and `clearinghouse.py`. Chain them, do not parallelize.
acceptance_criteria:
1. Every child bead is closed.
2. `backend/app/claims/stedi.py` no longer calls any `/change/medicalnetwork/*` endpoint.
3. The live lane passes against the SDK-backed implementation with assertions unchanged from the httpx-backed run.
4. `make check` passes (lint incl. mypy, plus tests).

title: Let an availability rule apply to one weekday, or one kind of appointment
description:
Availability rules cannot be scoped to a weekday or to a kind of appointment,
so several ordinary ways of running a practice cannot be configured at all.

max_per_day carries {"max": N} and nothing else — no day, no appointment type.
BLOCK_DAY_OF_WEEK blocks a day for everything. And the engine never reads an
appointment type: grep for appointment_type in the availability service and
there are no matches. Duration is the only thing about a type that reaches it,
and it arrives as a query argument rather than from the type.

What a practice can say today:

  nine to five Monday to Friday        yes — five working_hours rules, one per day
  a cap that applies to every day      yes
  a day off                            yes, for every kind of appointment at once

What it cannot say:

  "no more than four on Wednesdays"    the cap has no day_of_week, so the only
                                       way to get a lighter Wednesday is to cap
                                       every day at the Wednesday number
  "intakes on Tuesdays and Thursdays"  no rule is type-aware; blocking a day to
                                       protect intake slots also removes the
                                       ordinary sessions meant to stay
  "two intakes a day, sessions on top" the cap counts appointments, so a
                                       fifteen-minute screening call and a
                                       ninety-minute first session are one unit
                                       each against the same number

A practice running short consults, longer first sessions and ordinary sessions
— which is most of them — cannot express the shape of its own week. The
appointment types exist and carry duration and a self-bookable flag; the
availability rules simply cannot see them.

Characterization tests for each limitation landed with this bead, in
TestWhatTheCapCannotSay in test_availability_engine.py. They assert the
current behaviour and carry the limitation in their names, so whichever of
them has to change is the signal that the rule shape grew a scope.
acceptance_criteria:
1. Decide the scope model before adding fields. The three candidate axes are
   day-of-week, appointment type, and both together; picking "both" by default
   turns every rule into a matrix, so the reason for whichever is chosen is
   written down on this bead.
2. max_per_day gains the chosen scope, with the unscoped form still meaning
   "every day, every type" — existing rows keep working untouched.
3. A type-scoped rule refers to an appointment type by id, not by name.
   Session names are editable free text; a rule keyed on one silently stops
   applying the day somebody fixes a typo.
4. The engine reads the scope in BOTH paths — get_free_slots and check_conflicts
   — because a slot that is offered and then refused is worse than either
   answer alone. A test asserts the two agree for each new scope.
5. The characterization tests in TestWhatTheCapCannotSay are updated, not
   deleted: each becomes the positive statement of what the scope now does.
6. The params shape lands as the validated model from PABLO-vs1k rather than a
   fourth hand-kept copy, or this bead waits for that one.
7. The therapist can set it. A scope the engine honours and the availability
   UI cannot express is not shipped.

title: Integration modules leak state into each other; a module pair fails what each passes alone
design:
FOUND 2026-09-09 while landing PABLO-2g6.1, with a minimal reproducer.

Modules in tests_integration/ leak process state into each other, so a test's
result depends on which siblings ran before it. Each passes alone; a pair fails.

  # both pass alone
  pytest tests_integration/api/test_patients_api_e2e.py                    -> 2 passed
  pytest tests_integration/database/test_tenant_session_integration.py     -> 8 passed

  # together, in that order, two fail
  pytest tests_integration/database/test_tenant_session_integration.py \
         tests_integration/api/test_patients_api_e2e.py                    -> 2 failed, 8 passed

Reproduced identically on main and on the 2g6.1 branch, so it is not that
change. Earlier sightings recorded the same shape from the other direction:
test_alembic_idempotency and test_patient_charges_db were reported failing in a
whole-directory run while passing in isolation.

WHY IT IS WORTH FIXING RATHER THAN NOTING. The full suite currently passes, so
CI is green and nobody is blocked — which is exactly what makes this expensive
later. A result that depends on collection order means a genuine regression can
be masked by a sibling, and an innocent change can be blamed for a failure it
did not cause. Both happened during this epic: four alembic failures were chased
as a suspected regression before turning out to be an environment artifact, and
this pair was chased again a few hours later.

LIKELY MECHANISM, not yet confirmed. ``get_settings`` is a process-wide
``lru_cache`` and several modules mutate os.environ at import time to steer it.
Whichever module imports first wins, and the cache then serves that answer to
every module after it. PABLO-2g6.1 removed one such variable
(MULTI_TENANCY_ENABLED), which was the collision the
test_public_booking_tenant_scope_db fixture documented in its docstring — but
the pattern remains for ENVIRONMENT, PABLO_EDITION, AUDIT_DUAL_WRITE_ENABLED and
others, and the surviving failure shows at least one more collision exists.

Worth checking whether the fix is per-module settings isolation (an autouse
fixture that clears the cache and restores the environment), or removing
import-time env mutation in favour of a fixture, or both.
acceptance_criteria:
1. The reproducer above passes: running
   test_tenant_session_integration.py and test_patients_api_e2e.py in one
   invocation, in that order, gives the same result as running each alone.

2. A test proves the property rather than the instance — e.g. the suite runs
   under a randomised module order (pytest-randomly or an explicit shuffled
   run in CI) and still passes, so a NEW ordering dependency fails loudly
   instead of waiting to be tripped over.

3. No integration module mutates os.environ at import time to steer
   get_settings. Where a module needs different settings, it says so in a
   fixture that restores what it changed.

4. The full tests_integration/ suite still passes, and no test is skipped or
   deleted to achieve any of the above.

title: A deleted account's still-valid token returns 500 instead of 401
description:
verify_firebase_token() in backend/app/auth/service.py calls firebase_auth.verify_id_token(token, check_revoked=True). With check_revoked=True the Admin SDK fetches the user record to check revocation, and raises UserNotFoundError when the account no longer exists. The function handles ExpiredIdTokenError, RevokedIdTokenError, UserDisabledError and InvalidIdTokenError — but not UserNotFoundError, so it escapes as an unhandled 500.

This is the single largest source of server errors in the deployment: 67 occurrences in 7 days, every one of them a request that should have been a clean 401. A client holding a token for a deleted account cannot tell it needs to sign in again; it sees a server fault and retries.
design:
Add a UserNotFoundError handler to the same except-chain in backend/app/auth/service.py, mirroring the four handlers already there exactly: log a warning naming the reason only (never token material), then raise HTTPException(401) with detail.error.code 'USER_NOT_FOUND' and a message telling the client to sign in again.

Place it BEFORE the InvalidIdTokenError clause. UserNotFoundError and InvalidIdTokenError are unrelated classes so ordering is not a correctness constraint today, but keeping the specific-to-general shape matches the block's existing reading order.

No change to check_revoked=True — the revocation check is deliberate. No change to any caller: they already treat a 401 from this function as sign-in-required.
acceptance_criteria:
- A unit test patches firebase_auth.verify_id_token to raise UserNotFoundError and asserts HTTPException with status 401 and code 'USER_NOT_FOUND'.
- A test asserts the log line carries no token material.
- The four existing token-rejection tests stay green.
- make lint (ruff + mypy) and make test pass.
close_reason: Merged: oss#995 (deleted-account 401), oss#997 (empty transcript), oss#998 (route on unhandled). Shipped to dev via base bump saas#3020.

title: Saving professional info silently does not save it when the practice mapping is missing
description: PATCH /api/users/me/professional-info returns 200 having written nothing to the clinician profile whenever _resolve_practice_id_for(user) returns None — which happens for any account whose email has no platform.email_tenant_mappings row. _upsert_clinician_profile logs a warning and returns early (backend/app/routes/users.py:485-494); the route then mirrors the submitted values onto the response, so the client is told the save succeeded and shows the new values back to the clinician. The data is not there on the next load. This is how rendering_provider.npi comes back empty, which fails the claim scrub on every claim; proved by inserting the mapping row by hand, after which the identical claim scrubs clean and reaches validated.
design:
Read backend/app/routes/users.py (_upsert_clinician_profile and its early return, _resolve_practice_id_for, and update_professional_info's response mirroring), backend/app/auth/service.py (_resolve_practice_from_email), and how a practice mapping is created during onboarding.
THE DECISION THIS BEAD EXISTS TO MAKE is what SHOULD happen, and the current answer — pretend it worked — is the only clearly wrong one. Options: (a) refuse the write with a 409 naming the missing mapping, so the clinician learns immediately; (b) provision the mapping on demand, if a signed-in user without one is a state onboarding should never have produced; (c) persist the profile without a practice_id and attach it when the mapping appears. Pick one, implement it, and say in the commit why the others were rejected. Whatever is chosen, the route must never again report success for a write it did not perform.
ALSO: the response mirroring is what turns a skipped write into an invisible one. Mirror only what was actually persisted.
DO NOT TOUCH: the onboarding flow's own provisioning order (a sibling concern) unless option (b) is chosen, in which case say so plainly.
acceptance_criteria: 1. A PATCH that cannot persist no longer returns a success carrying the unsaved values. 2. A test covers the no-mapping path end to end and asserts the persisted state on a follow-up read, not just the response body. 3. The rejected options are named in the commit message with the reason. 4. An account WITH a mapping still saves exactly as it does today (regression test). 5. make check green.

title: The clearinghouse adapter's base URLs are module constants, so no deployment can point it anywhere else
description: backend/app/claims/stedi.py declares HEALTHCARE_API_BASE, PAYERS_API_BASE, CORE_API_BASE and ENROLLMENTS_API_BASE as module-level string constants. There is no setting and no environment override, so the adapter can only ever talk to the live vendor. Two consequences, one of them already blocking work: the end-to-end harness ships a fake clearinghouse and a CLEARINGHOUSE_BASE_URL entry in docker-compose.e2e.yml that the adapter never reads, so every claim submitted in the harness fails with ClearinghouseUnavailableError while the fake's inbox stays empty; and docs/design/e2e-harness.md states the base URL is a plain setting, which is not true of the current adapter. Verified empirically against the running compose stack.
design:
Read backend/app/claims/stedi.py (the four constants and every call site that interpolates them), backend/app/claims/credentials.py (ClearinghouseCredentials and mode_for_key — the existing seam for per-deployment clearinghouse configuration, which is where this belongs rather than a bare env read), backend/app/settings.py, and docker-compose.e2e.yml plus docs/design/e2e-harness.md (which currently describes behaviour the code does not have).
BUILD: make the four bases resolvable per deployment, defaulting to today's live values so nothing changes for an existing install. Prefer routing them through the credential provider that already answers 'which clearinghouse account is this' rather than introducing a second, parallel configuration path — one seam, not two. A deployment that sets nothing must behave exactly as it does now.
THEN: make the harness actually reach the fake — the compose entry becomes live rather than inert — and correct docs/design/e2e-harness.md so it describes the code as it is.
DECISIONS CLOSED: the default stays the live vendor, so this is not a behaviour change for any real deployment; overriding a base URL is a deployment concern and is never a per-request or per-practice value.
DO NOT TOUCH: the request/response parsing, the retry and error taxonomy, or the credential key-prefix mode inference.
acceptance_criteria: 1. With nothing configured, the adapter targets exactly the four URLs it targets today (assert the defaults in a test, so a typo in a refactor cannot silently redirect production traffic). 2. A configured base URL is used instead, proved by a test that points the adapter at a local server and sees the request arrive. 3. The e2e stack's claim submission reaches the fake clearinghouse and its inbox is non-empty. 4. docs/design/e2e-harness.md matches the code. 5. make check green.
close_reason: Merged: #989. ClearinghouseCredentials gains base_url, read from a CLEARINGHOUSE_BASE_URL setting; the four vendor constants stay as pinned defaults in the adapter and an ApiBases.resolve() swaps the origin while each API keeps its own version path. Routed through the existing credential seam rather than a second config path. Proved by getting a real claim through to the fake clearinghouse: POST /2024-04-01/.../submission appears in the fake's inbox, which was empty beforehand. A full browser-driven claim is still blocked on the rendering-NPI seam (PABLO-85ab).

title: The payment and clearinghouse webhooks have no integration test, and they are how money becomes real
description: backend/app/routes/payment_webhooks.py and backend/app/routes/claim_webhooks.py are each covered only by unit tests with a fake transport. Both are the moment an outside system tells us money moved: the payment webhook is what turns a pending charge into a succeeded one, and the claim webhook is what moves a claim on an acknowledgment. Their failure modes are exactly the ones a fake cannot show — a replayed delivery writing twice, a delivery arriving before the row it refers to was committed, a signature check passing on a body that was mutated in transit.
design:
SHARED RULES: testcontainers Postgres, NOBYPASSRLS 'pablo' role. Read backend/app/routes/payment_webhooks.py, backend/app/payments/reconcile.py (METADATA_CHARGE_ID and how a delivery finds its row), backend/app/routes/claim_webhooks.py, backend/app/claims/webhooks.py, backend/tests/test_payment_webhook.py and backend/tests/test_claim_webhooks.py (the unit cases to mirror, not duplicate), and backend/tests_integration/database/test_claim_pipeline_db.py (the closest existing integration shape).
BUILD backend/tests_integration/database/test_webhook_delivery_db.py proving, against a real database:
(a) IDEMPOTENCE: delivering the same event twice leaves exactly one state change and one ledger row — assert by counting rows, not by trusting a return value. Do this for both receivers.
(b) ORDERING: a delivery naming a charge or claim that does not exist yet is rejected or parked, and never creates a phantom row.
(c) SIGNATURE: a body mutated after signing is refused with the documented status, and a missing signature header is refused, both before the payload is read.
(d) TENANCY: a delivery cannot move a row belonging to another practice's schema.
DECISIONS CLOSED: use each vendor's real signing algorithm over a locally generated secret — never a stubbed verifier, since the verifier is part of what is under test. Fixtures carry no real vendor identifiers.
DO NOT TOUCH: the receivers themselves. A failure here is a finding to report.
acceptance_criteria: 1. A replayed delivery to each receiver produces exactly one state change, asserted by row count. 2. A delivery for an unknown charge or claim creates no row. 3. A tampered body and a missing signature are both refused, and the refusal happens before the payload is trusted. 4. A delivery cannot reach another practice's schema. 5. Runs under 'make test-integration' and passes. 6. No production file is modified.
close_reason: Merged: #985. 20 integration cases against real Postgres with real HMAC verifiers over generated secrets, two provisioned tenant schemas, NOBYPASSRLS role. Proved idempotence by row count (not by the deduped flag), ordering (a delivery for an uncommitted charge creates no phantom row), signature-before-parse (the same bad body answers 401 unsigned and 400 signed), and cross-tenant isolation with two practices holding the same PaymentIntent id. Found a real race: concurrent redelivery of one payment event returns 500 from an uncaught UniqueViolation - filed as PABLO-r7ae.

title: The money ledger has no integration test: constraints and isolation are believed, not proven
description: Nothing under backend/tests_integration/ touches patient_charges or the balance route. Every test of the charge ledger runs against in-process fakes, so three things are currently believed rather than demonstrated: (1) the CHECK constraints on the table actually reject bad rows in a real engine — a constraint that has only ever been read is a constraint you hope exists; (2) a clinician with no grant on a client cannot read that client's charges or balance through real HTTP; (3) the balance a real query returns matches the one the pure function returns over the same rows. The generic RLS invariant suite proves patient_charges has RLS enabled and is fail-closed with no GUC set, which is necessary and not sufficient — it says nothing about the columns or the routes.
design:
SHARED RULES: runs against testcontainers Postgres as the NOBYPASSRLS 'pablo' role, like every sibling in backend/tests_integration/database/. Money is integer cents. Read backend/tests_integration/database/test_patient_coverage_rls.py (the closest sibling: a per-tenant table's RLS proved through real SQL), test_patient_idor_http.py (the two-credential HTTP shape to mirror — note it tests the PATIENT principal with purpose-built stub routes, so it is a pattern to copy, not coverage to reuse), test_rls_invariants.py (what is already generic and must not be duplicated), and backend/app/db/models.py PatientChargeRow.
BUILD backend/tests_integration/database/test_patient_charges_db.py covering three things:
(a) CONSTRAINTS, against the real engine: a row with an unknown kind is rejected; a write_off with no reason is rejected; a non-write_off carrying a reason is rejected; a write_off WITH a reason is accepted; amount_cents <= 0 is rejected for every kind including contractual_adjustment and credit; the claim_id FK sets NULL rather than cascading when its claim is deleted.
(b) ISOLATION, through real HTTP with two clinicians and two clients in one provisioned schema: clinician A gets 404 (never 403) for B's client on GET /api/patients/{id}/charges and GET /api/patients/{id}/balance, and the symmetric case with the credentials swapped so nothing is keyed to A by luck.
(c) AGREEMENT: insert a ledger of every kind through the repository, read it back through the route, and assert the returned balance equals patient_balance() over the same rows — the pure function and the real round trip must not disagree.
DECISIONS CLOSED: this does NOT re-test what test_rls_invariants.py already asserts generically (RLS enabled, fail-closed with no GUC); it tests the columns and the routes, which that suite does not reach.
DO NOT TOUCH: app/payments/balance.py or the routes — this bead adds tests only. If a test fails, that is a finding to report, not a licence to change the code under it.
acceptance_criteria: 1. Every CHECK constraint on patient_charges has a test that inserts a violating row and asserts the database refuses it. 2. Cross-clinician reads of both /charges and /balance return 404 in both directions. 3. The route's balance equals patient_balance() over the same rows for a ledger containing every kind. 4. The suite runs under 'make test-integration' against a NOBYPASSRLS role and passes. 5. No production file is modified.

title: A detected carve-out should reach the claim, not just the badge
description: When eligibility finds that somebody other than the payer on the card administers the behavioral benefit, the chart shows a warning badge naming the administrator — and nothing else happens. The claim is still built against the coverage on file, so the app can tell a therapist the claim is about to go to the wrong company and then let them file it there anyway. A denial weeks later is the current feedback loop.
design:
Read backend/app/claims/eligibility.py (_carveout_administrator and what it returns), backend/app/models/eligibility.py (CarveoutAdministrator), backend/app/claims/assembly.py (how a claim picks its payer from the coverage), frontend/src/components/insurance/EligibilityBadge.tsx (today's warn state), and the coverage form.
BUILD: when a coverage's most recent eligibility summary names a carve-out administrator whose payer id differs from the coverage's payer, claim assembly's scrub raises a finding — a WARNING, never a hard refusal — naming the administrator and its payer id, and the Billing UI surfaces it on the claim before it is filed. The chart's coverage card gains a one-click action to add a second coverage naming the administrator, prefilled with its name and payer id; the therapist confirms and completes the member id, which the 271 does not supply.
DECISIONS CLOSED: PROPOSE, never adjudicate. The app never silently refiles a claim to a different payer, never edits the coverage on file, and never guesses a member id — a wrong payer is a denial and a wrong member id is a rejection, and neither is a decision to make on a therapist's behalf. The finding is a warning and the claim remains fileable, because the payer on the card is occasionally right and the therapist knows things the 271 does not.
DO NOT TOUCH: the eligibility parsing itself (sibling bead validates it); the remittance path.
acceptance_criteria: 1. A claim built on a coverage with a differing carve-out administrator carries a scrub WARNING naming the administrator and payer id; the claim is still fileable (test both halves). 2. No carve-out, or a carve-out whose payer id matches the coverage, raises nothing. 3. The coverage card action prefills name and payer id and leaves the member id empty and required. 4. Nothing in this change writes to a coverage row without the therapist confirming. 5. make check + frontend gates green.

title: Prove the behavioral carve-out detection against a real payer response, not a constructed fixture
description: The carve-out detection is the most specialty-specific logic in the eligibility path: a medical card names one payer, the behavioral benefit is often administered by somebody else, and a claim filed with the payer on the card is denied for 'not our benefit'. It has never seen a real payer response. backend/app/claims/eligibility.py says so plainly: the behavioral fixture is the vendor's PHARMACY carve-out line with the service type and entity swapped (eligibility_271_carveout_behavioral.json, constructed). So the code is tested against a document we wrote, which cannot tell us whether real payers answer in that shape at all.
design:
This is a verification task whose deliverable is a recorded fixture plus whatever code change the real response proves necessary. Read backend/app/claims/eligibility.py (module docstring: the two 271 shapes it reads), backend/app/claims/credentials.py (mode_for_key: a test_-prefixed key reaches the vendor's mock payers, an unprefixed key reaches real ones), and backend/tests/fixtures for how eligibility fixtures are stored.
STEPS: (1) run a real 270 for outpatient mental health (service type MH) against a real payer using a production clearinghouse key, for a plan whose behavioral benefit is known to be carved out; (2) record the 271 response as a fixture with every identifier scrubbed — no member id, no subscriber name, no date of birth, no address; (3) assert the existing detector finds the administrator's name and payer id in it; (4) fix the detector if the real shape differs from the constructed one, and say in the commit how it differed.
CONSENT AND SCOPE: run the check against the operator's OWN coverage. An eligibility check on a person the practice has no treatment or payment relationship with is not ours to make, whatever the intent, and a real 271 carries real PHI into whatever environment it is run from.
DECISIONS CLOSED: the recorded fixture is scrubbed before it is committed, never after; if the real payer's shape differs, the constructed fixture STAYS as a second case rather than being replaced — two shapes are more coverage than one.

CAPTURE IS POSSIBLE WITHOUT A REAL PAYER - corrected 2026-09-09.
Stedi mock payers answer through the REAL eligibility API with a TEST key
(`/healthcare/api-reference/mock-requests-eligibility-checks`), so a response
captured from them is a genuine capture: real endpoint, real serialisation,
real key names and envelope. That satisfies "captured, not authored" for
SHAPE, and needs no payer relationship - the live lane already has the key as
`CLEARINGHOUSE_TEST_API_KEY`.

Scenarios the mocks cover: Aetna, Cigna, UnitedHealthcare (active AND
inactive), Anthem BCBS CA and BCBS Texas and Oscar (dependent as spouse / as
child, and the case where the payer returns the dependent inside the
subscriber object), Ambetter and Humana (subscriber only), Kaiser NCal, CMS
(active + MBI lookup), Ameritas and MetLife (dental, service code 35). Plus
canned AAA errors 42, 43, 72, 73, 75 and 79 - exactly the codes the
disposition table in PABLO-os22 has to get right.

WHAT THE MOCKS DO NOT COVER: a behavioural carve-out. No mock payer returns
one, so `PABLO-d8ow.36` still needs a response from a real payer to prove the
carve-out reading. Do not let a mock capture be mistaken for closing it.

So the split is: SHAPE can be proven now against mocks; carve-out SEMANTICS
cannot.
acceptance_criteria: 1. A scrubbed real 271 is committed as a fixture and contains no member id, subscriber name, date of birth or address (assert this in a test, not by eye). 2. A test asserts the detector reads the administrator name and payer id out of the REAL fixture. 3. If the detector changed, the commit message says exactly how the real shape differed from the constructed one. 4. The constructed fixture and its test still exist. 5. make check green.
notes:
WHAT IT WOULD TAKE, checked 2026-09-10. Kurt asked whether he could run an
eligibility check against his own health insurance on the production account
to see a real behavioural carve-out. Answer: not today, and the blocker is one
specific thing.

The production clearinghouse account as it stands:

    key mode      PRODUCTION (32 chars, present in prod Secret Manager)
    provider      npi=1999999984  "Pablo Health Test Provider"
    enrollment    LIVE — Stedi Test Payer only

That NPI is a dummy: the 199999xxxx range is reserved for test values, and the
name says as much. A real payer validates the inquiring NPI against NPPES and
will refuse or AAA-error an inquiry from one that is not a registered
provider, so the request fails on the PROVIDER side before saying anything
about anyone's benefits.

So the blocker is a real, NPPES-registered NPI — an individual clinician's or
an organisational NPI for the practice entity. Everything else is easy:
- member id, name, date of birth, and the payer's Stedi payer id (keep the
  leading zeros — the vendor's docs call that out specifically);
- a mental-health service type code;
- no per-payer enrollment needed for eligibility in the general case (CMS is
  the documented exception);
- the vendor bills per production check, which is trivial for one call.

WORTH SAYING OUT LOUD: a 270 asserts that A PROVIDER is inquiring about this
person's benefits. The subject's consent covers the patient half of that, not
the provider half. An NPI that is not treating the person stretches the
payer's trading-partner agreement, which expects treatment/payment/operations.
The two clean shapes are (a) self-inquiry, where the same real person is both
the provider and the subject, or (b) a design partner running eligibility on a
consenting patient in the ordinary course — which is not a test at all, and is
what PABLO-zpon needs anyway.

ALSO ESTABLISHED: the vendor documents NOTHING about carve-outs. No
benefitsInformation code "U", no benefitsRelatedEntity, no worked example
(checked their llms.txt and llms-full.txt indexes, 2026-09-10). Our fixture
remains a pharmacy carve-out re-pointed at behavioural service types, so this
bead's premise stands: one real 271 from a plan with a genuine behavioural
carve-out is the only thing that tells us whether PABLO-d8ow.37 is aimed at
the right shape.

OPERATIONAL NOTE for whoever runs it: make it a DIRECT API call, not a trip
through the app. That captures the 271 without creating a patient record or
writing anyone's PHI into our database; scrub it, then commit it as the
fixture.

title: Export claims and payments for a period, as the practice's own records
description: A practice needs its own copy of what it billed and what it collected: for its accountant at year end, for a payer audit, for reconciliation against the bank, and to leave with the data if it leaves the product. Today the only export is the biller handoff for a single claim package.
design:
SHARED RULES: money is integer cents; loggable: ids, amounts, row counts; never member id, DX, subscriber demographics. Read backend/app/claims/export.py (the existing biller CSV, whose shape and quoting to mirror), backend/app/routes/billing_queue.py, backend/app/payments/balance.py, backend/app/services/audit_service.py.
BUILD: backend/app/payments/period_export.py (new file) rendering two deterministic CSVs for a [from, to] window: (a) claims — control number, client id, payer, dates of service, billed, allowed, paid, adjusted, patient responsibility, state, filed/paid dates; (b) payments — every ledger row with its kind, status, amount, visit, claim, write-off reason. GET /api/billing/export?from=&to=&kind=claims|payments streams the CSV with a content-disposition filename carrying the window. Byte-stable for a fixed input so a re-export can be diffed. Audited as an EXPORT with the window and the row count — the disclosure is the whole period, so the audit entry says so.
DECISIONS CLOSED: CSV only in v1 (no XLSX, no PDF); the export is the practice's own data and carries client ids, not names, unless the practice explicitly asks for names — decide that with the first real request rather than guessing; streaming rather than buffering, since a year of a busy practice will not fit comfortably in memory.
DO NOT TOUCH: the per-claim biller export (sibling surface); the statement PDF.
acceptance_criteria: 1. Both CSVs are byte-stable across two runs over the same data. 2. The window is inclusive at both ends and a row on the boundary appears exactly once (test). 3. The export is audited with the window and row count, and the audit entry is written even when the export is empty. 4. A practice with no claims exports a header-only file rather than a 404. 5. Streaming: the route does not materialise the whole result in memory (test with a large generated ledger). 6. make check green.

title: Practice financial report: aging, payer mix, collections rate, payment lag
description: The Billing page can list who owes (the Balances view), but a practice cannot answer the questions an owner actually asks at month end: how old is my receivable, which payers are slow, what share of what I billed did I collect, and how long does a claim take to turn into money. Every input already exists once the charge ledger carries kinds and claims carry their receipt timeline; nothing here needs a new source of truth.
design:
SHARED RULES: money is integer cents via backend/app/money.py; loggable: ids, amounts, kinds, claim state; never member id, DX, subscriber demographics. Read backend/app/payments/balance.py (the ledger arithmetic), backend/app/claims/tracker.py, backend/app/routes/billing_queue.py, backend/app/models/claims.py (claim states and the receipt timeline), frontend/src/components/billing/.
BUILD: a pure report module backend/app/payments/reporting.py (new file) computing, from ledger rows + claims, (a) A/R aging buckets by age of the owed row: 0-30, 31-60, 61-90, 90+, each with count and cents; (b) payer mix: billed and collected cents per payer over a window; (c) collections rate: collected / (billed - contractual_adjustment - write_off) over a window; (d) claim-to-payment lag: median and p90 days from submitted receipt to the 835 that paid it, per payer. GET /api/billing/report?from=&to= returns them together, audited, ids and amounts only. Billing page gains a Reports view rendering the four, each with an empty state that says what would populate it.
DECISIONS CLOSED: computed on read, never stored or cached — same reasoning as the balance; the window is explicit in the query, never an implicit 'this month'; percentages are computed in the frontend from the cents so the API stays exact.
DO NOT TOUCH: the balance module's own arithmetic (import it); remittance posting; the statement PDF.
acceptance_criteria: 1. Aging buckets sum to the practice's total owed (property test over generated ledgers). 2. Collections rate excludes contractual adjustments and write-offs from the denominator, with a unit test naming why. 3. Lag is computed from receipts, and a claim with no payment yet is excluded rather than counted as zero. 4. GET /api/billing/report is tenant-scoped and audited with ids only. 5. Empty practice renders every section's empty state, no division by zero. 6. make check green.

title: Gate main image publication on compose end-to-end tests
description: Make the End-to-end workflow reusable, invoke it from both main image publication workflows, and require it before backend, frontend, or pentest images are built and pushed. Preserve standalone nightly and relevant-PR runs. The workflow files are human-merge-only.

title: Claims setup checklist card until billing is ready
description: A therapist who opens Billing > Claims before setting anything up sees an empty tracker. Guidance today is reactive. Show a checklist card at the top of the Claims tab until every step is done: practice profile complete, at least one payer, coverage on at least one client, each linking to the page that does it. A deployment may append its own steps (e.g. payer enrollment) through a render slot. Builds on pablo#965 (BillingSetupGate: a slot that wraps the queue so a deployment can put processor setup in place of the work) — this checklist is NOT a gate: claims setup is progressive, so it sits above the Claims tab content and never hides the queue.
design:
Read pablo#965 first (frontend/src/components/billing/BillingSetupGate.tsx, BillingSetupSlot.tsx; the gate wraps the queue and ships empty in the base build) and keep this separate from it: the gate is for a prerequisite (a processor), the checklist is guidance. Then frontend/src/components/billing/ (BillingPage, the Claims tab), frontend/src/components/settings/BillingProfileBanner.tsx + billingProfileGaps.ts (reuse the gap logic; do not re-derive), and the payers and coverage APIs.

BUILD: a ClaimsSetupChecklist component rendered at the top of the Claims tab while incomplete: steps with done/not-done state, each a link (Practice profile, Insurance payers, a client's Insurance tab); an extraSteps render slot (the settings render-slot idiom in settingsSlots.extensions) so a downstream build can add steps such as payer enrollment without forking the card; hidden once every core step is done. Component tests for each step state and the hidden state. Frontend only. Branch from main after #965 merges.

DECISIONS CLOSED: never a gate; never hides the queue or tracker; reuses billingProfileGaps for the profile step.
acceptance_criteria: 1. Claims tab shows the checklist with correct step states from the APIs and hides it when complete (component tests). 2. Each step links to the right page. 3. A render slot exists for downstream steps. 4. The checklist never hides the queue or the tracker (test). 5. eslint/tsc/vitest green.
close_reason: Merged to main: #976 claims setup checklist, #977 claim detail reads the submission ledger, #978 charge ledger kinds + balance. Note on .28: the balance arithmetic shipped with a follow-up fix — a paid bill now nets to zero instead of reading as a credit, and the ledger gained a 'payment' kind so money can be collected against a bill another row raised.

title: Write-offs with a reason, and the practice's waiver policy
description: Waiving a copay or a balance must be a deliberate, recorded act: routine waivers are an inducement problem and a contract violation. Add a write-off with a required reason, a practice policy that gates courtesy waivers and small-balance thresholds, and an audit trail. Contractual adjustments from remittances are written off automatically and are never billable.
design:
SHARED RULES: money is integer cents via backend/app/money.py; per-tenant DDL ships with the same-commit alembic_tenants revision stacked on the CURRENT tenant head plus the regenerated tenant template; tables with patient_id use has_patient_access; loggable: ids, amounts, kinds, claim state; never member id, DX, subscriber demographics. Design: the private product design (not in this repo) sections E and F were summarised into this bead; everything needed is here. Public repo: commits, comments and PR bodies mention no other repo or tier.
Read backend/app/payments/balance.py and the ledger kinds (write_off row, write_off_reason CHECK), practice settings storage (grep practice_billing_profile or the settings service used by billing), backend/app/services/audit_service.py, the Balance tab from the balance bead.
BUILD: practice policy fields on practice_billing_profile (migration + template): allow_courtesy_writeoffs bool default false, small_balance_cents int default 500. POST /api/patients/{id}/write-offs {amount_cents, reason, note} -> write_off row; rules: reason in the CHECK set; 'courtesy' refused (403 with explanation) unless the policy allows; 'small_balance' refused unless the client's balance <= small_balance_cents; amount cannot exceed the balance; disclosure-grade audit event with actor, reason, amount, claim ids (never DX/member id). Settings > Billing > Practice profile gains a 'Waivers' section for the two policy fields with the compliance helper text. Balance tab gains Write off with the reason picker and note. No bulk write-off. Remittance's CO-group rows are kind='contractual_adjustment' (the remittance bead writes them; this bead only renders them as 'insurance adjustment, not owed').
DECISIONS CLOSED: courtesy waivers default off; write-offs are per client per amount, never a list; reasons are the fixed set.
DO NOT TOUCH: remittance posting internals; the copay action.
acceptance_criteria: 1. Write-off route enforces reason set, courtesy policy, small-balance threshold and amount <= balance (tests for each refusal). 2. Audit row per write-off with actor and reason, no PHI beyond ids. 3. Settings shows the two policy fields; Balance tab offers Write off with reason + note. 4. make check + frontend gates green.

title: Client balance, Charge balance, and a deterministic statement PDF
description: Once remittances post patient responsibility, a therapist needs to see what each client owes, charge it to the card on file, or hand the client a statement. None of that exists.
design:
SHARED RULES: money is integer cents via backend/app/money.py; per-tenant DDL ships with the same-commit alembic_tenants revision stacked on the CURRENT tenant head plus the regenerated tenant template; tables with patient_id use has_patient_access; loggable: ids, amounts, kinds, claim state; never member id, DX, subscriber demographics. Design: the private product design (not in this repo) sections E and F were summarised into this bead; everything needed is here. Public repo: commits, comments and PR bodies mention no other repo or tier.
Read backend/app/payments/balance.py (from the ledger-kinds bead), backend/app/claims/superbill.py (the deterministic PDF pattern to copy), the chart page components under frontend/src/components/patients/, frontend/src/components/billing/.
BUILD: chart header balance line ('Owes $62.00' / 'Credit $10.00' / nothing at zero) with a Balance tab listing ledger rows by visit (kind, date, amount, claim link); Charge balance button using the existing off-session charge path with kind='session' settlement rows referencing the patient_resp rows it settles (settled_by_charge_id on the rows; add to the ledger bead's columns if missing); Statement PDF (backend/app/payments/statement.py, reportlab, byte-stable under a fixed clock): per visit date of service, service, charge, insurance paid, adjusted, you paid, you owe; totals; practice block; audited download. Billing page gains a Balances view (clients with a non-zero balance, oldest first) reusing the same read model. Component + route + determinism tests.
DECISIONS CLOSED: statements are generated, never emailed by OSS (a deployment may send them through its own channels); no partial payments UI in v1 (charge full balance or nothing).
DO NOT TOUCH: the copay action; remittance; write-off UI (sibling beads).

VERIFIED BUILT 2026-09-09, audited against the acceptance criteria rather than
from memory. Everything this bead asked for exists:

design:
SHARED RULES: frontend only — every backend surface this bead needs already
shipped in pablo#960 and is read, never edited. The clearinghouse's own wording
(submission_findings[].description) may quote the field at fault and can carry
patient-identifying text, so it renders ONLY inside the audited claim detail
view: never in a tracker row, a queue row, a toast, a page title or a console
log. Public repo: commits, comments and PR bodies mention no other repo or tier.

Read backend/app/routes/claims.py (_to_detail, _hops, _to_findings, and the
ClaimDetailResponse / ClaimTrackerResponse it returns), backend/app/models/claims.py
(ClaimReceipt, ClaimHop, the response models — the field names are authoritative

frontend/src/types/claims.ts, frontend/src/lib/api/claims.ts, and the components

1. TYPES. frontend/src/types/claims.ts declares what pablo#960 added and the

vendor_claim_id, payer_claim_number, submission_pending_at, last_receipt_at,
status_checked_at; on ClaimTrackerItem — next_action and last_receipt_at. Mirror
the backend models exactly, including nullability.

2. TIMELINE FROM THE RECEIPT LEDGER. ClaimHops.tsx takes receipts: ClaimReceipt[]
instead of hops: ClaimHop[], ordered oldest first by occurred_at. A receipt whose
to_state differs from from_state is a HOP (kinds submitted, ch_accepted,
payer_accepted, rejected, stalled). A receipt whose to_state == from_state moved
nothing (acknowledged, status_checked, deadline_approaching, deadline_missed) and
renders as a dimmer NOTE on the same timeline, not a hop — keep the existing

DO NOT TOUCH: anything under backend/ (all of it already shipped); the scrub
