title: Trim comment prose to signal, one functional area per PR
description:
Comment and docstring density across the codebase runs high enough that the
signal gets lost in it: long narrative module docstrings, prose that restates
the line below it, and rationale paragraphs defending decisions rather than
stating them.

The insurance-billing and Stripe surface has been done (see the trim PR) and
came out at roughly 800 lines of prose removed for 400 added, with no
behaviour change. This is the same pass, one functional area per PR so each
stays reviewable.

The rule that worked:

* KEEP anything naming a trap, a decision that looks wrong until explained,
  a standards citation, or a "this is deliberately NOT done because".
* CUT prose restating the code, bolded multi-paragraph essays before the
  first line of a module, test docstrings repeating the assertion below
  them, and any comment justifying a design instead of fixing it.
* Comments should read as notes a colleague left, not as documentation
  written for an audience that does not exist.

No behaviour changes and no bug fixes in these PRs. Anything that looks like
a real defect gets its own bead.
acceptance_criteria: Every child closed. No behaviour change in any of them. make check green on each.
notes:
PR DESCRIPTION STYLE for every child of this epic (Kurt's ask, 2026-09-11).

A line or two of personality — not the full routine pablo#1100 ran. That one
was the flagship and earned a Kirk Lazarus epigraph; these are follow-ups and
should read as the same person on a quieter day.

What that means concretely:

* Open with one fitting quote, or skip it if none lands. Canon Kurt has cited:
  Trading Places, Tropic Thunder, Vegas Vacation, Weird Science, Beverly Hills
  Cop 3. A quote only works if both parties know the scene — do not reach for
  obscure ones to fill the slot.
* Include one honest self-roast where there IS one: the specific thing that
  was wrong, quoted from the diff. "I wrote X, here is why that was daft"
  beats a generic line about verbosity. If nothing embarrassing turned up in
  that area, say so plainly and move on rather than manufacturing a bit.
* Keep the rest factual and short: what was cut, what was kept and why, the
  line count, and the checks that ran.

These may get posted publicly, so no real names, no client detail, nothing
that reads as a dig at anyone but the author.

NOT in bug reports, incident comments or anything someone will read while
hunting the problem six months from now. Straight prose there.

title: Find what holds the persistent row lock on claims during a pipeline run
description:
A live deployment showed a lock timeout on the same `claims` row on every
pipeline pass:

    canceling statement due to lock timeout
    CONTEXT: while updating tuple (0,8) in relation "claims"
      poll_acknowledgments -> _apply_feed -> apply_fetched

It persisted across a service roll, so it is not one stuck connection belonging
to a single long-lived process.

The reconcile loop it triggered is fixed (PABLO-02vb): a stage failure can no
longer roll back an earlier stage's committed work. But the contention itself
was never explained, and a pipeline that reliably fails one stage for one
practice on every run is still wrong — it just fails less destructively now.

Two candidates worth checking first:

- An idle-in-transaction session holding the row. `pg_stat_activity` will say,
  along with `pg_locks` joined against it.
- Two clinician runs contending. `practice_user_ids` falls back to EVERY
  platform user when a practice has no `email_tenant_mappings` rows, and a run
  reporting `clinicians=1553` across 78 practices suggests that fallback is
  firing widely. The dispatch fires every five minutes; if a sweep takes longer
  than the interval, two runs overlap and contend on the same rows.

The second would also mean the pipeline is doing hugely more work than it
needs to, which is worth knowing independently of the lock.

title: Batch the per-patient coverage lookup in the unbilled queue
design:
SCOPE: remove the one true N+1 on the unbilled queue and the two compounding costs in the same route.

VERIFIED POINTERS (re-locate on current main before editing): backend/app/routes/billing_queue.py:120-124 calls coverage_repo.get_active(patient_id) inside a dict comprehension over patient_ids (one SELECT per patient); :96 notes_repo.list_finalized(user.id) passes no limit though the repository accepts one (backend/app/repositories/note.py:90, limit keyword documented at :82-86); :174 audit.log_session_action(SESSION_VIEWED, ...) sits INSIDE the item loop, and SESSION_VIEWED is in _COALESCED_READ_ACTIONS (backend/app/services/audit_service.py:37), so each call is a Redis round trip plus a possible insert. Coverage repository: abstract get_active at backend/app/repositories/coverage.py:66, in-memory twin at :122, Postgres at backend/app/repositories/postgres/coverage.py:135. Audit-hoist precedent to copy: backend/app/routes/practice_balances.py:92-102 logs ONE row for the whole list.

PLAN: (1) add get_active_for_patients(patient_ids) returning dict[str, PatientCoverage] to the abstract interface, the in-memory repository, and the Postgres repository -- one SELECT WHERE patient_id IN (...) with the same active-row semantics get_active has -- and use it at :120; (2) pass a limit to list_finalized -- PRE-ANSWERED: a module constant UNBILLED_QUEUE_NOTE_LIMIT = 500, an order of magnitude above a busy year's unbilled sessions; the queue surfaces recent unbilled work, and an unbounded read is the bug; (3) hoist the audit out of the loop into ONE log call per request naming the surviving session ids (mirror practice_balances.py:92-102), keeping the payload to ids only.

OUT OF SCOPE: changing which rows the queue shows or their order; touching _COALESCED_READ_ACTIONS; any frontend change; index work (separate).

FILES: backend/app/routes/billing_queue.py, backend/app/repositories/coverage.py, backend/app/repositories/postgres/coverage.py, backend/tests/ (route tests), backend/tests_integration/ if a query-count assertion needs real Postgres.

Commit and PR text: plain and human-toned, describing the batching; no tracker ids.
acceptance_criteria: 1. A test with 3+ patients asserts the coverage repository is hit ONCE for the batch, not once per patient (spy or query counter). 2. The queue returns the same rows, in the same order, as before (existing route tests stay green; add a fixture with mixed settled/claimed/unbilled rows if none exists). 3. Exactly one audit row per request, naming the session ids; a test asserts the audit call count does not scale with the number of items. 4. The audit payload carries no PHI (ids only). 5. list_finalized is called with UNBILLED_QUEUE_NOTE_LIMIT and the constant is 500. DONE SIGNAL: the batch-call and single-audit tests fail against current main and pass with the change; full backend suite green.
notes: Filed by the eng-head pass 2026-09-10 (evening, interactive) from the SaaS board's spec (re-homed here because the work lands in this repo). Six-gate walk recorded on the SaaS twin. Read-path performance + audit hoist only; no change to which rows the queue shows.

title: The unbilled queue loads a practice's entire billing history, every time
description:
GET /api/billing/unbilled-sessions has no limit and no pagination.

It lists EVERY finalized note for the user (notes_repo.list_finalized, no
limit passed), then multi-gets sessions, appointments, succeeded charge kinds,
latest claims, patients, coverage and appointment types for all of them, and
returns the lot. The page renders every row.

The size grows with practice history and never shrinks, because a visit can
only leave the queue by being billed (see sibling bead) — so today's list is
every session a practice has ever finalized and not billed.

Measured on the dev test tenant 2026-09-10: 375 rows. That is enough to make
the Billing page slow enough that an e2e racing it fails in a different place
each run. A real practice reaches those numbers in months, and reaches them on
the page they open every day.
design:
Page it, or window it, or both — but measure before choosing.

1. list_finalized already accepts `limit`; the route passes none. The cheapest
   first move is a bounded page with a "show more", which is honest about
   there being more rather than pretending the list is the whole truth.
2. A date window is the better product answer if the sibling bead lands
   ("from when did you start billing"), because then the list is naturally
   short.
3. Whichever is chosen, the per-row fan-out (six repository calls over the
   whole set) should be bounded by the same page rather than the whole
   history.

DO NOT paginate in the frontend over a full-history response. That fixes the
render and leaves the query.
acceptance_criteria: 1. The unbilled endpoint returns a bounded page rather than every finalized session. 2. The supporting repository calls are bounded by that page. 3. A tenant with hundreds of unbilled visits renders the Billing page without the list being the slow part. 4. make check passes.

title: A therapist cannot say "I am not billing this visit"
description:
There is no way to say "I am not billing this one".

Checked 2026-09-10: routes/billing_queue.py and components/billing/UnbilledQueue.tsx
contain no dismiss, skip, hide, or not-billable action of any kind. A visit
with a finalized note leaves the queue only by acquiring a succeeded charge or
a claim in state `paid`. Anything else keeps the row forever.

Therapists decline to bill for real reasons — a session they will not charge
for, a client they are seeing pro bono, a visit already settled outside Pablo.
Today each of those is a row that never goes away, and the queue slowly stops
being a to-do list.

Kurt's framing, which shapes the fix: they probably SHOULD still be tracked as
potential income and then discounted, rather than made to disappear. So the
resolution wanted here is DECIDE, not HIDE: bill it, write it off with a
reason, or mark it not billable with a reason — each of which leaves the money
accounted for.
design:
Give an unbilled visit a third answer besides "bill" and "leave it there".

DECISIONS CLOSED:
- The action records a REASON. A row that leaves the queue without one is
  indistinguishable from a bug, and unpickable a year later.
- It is not a delete. The visit stays queryable, and the practice financial
  report should be able to show what was declined and why — that is the
  "potential income, then discounted" view Kurt described.
- This is adjacent to the existing write-off work (pablo#1060, "Let a practice
  write off a client's balance, with a reason"). Read it before designing a
  second vocabulary for the same idea; reuse its reasons if they fit.

OPEN QUESTION worth settling before building: is "not billable" a property of
the VISIT or a zero-amount write-off on the client's ledger? The second keeps
one money model instead of two, and is probably right, but it needs saying
out loud.
acceptance_criteria: 1. An unbilled visit can be resolved without filing a claim or taking a charge. 2. The resolution records a reason. 3. The visit remains queryable and reportable rather than deleted. 4. The row leaves the unbilled queue. 5. make check passes.

title: Turning billing on shows every session the practice ever wrote
description:
A practice that has used Pablo for a year without billing, and then turns
billing on, is shown EVERY finalized session it has ever written as unbilled.

The queue is derived, not stored: get_unbilled_sessions lists every finalized
note and removes only the visits already settled by a succeeded charge or a
paid claim (routes/billing_queue.py). Nothing scopes it to "since you started
billing", because there is no such moment recorded.

That is not a work queue, it is an accusation — a year of sessions presented
as things the therapist failed to bill. And it is a real number: the dev test
tenant currently shows 375 rows, which is simply every session anyone has
seeded since the feature landed.

The practice-inbox and calendar connect flows both ask before they act. Billing
does not ask anything; it is on, and the backlog is already there.
design:
Ask "from when" as part of turning billing on, and honour the answer.

DECISIONS TO CLOSE FIRST:
- Where does the answer live? A billing-start date on the practice billing
  profile is the obvious home, and the queue then filters on session date.
- What is the default? Suggest a date rather than defaulting silently — the
  first session of the current month is a reasonable suggestion; "everything"
  must be a deliberate choice, not the fallback.
- Sessions BEFORE the date are not deleted or hidden forever. Kurt's point,
  and it is the right one: a therapist may still want them counted as
  potential income and then discounted, rather than vanished. So the earlier
  work should be reachable — a "before I started billing" view, or simply the
  ability to move the date back — not erased.

DO NOT solve this by adding a "dismiss" that only hides a row. Hiding money is
how a practice loses track of it; see the sibling bead.

Model + migration ship together if this adds a column.
acceptance_criteria: 1. Enabling billing asks from when, with a suggested date rather than a silent default. 2. The unbilled queue only shows visits on or after that date. 3. Choosing 'everything' is possible but deliberate. 4. Earlier sessions remain reachable rather than erased. 5. make check passes.

title: A claim that never reaches the payer tells us nothing — we do not subscribe to file.failed
description:
The clearinghouse emits three event types. We subscribe to one of them.

    transaction.processed   a payer response or a submission was translated   SUBSCRIBED
    file.delivered          the clearinghouse delivered a claim to the payer  not subscribed
    file.failed             processing or delivery FAILED                     not subscribed

Read back from the vendor 2026-09-10: the dev destination
(dst_01a08967-20e0-76e3-a47f-e59bb41b61eb) lists eventTypes
["event.ping", "transaction.processed"]. The production destination was
registered the same way.

So when a claim is accepted by the clearinghouse and then FAILS to reach the
payer, nothing tells us. No event arrives, no state changes, and the claim
sits where it was. The only thing that eventually notices is the watchdog
timing it out — which reports "nobody answered" when the truth is "it never
got there". Those want different actions from a practice: one is waiting, the
other is refiling.

This is the same shape as every other defect found on 2026-09-10: a real
failure arriving as silence.
design:
Two halves, and the first is worth doing even without the second.

1. SUBSCRIBE. Add file.failed to both destinations' eventTypes (dev first).
   That is a vendor-side configuration change, not code — the destination
   update endpoint takes the event type list.

2. HANDLE IT. The webhook route currently answers anything that is not
   transaction.processed with "ignored" and a 200 (routes/claim_webhooks.py).
   A file.failed needs to reach the claim: record a receipt saying the
   clearinghouse could not deliver it, and put the claim in front of the
   clinician as something to act on rather than something to wait for.

DECISIONS TO CLOSE FIRST, not while building:
- What state does a delivery failure put a claim in? "stalled" already means
  "nobody has answered", which is precisely the wrong story. It may want its
  own state, or a receipt kind with no transition — decide deliberately, and
  note that TERMINAL_STATES and the watchdog both read state.
- file.delivered is the happy-path twin and is NOT obviously worth having: it
  says a claim reached the payer, which the 277CA already says with more
  detail. Subscribing to it adds volume for little signal. Default to leaving
  it off unless somebody argues otherwise.
- Confirm the exact payload shape of file.failed from the vendor before
  parsing it. Do not build against a guess — the whole reason PABLO-1qox took
  a day is that both sides of a seam were imagined rather than observed.

DO NOT subscribe production until dev has seen one and the handler is proven.
acceptance_criteria: 1. The dev destination subscribes to file.failed. 2. A file.failed delivery records a receipt against the named claim rather than being answered 'ignored'. 3. The resulting claim state distinguishes 'the clearinghouse could not deliver this' from 'nobody has answered yet'. 4. The payload shape is confirmed against a real vendor event, not assumed. 5. Production is unchanged until dev has seen one. 6. make check passes.

title: A control number repeated in 200 draws — 1-in-54,000, so probably not chance
description:
tests/test_claim_assembly.py::test_control_numbers_do_not_repeat failed in CI
on 2026-09-10 (pablo#1073, run 34507962961):

    numbers = {new_control_number(_NOW) for _ in range(200)}
    assert len(numbers) == 200
    AssertionError: assert 199 == 200

Two of two hundred control numbers were identical.

DO NOT file this as an ordinary flaky test without reading the numbers first.
The test pins `now`, so the base32 timestamp prefix is constant and uniqueness
rests entirely on the random suffix: _CONTROL_RANDOM_LENGTH = 6 characters
from a 32-character alphabet, which is 1,073,741,824 possibilities.

    P(collision in 200 draws) = 0.00002   (~1 in 54,000 runs)

So "it is just the birthday problem" does not explain it. Either we witnessed
a 1-in-54,000 event, or something is wrong with the entropy the suffix is
drawn from — assembly.py uses secrets.choice, which reads the OS CSPRNG, and a
CI container with a degraded entropy source is the kind of thing that would
produce exactly this and nothing else.

Why it matters beyond a red build: the control number is what every
acknowledgement and remittance is matched on. Two claims sharing one would
have a payer's money posted against the wrong visit. The claims.control_number
unique constraint is the backstop and would refuse the second INSERT, so the
blast radius is a failed claim rather than a misposted payment — but the
generator is supposed to make that constraint unreachable, and here it did not.
design:
Investigate before changing anything.

1. Re-run the test in a loop (10k iterations) locally and in a CI container.
   If collisions appear at anything like the observed rate, it is the entropy
   source, not chance.
2. If it reproduces in CI only, look at the runner image's /dev/urandom and
   whether anything reseeds or sandboxes it.
3. Only if 1 and 2 come back clean should this be treated as the rare event it
   is statistically allowed to be — and even then, consider widening the
   suffix, because a generator whose collisions are refused by a database
   constraint is a claim that silently fails to file.

DO NOT "fix" this by loosening the assertion to `>= 199` or by seeding the
test. The assertion is correct; it caught something.
acceptance_criteria: 1. The collision either reproduces under a loop test (entropy problem, fixed at the source) or is shown not to reproduce in 10k+ runs locally and in a CI container. 2. The finding is recorded on the bead either way. 3. The test's assertion is unchanged — it is not loosened to make the build green.
notes:
LOCAL LOOP TEST 2026-09-10: 20,000 trials of 200 draws on this Mac, using the same alphabet and suffix length through secrets.choice — ZERO collisions. Expected count at the calculated rate is 0.37, so zero is the most likely outcome and this neither confirms nor refutes anything; it does rule out a grossly broken local entropy source.

What it leaves: the collision was observed only in a GitHub Actions runner. Step 2 of the design (look at the runner container's entropy) is now the live question, not step 1. If it never recurs, the honest conclusion is the rare event — but this bead should stay open long enough to see whether it does, because the cost of being wrong is a claim that cannot file.
PROPOSED REMEDY 2026-09-10 (Kurt): stamp MILLISECONDS, not seconds.

Kurt asked whether control numbers should simply be strictly increasing —
00001, 00002 — and answered his own question: too guessable. That is right,
and the reason is worth writing down so nobody re-opens it:

- Spoofing is NOT the risk. Nothing user-facing looks a claim up by control
  number (the app keys on the claim's UUID), and inbound matching only happens
  on a signature-verified webhook. Verified 2026-09-10.
- LEAKAGE is the risk. A sequence publishes volume. Anyone holding two of a
  practice's remittances — a payer, a clearinghouse — learns how many claims
  were filed between them. For a solo therapy practice that is patient volume,
  which is revenue, and it is printed on every EOB.
- A strict sequence also needs a counter: per-practice means a lock on every
  build and still leaks that practice's volume; global means a cross-tenant
  write bottleneck and a shared object reachable from every schema, against
  the isolation model.
- X12 does not want it either. CLM01 must be UNIQUE to the provider, not
  sequential. The field that conventionally ascends is ISA13/GS06, the
  interchange envelope, which the vendor builds — not us.

So monotonic-to-the-instant plus randomness is the right shape (this is the
ULID / UUIDv7 pattern). The defect is not the shape, it is the RESOLUTION:

    stamp = int((now or utc_now()).timestamp())      # assembly.py — SECONDS

Two claims built in the same second rest entirely on the six random
characters, which is exactly the surface this bead is about. Milliseconds
shrink that window by ~1000x and sharpen the ordering, and they attack WHY two
numbers can collide rather than merely making it rarer — which is what
widening the random part would do.

THE LENGTH BUDGET, checked rather than assumed (2026-09-10):
- CLAIM_CONTROL_NUMBER_MAX_LENGTH = 17 (db/models.py:2198), enforced on CLM01
  by scrub.py:454.
- Second-resolution today: 7-char base32 prefix + 6 random = 13.
- Millisecond resolution: 9-char prefix (32^9 = 3.5e13 > any ms timestamp
  this century) + 6 random = 15. Inside 17.
- Line numbers derive as f"{control}L{n}", so 15 + "L1" = 17, and 18 for a
  two-digit line. I thought that was a blocker; it is not. The scrub's line
  rule (scrub.py:465-476) checks presence, X12 charset and distinctness and
  does NOT bound length, and REF02 in 005010 is AN 1/50 on the wire. So the
  derived line number has room.

DO NOT widen _CONTROL_RANDOM_LENGTH instead. It papers over the same-second
window rather than shrinking it, and it spends the character budget on the
part that is already the stronger half.

Still open regardless of this remedy: the observed collision was in a fixed-
`now` test, so its prefix was constant by construction and milliseconds would
NOT have prevented it. This remedy reduces production risk; it does not
explain the CI observation. Both halves of this bead stand.

title: The claims pipeline's polling stage cannot read the harness's answers (DiscriminatorError every run)
description:
Found 2026-09-10 alongside the webhook 400. Every time the in-process claims pipeline runs against the e2e stack it logs, five times per pass:

  clearinghouse_sdk_error_untranslated type=DiscriminatorError

from backend.app.claims.sdk_runtime. The submission stage works — the claim reaches the fake on the native endpoint and comes back accepted — so this is the stage that asks about a claim afterwards failing to deserialize what the harness answers.

Two things are wrong and both are worth fixing. The SDK cannot read the answer, and our own error translation does not recognise the failure either, so it surfaces as an untranslated warning with no claim id, no endpoint and no hint of which payload failed.
design:
Two separable pieces:

(a) The translation gap. sdk_runtime logs 'untranslated' and drops it. A DiscriminatorError is the SDK failing to pick a variant for a union, which is a response-shape problem, not a transport one — it should map to something the caller can act on and the log line should carry the endpoint, so the next person does not have to guess which call failed.

(b) The shape gap. Find which endpoint the pipeline is polling and what the harness answers, then decide which is wrong against the vendor's own recordings in backend/tests/fixtures/clearinghouse/ — claim_timeline_paid_in_full.json is a real capture and is the reference for the native lifecycle API.

Related: PABLO-zz6p.4 moves this stage onto the claim-lifecycle API, which may replace the failing call outright. Check whether that bead subsumes (b) before doing (b).
acceptance_criteria:
1. A full claims-pipeline pass against the compose stack logs no DiscriminatorError.
2. A response the SDK cannot deserialize maps to a typed clearinghouse error and its log line names the endpoint.
3. A unit test covers that translation, driven by a response the SDK genuinely rejects rather than a hand-built exception.
notes:
PARTLY FIXED 2026-09-10 on branch enrollment-tasks (pablo#1056).

(a) The translation gap is closed. An answer the SDK cannot parse is no longer
reported as 'unavailable' — which was wrong in a way that mattered, since
retrying an unreadable answer produces the same unreadable answer. It now maps
to ClearinghouseValidationError, and the log names the call:

  clearinghouse_sdk_answer_unreadable operation=get_claim_timeline type=DiscriminatorError

That one word is what turned this from a mystery into a morning.

(b) The shape gap: the harness never served the claim-lifecycle timeline at
all, which the remittance stage has called since the SDK move. It now serves
GET /2025-03-07/claims/{id}/timeline from claim_timeline_paid_in_full.json —
a real capture — trimmed to what has actually happened to the claim being
asked about, and refuses an unknown claim in the vendor's error envelope
rather than the framework's (the SDK parses the refusal too, and could not
read a FastAPI {detail: ...}).

STILL TO CONFIRM: the surviving DiscriminatorErrors in the log were all
timestamped before the harness rebuild landed, and the window after it is thin.
Run the pipeline against the stack for a few minutes and confirm the line is
gone for claims the harness knows. If any remain, the endpoint is answering
something the SDK still cannot read — curl it and compare against the SDK's
CLAIM_TIMELINE_EVENTS union members, which are the five keys in
stedi/_private/schemas.py around line 5798.

title: Refresh enrollment status on a schedule, and tell the therapist when a payer wants something
description: A refresh button makes enrollment status right when somebody looks. It does not tell a therapist that a payer is waiting on them, which is the state that actually blocks an enrollment.
design:
Follows PABLO-5zlm, which adds the button and the route. This adds the part a
button cannot do.

THE JOB. `backend/app/jobs/payer_enrollment_refresh.py` already exists,
bounded by `--max-tenants` and `--max-per-tenant`, with tests
(`test_payer_enrollment_refresh_job.py`). It is not scheduled in either
project — checked directly against Cloud Scheduler on 2026-09-09, where the
sibling crons (compliance-reminder-cron, audit-outbox-shipper-cron,
practice-inbox-poll-cron) all exist. So: a Cloud Run job plus a Scheduler
entry in both projects, following an existing daily cron in
`.github/workflows/deploy.yml` (pablo-saas). `compliance-reminder-cron` is the
closest sibling, since the reminder it delivers is what this job produces.
Daily is right; the vendor moves in days, not minutes.

THE NOTIFICATION. `refresh_enrollments` already raises
`enrollment_action_required` and the default listener already turns it into a
compliance reminder — so in-app is done the moment the job runs. What is not
done is telling somebody who is not looking at the app. Decide the channel
deliberately: the reminder surface may be enough for a first customer, and an
email about payer paperwork is a small, safe, non-PHI message if it is not.

SOONER, AND BETTER THAN POLLING: the vendor publishes
`enrollment.task.assigned`, which IS this event, pushed. Subscribing turns
"within a day" into "within seconds". Both destinations are registered
already (dev dst_01a08967-20e0-76e3-a47f-e59bb41b61eb, prod
dst_01a0896e-4d1c-7783-8055-d17f2b5ebbfd) and subscribe to
transaction.processed and event.ping only. That work is PABLO-zxaq; do not
duplicate it here. The job remains worth having regardless, as the backstop
for a delivery that never arrives.

NOTE FOR TESTING: the vendor refuses test-mode keys on the enrollment API
(403), so the dev cron will run and find nothing it can act on. Schedule it
anyway - the wiring is what is being proven.
acceptance_criteria:
1. A Cloud Run job and a daily Scheduler entry exist in both projects.
2. A run records vendor status, mirrors payer status, and raises the event for a request needing provider action.
3. The compliance reminder carries the vendor instructions and resolves when the request moves on.
4. A vendor error in one practice is logged and the run continues to the next.
5. The notification channel beyond the in-app reminder is decided in writing, with the reason.

title: Assert the 835 balances before believing any number in it
description: An 835 is a balanced transaction: the adjustments must account for the whole gap between charged and paid. Checking that is the one validation that needs no real payer, and a failure means our parse is wrong or the payer's file is.
design:
Guaranteed by TR3 005010X221A1 section 1.10.2 (SNIP level 3). Assume the
vendor does not enforce it on inbound files.

Hard invariants - a failure means do not trust the document:
* LINE: SVC02 (charge) - sum(every CAS amount on the line, all group codes,
  all six triplets, signed) == SVC03 (paid)
* CLAIM: CLP03 - sum(claim-level CAS) - sum(all line CAS) == CLP04
* TRANSACTION: sum(CLP04) - sum(PLB amounts) == BPR02
* A reversal (CLP02 = 22) negates a prior adjudication: amounts are the
  negation of what was posted before.

Soft checks - warn, never fail:
* CARC / group-code pairing against the CAQH CORE Rule 360 code-combination
  table (free download). A `PR*253` or a `CO*1` is either a payer bug or a
  parse bug; either way stop and look.
* sum(PR) <= charge on a non-reversal claim. NOTE: "PR <= allowed" is NOT
  true in general - out of network, PR45 can push patient responsibility
  above the allowed amount.

Worth pairing with property-based testing: generate from a domain model
(fee schedule, deductible remaining, coinsurance, copay, out-of-network flag,
sequestration flag), render to an 835, parse it back, and assert both the
invariants and that the posted patient responsibility equals what the model
says the client owes. The model encodes the definition; the parser encodes our
code; the render-parse round trip is where the bugs are.

REVIEW FINDINGS 2026-09-09, two independent reviewers. The single highest-value
check, and it needs no real payer:

CLP05 (claim-level patient responsibility) SHOULD EQUAL the sum of the PR
adjustments across the claim. X12 RFI #2548 addresses exactly this. It matters
more than any other invariant here because it is an INDEPENDENT, PAYER-SUPPLIED
cross-check on precisely the half of our split that bills a client - the payer
states the total separately from the itemisation, so a mis-classified
adjustment shows up as a mismatch. And it fires on the FIRST real remittance we
ever receive rather than waiting for us to reason about it.

We already parse both sides: RemittanceClaim.patient_responsibility_cents is
CLP05, and the PR total comes from the line adjustments. The check is cheap.

Balancing identities, from TR3 005010X221A1 section 1.10.2 (SNIP level 3);
assume the vendor does not enforce them on inbound files:
* LINE: SVC02 (charge) - sum(every CAS amount on the line, all groups, all six
  triplets, signed) == SVC03 (paid)
* CLAIM: CLP03 - sum(claim-level CAS) - sum(all line CAS) == CLP04
* TRANSACTION: sum(CLP04) - sum(PLB) == BPR02

FREE AUTHORITATIVE SOURCES - verified accessible, no login:
* x12.org/examples/005010x221 - eight worked examples. Coverage is UNEVEN:
  some pages carry full narrative and EDI, at least one (Example 07, COB)
  defers to the licensed TR3. Treat as a partial free deck. Example 05,
  "Line Service Penalty Tax or Bonuses impacting payment only", is the
  standards body's own counterexample to deriving allowed from charge minus
  contractual.
* x12.org RFI database - the edge cases we worry about have already been
  formally adjudicated. RFI 2601 (charged vs allowed vs PR45), 2548 (CLP05 vs
  PR sum), 2551 (bundling), 2535/2570/2143 (secondary, OA23), 2348, 2371, 1705.
  A fixture built from an RFI ANSWER is not circular: the belief that wrote it
  came from the standards body.
* CAQH CORE Rule 360 code-combination table - ACA-mandated, the only public
  normative source for which group code may pair with which CARC.

COPYRIGHT, and it is load-bearing because pablo is world-readable: the TR3
itself is licensed and paid; the examples pages are free but still carry
"All X12 work products are copyrighted". Do NOT copy their EDI into this repo
and change the amounts - starting from their expression and editing it is a
derivative work. Read them for the SCENARIOS (which are facts about the
standard, not expression) and construct our own fixtures independently. Our
fixtures are the vendor's JSON rather than X12 anyway, which defuses most of
this.

RFI #2548 read directly, 2026-09-09. Confirms the CLP05 check and adds an
exception that is now implemented:

"CLP05 must equal the sum of all claim and service line adjustments with
Claim Adjustment Group Code PR. The exception is reversals (see section
1.10.2.8 of the 835 5010 TR3 guide). Note, CLP05 is not part of the
transaction balancing."

That last sentence is why the check is worth having: CLP05 is an INDEPENDENT
statement of the number rather than a restatement that the balancing
identities already constrain. Landed in pablo#1039 including the reversal
exemption.

Other RFIs worth reading before building the balancing invariants:
* #2348 - when the SVC segment is required at all (line-level pricing).
* #2320 - bundling; also the SVC06 down-coding rule (match on SVC06, not
  SVC01, or a down-coded line matches nothing).
* #1917 - line item control number, which is what we match on.
* #2399 / #2165 - splitting claim lines vs unbundling; a claim's lines can
  arrive across more than one remittance.
* #2371 - payers that decline to report an actual coinsurance amount.
* #2048 - group code CO used with coinsurance.
acceptance_criteria:
1. The line, claim and transaction balancing identities are asserted on every parsed remittance.
2. A failing identity is surfaced (and feeds the quarantine bead) rather than silently ignored.
3. The CARC/group pairing check exists as a warning against the CORE 360 table.
4. Property-based tests generate remittances from a domain model and assert posted patient responsibility matches the model.
5. `make check` passes.
notes:
VERIFIED 2026-09-10: half of this bead is already written and simply never
called.

app/claims/remittance_lines.py:146 patient_responsibility_agrees() compares
the payer's stated CLP05 total against the same figure itemised across the
service lines and claim-level adjustments — two independent statements of
one number — and exempts reversals (CLP02=22). It is correct, documented,
and covered by tests.

It has ZERO production callers. Only tests/test_remittance_lines.py and
tests/test_fake_clearinghouse.py call it. apply_posting writes the client's
ledger row without ever asking it. Its own docstring says "It fires on the
very first real remittance rather than waiting for anybody to reason about
it" — today it fires on none.

So the first increment here is wiring, not arithmetic: call it on the
posting path and decide what a disagreement does (refuse to post? post and
flag? quarantine, per PABLO-7awq?). That decision is the actual work.

Of the three X12 balances, the codebase can compute two from today's
dataclasses with no new fields:
  line:  SVC02 = SVC03 + sum(line CAS)
  claim: CLP03 = CLP04 + sum(all CAS on the claim)
The third — BPR02 = sum(CLP04) - sum(PLB) — is not computable: there is no
PLB model, field, or parser branch anywhere. Also absent: a stated sign
convention for CAS/PLB amounts (responses.py:143 runs dollars_to_cents raw,
so negative CAS works by accident, not by design), BPR01
transactionHandlingCode (an 'H' zero-dollar advice would fail a naive
balance check), and any column to record a balance outcome on.

Evidence note: no complete, unambiguously public-domain 835 carrying
service-line CO-45 appears to exist to test against — see
pablo-saas docs/internal/era-data-sourcing.md for the search. The rule is
free to implement; the realistic fixture is not.
SETTLED BY QUERY 2026-09-10, not by reading docs. Kurt pushed on whether the
vendor really has no test-mode lever for a denial or a partial payment, on the
grounds that the claim rested on documentation — and documentation had already
been wrong twice today. So the payer network was asked directly with our own
test key.

    payer search "test"  -> FRCPB  "Stedi Test Payer"   (ONE result)
    payer search "mock"  -> nothing
    payer search "demo"  -> real payers whose NAMES contain "demo"
                            (Caresource Military and Veterans, TRISTAR
                            Insurance Group), not fixtures

THERE IS EXACTLY ONE TEST PAYER. No denial variant, no partial-payment
variant, no second mock to point a claim at. Its declared support:

    professionalClaimSubmission  SUPPORTED
    eligibilityCheck             SUPPORTED
    claimPayment                 ENROLLMENT_REQUIRED
    coordinationOfBenefits       NOT_SUPPORTED

So what test mode CAN and CANNOT produce, with the evidence for each:

  claim REJECTION      YES. "Stedi doesn't forward test claims to payers.
                       Instead, we apply our entire catalog of edits and
                       repairs and then generate a test 277CA claim
                       acknowledgment indicating whether the test claim passed
                       our validation." Proven by our own three captured
                       837p_submission_edit_rejected_* fixtures, which were
                       made by submitting genuinely invalid claims.

  eligibility failures YES. Documented mock members; we hold captures of
                       inactive coverage and of an AAA error.

  DENIAL (CLP02=4)     NO lever found.
  PARTIAL / CO-45      NO lever found.

The remaining honest limit: "the test 835 always pays in full, with the same
charge amounts you submitted" is still vendor documentation plus our single
capture, not something a query can prove. What the query DID rule out is the
most plausible way that could have been wrong — an alternate payer to aim at.

CONSEQUENCE, and it is the same conclusion this bead already reached from the
fixture side: rejections are testable for real, adjudication outcomes are not.
A denial, a partial payment, or a contractual write-off can only come from a
real payer, which is PABLO-zpon.

title: Quarantine remittance shapes no real payer has shown us yet
description: Every adjustment scenario in the suite is a fixture we wrote, because the vendor test payer pays in full and adjusts nothing. Rather than guess, refuse to move client money on a shape that has never been observed.
design:
Posting a wrong client balance is the expensive failure. Until a real payer
has shown us a shape, record the remittance and post NOTHING to the client,
surfacing it for review instead.

Quarantine when any of these hold:
* a balancing invariant fails (see the invariants bead)
* CLP02 (claim status) is not 1 (processed as primary) or 4 (denied)
* claim-level CAS is present (do not allocate claim-level patient
  responsibility across lines - there is no correct way to)
* a negative CAS amount outside a reversal
* PR45, OA23 or PI present - out-of-network, secondary, payer-initiated
* the payer-reported allowed amount disagrees with paid + sum(PR) by more than
  a cent

Relax each shape as a real payer proves it. This turns "we cannot validate
without a real payer" into "we will not act until a real payer has been seen",
which is the right posture for a number that bills a client.

REVIEW FINDING 2026-09-09: unknown and zero are currently conflated, and they
mean opposite things.

AMT*B6 (allowed) is "required when the value is non-zero" - the standard says
send one for each applicable NON-ZERO value and do not report zeros. So a
fully denied line, a bundled or incidental line, and a non-covered service all
arrive with NO allowed amount, and pablo#1038 reports None ("we do not know")
where the truth is zero ("the payer allowed nothing"). A report cannot tell
those apart.

DELIBERATELY NOT FIXED YET, and the reasoning should not be lost: the proposed
fix is to classify a line as denied/bundled from its CARC set and assert zero.
That is another inference of exactly the kind pablo#1038 removed - it depends
on knowing which CARC sets really mean "denied", which is payer behaviour we
cannot validate. Allowed is informational and bills nobody, so a blank costs
little while a confident wrong zero costs a misleading report. Decide it
against real ERAs (PABLO-zpon), not against reasoning.

Same reasoning for claim-level allowed: the vendor DOES surface
paymentInfo[].claimSupplementalInformation.coverageAmount, but that is AMT*AU
(total covered charges - excludes non-covered, includes deductible), which is
NOT the same quantity as AMT*B6 (payer payment plus assigned patient
responsibility). Mapping one onto the other is a third inference. Verify
against a real ERA before using it.

RFI FINDINGS 2026-09-09, read directly from the X12 interpretations. Two of
these CORRECT assumptions written above.

CORRECTION - "a negative CAS outside a reversal" is NOT inherently suspicious
and must not quarantine on its own. RFI #2320 (835 SVC06 Requirement) has
bundling produce exactly that: the bundled-away lines carry CARC 97 with an
adjustment equal to the submitted charge, and the surviving line is adjusted
UP by the sum of the other line charges, reported as group OA reason 94
("Processed in Excess of Charges") with a NEGATIVE amount. A perfectly
ordinary bundled claim would trip that rule.

CORRECTION - secondary/COB is a DOUBLE-BILLING risk, not merely an unseen
shape, and it is the most dangerous thing on this list. RFI #2548: "The
secondary payer should not re-report prior payer patient responsibility
amounts. The secondary payer should report PR adjustments that they have
assigned per their adjudication." So each remittance carries only THAT
payer's own assignment. Our ledger writes a patient_resp row per posting, so
a secondary remittance arriving for a claim we already posted would write a
SECOND row - billing the client twice for one session. The fix is not to sum
across remittances; a later payer's assignment supersedes the earlier one.
Quarantine COB until that is modelled.

RFI #2570 - OA-23 may be reported at claim level OR line level but never
both: "Service level adjustments are not repeated at the claim level." Which
also confirms that adding claim-level and line-level PR together is correct
rather than double counting.

RFI #2535 - OA-23 is "the payments and contractual reductions that have
already been posted to the AR by the provider". It is a restatement of what
we already recorded from the primary, so it must never be posted again.
acceptance_criteria:
1. A quarantined remittance records the claim-level posting and writes no patient_resp ledger row.
2. Each listed shape has a test that proves it quarantines.
3. A quarantined remittance is visible for review, not merely logged.
4. An ordinary in-network paid claim is NOT quarantined.
5. `make check` passes.

title: Move claim submission to the vendor native API, so filed claims have a timeline
description: Claim submission is the one keyed operation: the caller mints an idempotency key, persists it, and depends on documented replay semantics (same key and body replays; different body is refused; in-flight is a 409 with a retry hint). The SDK does not document control of that header, so submission moves last and only if it can.
design:
LAST child of this epic. Do not start until the eligibility and claim-lifecycle
beads are closed.

First establish whether the SDK can set `Idempotency-Key` on
`CreateProfessionalClaim`. Its documented config surface is only `api_key` and
`retry_strategy`, and it exposes no transport injection, so this may be
impossible.

If it CAN: move `submit_claim` to the SDK, preserving the caller-minted key and
the existing typed errors - `ClearinghouseRequestChangedError` (422),
`ClearinghouseInFlightError` (409 with `retry_after`).

If it CANNOT: leave `submit_claim` on httpx, write down why in the bead notes,
and close. That is a legitimate outcome, not a failure. A mixed adapter is
correct here.

Also check whether the per-claim `usageIndicator: "T"` (`backend/app/claims/
wire.py:97`) is still needed now that test mode is derived from the key, or
whether it now conflicts. Answer it with a call against test mode, not by
reading docs.

Do NOT relax the idempotency contract to fit the SDK. If the SDK cannot honour
it, the SDK does not get this method.

BLOCKER RESOLVED — probed live 2026-09-09. `idempotency_key` is a first-class
field on `CreateProfessionalClaimSubmissionInput`, so the KEYED submit this
bead was gated on is supported. The gate is closed; this is buildable.

It is also now a PREREQUISITE rather than the last step: the claim-lifecycle
API only knows claims submitted through its own endpoint (see PABLO-zz6p.4),
so the remittance reader stays dark until this lands.

Request-shape notes from the probe, so nobody re-derives them:
- `authorization` is REQUIRED despite being optional in the SDK type. Its
  four fields are legible enums (patient_releases_medical_info=YES,
  insured_authorizes_assignment=YES, provider_accepts_assignment=ASSIGNED,
  provider_signature=ON_FILE) rather than the X12 single letters.
- Service lines carry `diagnosis_codes` as actual codes, not pointers into a
  claim-level list. That removes the pointer-mismatch class of edit rejection
  entirely.
- Dates are ISO (`2026-09-01`), not `YYYYMMDD`.
- `patient` is omitted when the patient is the subscriber; the subscriber is
  `insured`.
- Validation failures come back field-by-field with a JSON path, which is a
  far better scrub signal than the legacy edit rejections.

DONE 2026-09-09, pablo#1032. Submission now goes to the vendor native claim
API through the SDK; the stored vendor_claim_id is the vendor CLAIM id (stable
across resubmissions), which is what GetClaimTimeline is keyed on.

Proven live end to end: file -> 277CA -> 835 -> a `pay` posting for the full
charge with its trace number, in about 30 seconds, through production code.
The durable version is
backend/tests_integration/clearinghouse_live/test_native_round_trip.py.

Facts established against the vendor, so nobody re-derives them:
- Same idempotency key + same claim REPLAYS the original claim id, files
  nothing new. Same key + changed claim is refused. Both verified live.
- A refused claim arrives two ways under ONE exception type: a JSON-schema
  failure carrying field paths, and a whole-claim rule carrying only a
  sentence. Both now reject the claim with the reason attached rather than
  stalling it. A reused key is the exception that still raises.
- A one-day session must send dates_of_service.start only. Sending start==end
  makes it an X12 range segment and the 835 comes back WITHOUT the service
  date the legacy 835 reader looks for.
- Acknowledgement matching was NOT broken by the switch: 277CAs are matched on
  the patient control number, not the vendor claim id.

Genuinely lost, and accepted: native edit rejections carry no numeric code and
no follow-up action, and an unenrolled payer is no longer distinguishable from
a key that may not file claims (both are a refusal to serve). Both still stall
or reject with text a biller can read.

CORRECTION 2026-09-09, probed live. The two things recorded above as
"genuinely lost" were overstated. Both were checked against the API.

EDIT REJECTION CODES - not a loss. The native rejection carries prose instead
of a code, and the prose is strictly more useful than what it replaced. A real
one: "Invalid ICD-10-CM Diagnosis Code. The submitted principal diagnosis code
must be valid and to the highest level of specificity. Diagnosis code F41 is
category codes and considered non-billable. Correct and resubmit." The legacy
code was `33`, a generic "failed front-end edits" bucket naming neither the
field nor the reason. Do NOT reverse-engineer codes out of that text: it is
fragile, it gains nothing, and the sentence is the useful part. Checked
whether structured codes survive elsewhere - the rejection 277CA IS on the
claim timeline with status REJECTED, but neither GetClaimTimeline nor GetClaim
exposes its X12 status codes.

UNENROLLED vs BAD KEY - the distinction no longer exists at submit time, and
does not need to. Filed a claim to Aetna (60054), a payer this account is not
enrolled with: ACCEPTED, clm_7DKP0R8JVVAYYR8QE5HFZAKV8B, no errors. The claim
API does not check enrollment synchronously at all; an enrollment problem
surfaces later as a 277CA rejection on the timeline.
ClearinghouseNotProvisionedError was mapping a failure mode this endpoint does
not produce. Nothing was lost because there was nothing to distinguish.
acceptance_criteria:
1. The bead notes state, from an actual test-mode call, whether the SDK can set `Idempotency-Key`.
2. Either submission is on the SDK with the caller-minted key and both typed errors still raised for their vendor conditions; or it remains on httpx with the reason recorded.
3. The behaviour of `usageIndicator` under key-derived test mode is recorded from an observed call.
4. The live lane submission tests, including the reject and dependent cases, pass.
5. `make check` passes.

title: Check a claim against the vendor edit database before submitting it
description: Our scrub is roughly 600 lines of edit rules with no external check. The vendor exposes a validate operation that runs a claim against its own edit database without submitting it, and test mode now supports the full claims workflow, so this costs nothing per call.
design:
Add a `validate_claim` method to `ClearinghouseClient` backed by the SDK
`ValidateProfessionalClaim` operation, and use it as an oracle for
`backend/app/claims/scrub.py` in tests: build claims that our scrub passes, and
assert the vendor also accepts them; build claims our scrub rejects, and record
what the vendor says.

The value here is test signal, not a new product surface. Do NOT wire validation
into the live submission path in this bead - that is a product decision about
latency and failure modes that has not been made.

Depends on the async protocol bead and the SDK being wired at all.

Related, and worth doing in the same diff only if it stays small: the vendor
professional-claim JSON is modelled on the CMS-1500 form, and we already model
that form in `backend/app/claims/cms1500.py` and `cms1500_layout.py`. If the
mapping is close, say so in the notes; if it is not, do not force it.

1. `validate_claim` exists on the protocol and is implemented against the SDK.
2. A test in the live lane validates at least one claim our scrub accepts and asserts the vendor accepts it too.
3. Any disagreement between our scrub and the vendor edit database is written down in the bead notes, whether or not it is fixed here.
4. Nothing in the live submission path calls validate.
5. `make check` passes.

title: Compute bookable slots in one place, not once per booking surface
description:
Every booking surface computes its own answer to "what may be booked", and
they have already drifted apart.

Each one starts from AvailabilityEngine.get_free_slots and then narrows the
result its own way — the minimum-notice window, the booking horizon, whether
over-cap slots are offered, and what a returned timestamp is taken to mean.

The two in-tree surfaces disagree on two of those today:

- public_booking filters over_cap out unconditionally (_public_slots), on the
  stated grounds that an unauthenticated path must never hand out a soft cap
  deliberately. patient_booking keeps them.
- public_booking calls get_free_slots with no tz and documents the result as
  the practice local wall-clock with a cosmetic Z suffix. patient_booking
  passes the clinician timezone and returns genuine instants.

Both are individually defensible and both are documented. Together they mean a
caller cannot reason about "the bookable set" without first knowing which route
answered, and a fix to one does not reach the other. This is the same shape as
the rule-params duplication in PABLO-vs1k: the defect is that the rule lives in
several hand-kept copies, not that any one copy is currently wrong.

The cost is not hypothetical. patient_booking landed with the availability
check missing entirely; its tests still passed, because the listing endpoint
honoured the rules and every test booked a slot it had been offered. Two
computations that are supposed to agree, verified only against each other,
agree right up until one of them is absent.
acceptance_criteria:
1. One offer function in the scheduling-engine layer, taking the engine, the
   user, the date, the duration, the notice/horizon window, the timezone and an
   explicit over-cap policy, returning the slots that may be offered.
2. Both routes call it and do no further narrowing of their own. A route that
   still filters the result afterwards has not adopted the seam.
3. The timestamp convention is decided once, stated once, and applied by the
   seam — not chosen per route. Whichever way it goes, the choice and its
   reason are written down where the function lives.
4. Over-cap handling is a parameter with an explicit default, not a per-route
   habit. public_booking keeping its stricter setting is fine; keeping it as
   private local code is not.
5. A test per surface pins that what GET offers is exactly what POST accepts —
   the property the duplication is currently relied upon to provide by accident.
6. No behaviour change to existing public booking links unless it is chosen
   deliberately and called out; this is a consolidation, not a redesign.

title: Recovery-code redemption shares a rate-limit budget with passkey login
description:
Five endpoints share one pre-auth limiter keyed on client IP at 10 requests per 60 seconds (rate_limit.py: _get_preauth_limiter, max_requests=10, window_seconds=60):

  POST /api/auth/native/code
  POST /api/auth/native/exchange
  POST /api/auth/passkey/authenticate/begin
  POST /api/auth/passkey/authenticate/finish
  POST /api/auth/passkey/recovery-code/redeem

A single passkey sign-in spends two of those (begin + finish), so the shared window is roughly five sign-ins per minute for everyone sharing an egress IP.

THE INTERACTION THAT MATTERS

Recovery-code redemption is what a user reaches for when their passkey is not working. Because it draws on the same budget as the sign-in attempts they just made, the failure is self-reinforcing: authentication struggles, the user retries, the retries consume the window, and the recovery path is then refused with 429 — precisely at the moment it is needed. Behind a shared office address or carrier NAT, a colleague's sign-ins can close the escape hatch for someone else.

This is the same argument rate_limit.py already makes, two blocks below, for public booking:

  'Sharing was wrong in both directions - browsing two weeks of availability is
   ~15 requests and would exhaust a 10/60s login budget, and booking traffic from
   one NAT'd address would lock out logins for everyone behind it. Two windows
   with *distinct key namespaces*.'

The reasoning transfers directly. Recovery is lower-volume and higher-stakes than browsing, and it should not be starved by sign-in traffic it does not control.

HOW IT SURFACED

The end-to-end suite runs from a single egress address, so the whole run shares one window. Both recovery specs failed on 2026-09-09 with 429 where they assert 401 and 200 respectively — the limiter, not the behaviour under test. The specs had been green for a week, which is why this looked at first like a regression rather than a budget that had simply been crossed.

SUGGESTED FIX

Give redemption its own key namespace, following the public-booking precedent: a separate limiter with its own prefix so it cannot be drained by sign-in traffic. The window itself should stay tight — redemption is a second factor and brute force is the thing the limit exists to stop — but it should be spent only by redemption attempts.

Note the namespace caveat already recorded in that file: the limiter keys purely on the string it is handed, so two limiters given the same key silently share one window. The prefix has to differ, not just the limiter object.

Choosing the number is a judgement call worth making deliberately rather than inheriting.

title: Integration suites stub practice resolution instead of seeding it
description:
Four integration suites replace _resolve_schema_from_request with a lambda:

  backend/tests_integration/database/test_patient_charges_db.py   (21 tests)
  backend/tests_integration/api/test_chat_real_db.py              (7 tests)
  backend/tests_integration/api/test_soap_async_upload_e2e.py     (3 tests)
  backend/tests_integration/api/test_patients_api_e2e.py          (2 tests)

The 33 tests themselves are worth keeping — charge-constraint behaviour against real Postgres, cross-patient 404s, a worker writing into one tenant only, and an assertion that no transaction is open when the model gateway is called. None of that is in question.

The problem is narrower: because resolution is stubbed, none of these exercises it, so none of them can fail when resolution breaks — while sitting in suites that otherwise look like end-to-end multi-tenant coverage. They also break on changes they do not care about; adding a return value to the resolver required editing all four.

One monkeypatch site per file. This is a setup change, not a rewrite.
design:
Replace each lambda with a seeded practice, so the tests drive the real lookup.

The helper already exists: _seeded_practice in
backend/tests_integration/database/test_tenant_resolution_db.py provisions the schema and inserts the practice, platform user and email mapping rows that resolution reads. test_webhook_delivery_db.py has the same shape and predates it. Reuse one of those rather than writing a third.

Do the three single-tenant files first: charges, chat, patients. Each is a
straight swap of the patch for a seeded fixture whose email the request's
identity already carries.

test_soap_async_upload_e2e is the awkward one and should go LAST: it patches to
tenant_a_schema specifically because it asserts a worker writes into tenant A
only, so it needs TWO seeded practices, not one. Getting that wrong would
weaken a cross-tenant assertion, which is worse than leaving it patched — if it
does not come out clean, leave it and say so.

Do not change any assertion. If a test fails after seeding, that is a finding
about resolution or about the test's assumptions, and it wants reading, not
adjusting until green.
acceptance_criteria:
- The three single-tenant suites seed a real practice and no longer patch the resolver.
- All 33 existing tests still pass, with their assertions unchanged.
- Deliberately breaking resolution (e.g. deleting the seeded mapping) fails at least one test in each converted suite — proof the coverage is now real.
- test_soap_async_upload_e2e either seeds two practices with its tenant-A-only assertion intact, or is left patched with the reason recorded here.
- make lint and the integration lane pass.

PR merged (https://github.com/pablo-health/pablo/pull/1010) — reconciled

title: The unhandled-exception log line loses the route it happened on
description:
_unhandled_exception_handler in backend/app/api_errors.py documents that it logs the request-scoped route_template alongside error_class and exc_info. In practice the field is absent from those log lines: sampled over 7 days of deployment logs, every pablo.unhandled entry carried only error_class, exc_info, level, logger, message and timestamp — no route_template and no request_id.

The values come from contextvars, and they are empty by the time this handler runs. The clearest case is an exception raised under run_sync_in_worker_thread: a sync route runs in a threadpool, which does not inherit the request's context, so the contextvar reads empty. Entries logged inline from async request code (for example the auth service's rejection warnings) do carry both fields, which is what makes the difference visible.

The result is that the single most useful log line we emit — the one with the traceback on it — cannot be attributed to an endpoint.
design:
The handler already receives the FastAPI Request. Read the route from it rather than from a contextvar that may be empty: request.scope.get('route') exposes the matched route, whose .path is the template ('/api/patients/{patient_id}/notes'). Fall back to the contextvar, then to no field at all, so nothing regresses where the contextvar does work.

Log the TEMPLATE, never request.url.path — the populated path carries record ids and this line goes to a log stream we read outside the request context.

Do not change what the client receives, and do not widen the log line with any other request-derived field.
acceptance_criteria:
- A test that raises from a SYNC route asserts the emitted pablo.unhandled record carries route_template equal to the route's template.
- A test that raises from an async route asserts the same.
- A test asserts the logged value is the template and never a populated path containing an id.
- The existing api_errors tests stay green.
- make lint (ruff + mypy) and make test pass.
notes: Blocks the route-join in the log-incident enricher: without route_template these tracebacks file as no-route/<ExceptionType> instead of attaching to the endpoint's incident.
close_reason: Merged: oss#995 (deleted-account 401), oss#997 (empty transcript), oss#998 (route on unhandled). Shipped to dev via base bump saas#3020.

title: An empty transcript crashes the transcription poll instead of finishing the session
description:
backend/app/routes/internal_transcription.py:297 builds UploadTranscriptToSessionRequest(format=..., content=transcript_content). The model requires at least one character, so when the provider returns an empty transcript — silent audio, a recording with no speech — pydantic raises ValidationError and the route 500s.

The caller is Cloud Tasks, which retries, so one silent recording produces a burst: 40 occurrences in 7 days, the second-largest error source in the deployment. The session is left stuck rather than being resolved, and the queue keeps re-driving the same failure.
design:
Handle the empty transcript as a real outcome instead of letting it reach the model.

Before constructing UploadTranscriptToSessionRequest, check whether transcript_content is empty or whitespace-only. If it is, do not build the request: log at INFO naming the session id and the empty-transcript reason (no transcript text in the log), move the session to the terminal status the product already uses for 'nothing to transcribe' rather than leaving it PROCESSING, and return the same success-shaped response the already-processed branch returns so Cloud Tasks stops retrying.

Pick the terminal status by reading SessionStatus and matching what the failure path already does — do not invent a new status value, and do not mark it FAILED if the product distinguishes 'failed' from 'empty'. If no existing status fits, stop and say so rather than guessing.
acceptance_criteria:
- A unit/route test posts a transcription result with content='' and asserts: HTTP 200, no ValidationError, the session left in a terminal status, and no generate-soap task enqueued.
- A test with whitespace-only content behaves the same.
- A test with normal content still persists the transcript and enqueues generation (no regression).
- make lint (ruff + mypy) and make test pass.
close_reason: Merged: oss#995 (deleted-account 401), oss#997 (empty transcript), oss#998 (route on unhandled). Shipped to dev via base bump saas#3020.

title: Concurrent redelivery of one payment event raises an unhandled 500
description: Two simultaneous deliveries of the same payment event both pass the dedupe read, because event_already_processed() and record_processed_event() are two statements in two transactions. The ledger stays correct — SELECT ... FOR UPDATE in apply_charge_outcome lets exactly one delivery move the row, and the primary key lets exactly one record the event — but the loser raises an uncaught UniqueViolation from record_processed_event inserting into platform.processed_payment_events. Observed statuses [200, 500], reproduced deterministically against a real database. Self-healing in practice: the processor redelivers, the dedupe read now sees the row, and the retry is a clean 200. So the cost is an unhandled-exception log line and a wasted redelivery, not a wrong ledger — which is why this is P2 and not higher. Found by the webhook delivery integration suite, which asserts the invariants (one row, one state change) and deliberately does NOT assert the status, so it neither blesses the 500 nor breaks when this is fixed.
design:
Read backend/app/payments/reconcile.py (event_already_processed and record_processed_event — the check-then-insert pair), backend/app/routes/payment_webhooks.py (where the exception escapes), and backend/tests_integration/database/test_webhook_delivery_db.py (the suite that found it; its concurrent-redelivery case is where a fix is demonstrated).
BUILD: make record_processed_event conflict-tolerant — an INSERT ... ON CONFLICT DO NOTHING on the event id — so the losing delivery records nothing and returns the same success the winner does. The dedupe read stays as it is: it is a cheap fast path, not the correctness boundary, and the primary key is what actually enforces exactly-once.
THEN TIGHTEN THE TEST that found this: once the race cannot raise, the concurrent case may assert BOTH statuses are 200, rather than only the invariants. Do that in the same change, so the fix is pinned by an assertion that would have failed before it.
DECISIONS CLOSED: do not serialise the two statements behind a lock or a transaction spanning the processor call — the ledger already has its own FOR UPDATE guard and a second locking scheme would be a new deadlock surface for a race whose only cost today is a log line.
DO NOT TOUCH: apply_charge_outcome's FOR UPDATE guard, the signature verification, or the dedupe table's schema.
acceptance_criteria: 1. Two simultaneous deliveries of one payment event both return 200, with exactly one processed_payment_events row and one ledger state change. 2. The integration suite's concurrent case asserts the statuses, and that assertion fails without the fix (demonstrate it). 3. A single delivery, a replay after completion, and an unknown-charge delivery all behave exactly as they do today (regression). 4. make check and make test-integration green.

title: The e2e stack cannot save a tax id: the calendar encryption key is unset in compose
description: PATCH /api/practice/billing-profile with a tax_id returns 500 (TokenEncryptionError) against the end-to-end compose stack, because GOOGLE_CALENDAR_ENCRYPTION_KEY is not set in docker-compose.e2e.yml and the tax id is stored encrypted through that same key. The practice billing profile is a prerequisite for filing a claim, so this blocks any end-to-end coverage of the claims path even once the clearinghouse adapter becomes reachable. Found while building the public-booking spec; a one-line compose fix, deliberately not smuggled into that PR.
design:
Read docker-compose.e2e.yml (the backend service's environment block), .env.e2e, backend/app/services/token_encryption.py (which key is used and how it is derived), and backend/app/routes/practice_billing.py (where the tax id is encrypted).
BUILD: set a deterministic, obviously-fake test key in the e2e stack's environment, alongside the other test-only values already there. It must be plainly a fixture — never anything shaped like a real key, so a secret scanner and a human reader both classify it correctly at a glance.
NOTE THE NAMING SMELL, do not fix it here: the tax id is encrypted under a variable named for the calendar integration. That is a real seam problem worth its own bead if it is more than a name.
acceptance_criteria: 1. PATCH /api/practice/billing-profile with a tax id succeeds against the e2e stack and the value round-trips. 2. The key in compose is obviously a fixture and passes gitleaks. 3. If the naming smell is more than cosmetic, it is filed as its own bead and referenced in the PR. 4. The e2e lane stays green.
close_reason: Merged in #989. GOOGLE_CALENDAR_ENCRYPTION_KEY set in docker-compose.e2e.yml; verified by saving a tax id and reading it back, and by confirming that clearing the key reproduces TokenEncryptionError. First fixture value failed gitleaks at entropy 4.65 - the shipped one is a literal placeholder matching the repo allowlist. Noted but not fixed: the tax id is encrypted under a variable named for the calendar integration, via encrypt_tokens whose docstring is about OAuth tokens, and derive_subkey exists for purpose separation but this path does not use it.

title: GET /openapi.json returns 500 on main
description: Schema generation raises PydanticUserError: Annotated["CoverageRepo", Depends(...)] in backend/app/routes/coverage.py is a string forward reference under 'from __future__ import annotations' that is never rebuilt, so FastAPI cannot resolve it when it builds the OpenAPI document. The application's own routes work — only schema generation is broken — which is why nothing has caught it: no test requests the schema. Anything that consumes the spec (a generated client, an API console, contract tooling, a security scanner enumerating routes) sees a 500.
design:
Read backend/app/routes/coverage.py (the Annotated string-forward-reference dependency declarations) and compare with backend/app/routes/claim_status.py, which documents the same hazard in a comment: a bare unresolvable name in a signature is silently read as a query parameter by the framework. Resolve the reference so the schema builds — either import the type properly for runtime resolution or rebuild the model — matching whichever approach the rest of the route layer already uses.
THEN ADD THE TEST THAT WOULD HAVE CAUGHT IT: a single request to /openapi.json asserting 200. Its absence is the actual defect here; the broken annotation is just what got in first. Sweep the other route modules for the same shape while you are there and say what you found.
acceptance_criteria: 1. GET /openapi.json returns 200 and the document contains the coverage routes. 2. A test requests /openapi.json and asserts 200, so this cannot regress unnoticed. 3. The sweep's result is stated in the PR, whether or not it found more. 4. make check green.
close_reason: Merged: #987. The reported cause was wrong and the agent found the real one: a TYPE_CHECKING-only UserRepository in a Depends() default made inspect.signature(eval_str=True) raise, and Python 3.14's FORWARDREF fallback then left EVERY annotation in that signature as a raw string - so CoverageRepo, payers and patients all silently became required query parameters. One bad annotation poisons its neighbours. Fixed with the same Annotated alias claims.py already uses. Added a test that requests /openapi.json, whose absence was the actual defect. Swept 201 routed dependants and found no other instance, distinguishing the 42 benign forward refs (return annotations and Depends defaults) from the one breaking shape.

title: End-to-end: a client's balance, from a charge through a statement
description: The money surfaces are about to exist end to end — the ledger carries kinds, the chart shows a balance, a client can be charged and a statement rendered — and no browser test walks that path. The unit and component tests each prove a piece against a fake; only an end-to-end run proves the pieces agree about the same dollar.
design:
Read frontend/e2e/ (the harness from the compose-stack work: fixtures/auth.ts, fixtures/scenarios.ts, fixtures/api.ts, fixtures/stack.ts, playwright.config.ts) and mirror the closest sibling spec. Read frontend/e2e/specs/chart.spec.ts for the chart navigation idiom.
BUILD frontend/e2e/specs/client-balance.spec.ts walking one client through: a visit with a charge on file -> the chart header shows what is owed -> the Balance tab lists the rows behind that number -> collecting the balance -> the header reads zero -> a statement renders and lists the visit with what was charged, paid and owed.
ASSERT THE NUMBER, NOT THE PIXEL: the point of this spec is that the header, the Balance tab and the statement agree about one figure, so assert the figure in each place rather than that an element exists. A spec that passes without checking the arithmetic is worse than no spec, because it reports safety it does not provide.
DECISIONS CLOSED: uses the existing e2e harness and its fixtures, never a second one; the statement is checked for its line values, not byte-compared (determinism is the unit suite's job); no real payment processor is contacted — the harness's fake stands in.
DO NOT TOUCH: the balance arithmetic or the statement renderer.

HARNESS GAPS FOUND 2026-09-09 BY RUNNING IT. Read this before starting: the
e2e lane itself is healthy (33 specs pass in ~30s against
docker-compose.e2e.yml), but a BILLING spec cannot be written against it as
it stands. Three things are missing, and none of them is in this bead.

1. THE FAKE CLEARINGHOUSE ONLY PAYS IN FULL. `scripts/fake_clearinghouse.py`
   `_build_835_report` is documented as "paying the claim in full for what it
   charged", so no run of the harness can produce patient responsibility at
   all - the exact number a balance spec exists to check. Needs a new
   control-number rule alongside the existing REJ-DX / REJ-PTR / REJ-SUB
   convention, e.g. `PART-` -> an 835 that pays part and assigns the rest as
   PR, and ideally `DENY-` for a denial that leaves the client owing the
   charge.

2. NOTHING DRIVES REMITTANCE POSTING PROMPTLY. The clearinghouse webhook
   (`backend/app/routes/claim_webhooks.py` -> `app/claims/fanout.py`) handles
   277CA acknowledgements ONLY - "an inbound document that is not a 277CA is
   ignored". The 835 is posted by the pipeline's remit stage, which runs in
   process on `CLAIMS_PIPELINE_INTERVAL_MINUTES` (default 5) and is not
   configured in docker-compose.e2e.yml. So a claim reaches paid minutes
   later, well past a 60s Playwright timeout.

   Worth noticing that this is not only a test problem: in production a
   practice waits up to five minutes after a payer pays before the app says
   so. Teaching the webhook to post an 835 the way it posts a 277CA would fix
   both, and is the better fix than shortening the timer.

3. CARD CHARGES ARE NOT EXERCISABLE. There is no Stripe fake in the compose
   stack, so the self-pay half of a balance (a session charge on a card)
   cannot be driven from a browser. The insurance half needs no card, because
   remittance posting writes the ledger row directly - so an insurance-first
   spec is the one that can be written.

SUGGESTED ORDER: fix (1) and (2) in their own PR, then this spec becomes
straightforward. Do not work around them inside the spec with sleeps or by
reaching into the database - a spec that waits five minutes will be deleted
by whoever next runs the suite.
acceptance_criteria: 1. The spec drives a real browser through charge -> balance -> collect -> statement against the compose harness. 2. The owed figure is asserted in the chart header, the Balance tab and the statement, and the three agree. 3. After collecting, the header reads zero rather than a credit. 4. The spec fails if the balance arithmetic regresses — demonstrate this by breaking the sign locally and showing it goes red. 5. Green in the e2e lane.

What would unblock this bead: a follow-up PR that (a) gives the e2e stack a synchronous or fast-interval way to run the claims-pipeline submit stage, and (b) gives an e2e-driven claim a way to land in the clearinghouse's PART-/DENY- bucket — likely by keying the fake clearinghouse's behavior off something already client-controllable (e.g. payer id) rather than the opaque control number, or by adding a narrow, test-only override for the control number itself.

The `PART-`/`DENY-` rules added in #1061 are only reachable by constructing a `Claim` row directly in the database, which is explicitly out of bounds for an e2e spec. Fixing either path (a Stripe fake service, or a reviewed control-number override hook) is an infra/product decision well outside "write one spec file," touches files the spec doesn't name, and needs a human call on approach. title: The practice address is write-only, so nothing can read it back

design:
Read backend/app/routes/users.py (the professional-info write at the business_address mapping, and the /me/status response model), backend/app/models/user.py, frontend/src/lib/api/users.ts (UserStatusBase), and frontend/src/components/settings/BillingProfileCard.tsx (prefillFromProfile, which is where the address becomes usable once it is readable).
BUILD: expose the practice address on /api/users/me/status alongside practice_name and practice_phone, declare it in UserStatusBase, and complete prefillFromProfile so 'Use my profile details' fills the address too.
THE MAPPING IS THE REAL DECISION: practices.address is a single free-text String(500); the billing profile wants structured address_line1 / line2 / city / state / postal_code. A copy is lossy whichever way it goes. Decide between (a) returning the free text and filling address_line1 with it, leaving the therapist to split it — honest, slightly annoying; or (b) structuring practices.address at the source, which is a migration and a form change and touches every existing row. 'Use my profile details' fills the address, and still copies neither the tax id nor the NPI (extend the existing test). 4. The chosen mapping is stated in the commit message. 5. make check + frontend gates green.
